records.title: Runbook: enable customer-managed audit log export (Hosted)
records.text:
Runbook: enable customer-managed audit log export (Hosted)

# Summary
This runbook describes how to enable **customer-managed audit log export** for a **Hosted** customer (multi-tenant control plane).

Do not proceed unless the request has passed the approval gates in the Security controls page.

# Preconditions
- An internal-support Jira ticket exists and includes:
  - customer company + org_id
  - deployment mode: Hosted
  - destination type: S3/GCS/Azure Blob
  - destination identifiers (bucket/container, prefix, region)
  - auth method (assume-role / workload identity)
  - Security approval comment
- Customer has completed destination setup (bucket/container created, encryption enabled).

# Ownership
- Primary: Eng Platform Oncall
- Consult: Security (for IAM/policy), SRE (if widespread connector alerts)
- Customer comms: Customer Success (CS)

# Procedure
## 1) Confirm export eligibility
1. Verify customer tier and contract entitlement (CS confirmation in ticket).
2. Verify this request is for **platform audit logs only** (no inference payload logging).
3. Confirm region alignment (no cross-region unless explicitly approved by Security + Legal).

## 2) Configure tenant export settings
All changes are made via the internal admin CLI `rdw-admin`.

1. Fetch org details:
```bash
rdw-admin org get --org-id <ORG_ID>
```
2. Create (or update) export destination:
```bash
rdw-admin audit-export destination upsert \
  --org-id <ORG_ID> \
  --sink <s3|gcs|azure> \
  --region <REGION> \
  --bucket-or-container <NAME> \
  --prefix <PREFIX> \
  --auth-mode <assume-role|workload-identity> \
  --external-role-arn-or-binding <VALUE>
```
3. Enable export:
```bash
rdw-admin audit-export enable --org-id <ORG_ID>
```

## 3) Feature flag verification
Hosted uses a per-tenant flag to control connector activation:
- Flag name: `audit_export_customer_sink_enabled`

Verify it is set:
```bash
rdw-admin flags get --org-id <ORG_ID> --name audit_export_customer_sink_enabled
```
If not set, set it:
```bash
rdw-admin flags set --org-id <ORG_ID> --name audit_export_customer_sink_enabled --value true
```

## 4) Validation
### 4.1 Internal health
- Confirm connector has created a consumer for this org:
  - Dashboard: `Observability / Audit Export Connector / Tenant View`
  - Look for non-zero `delivery_success_rate` and decreasing `delivery_lag_seconds`.

### 4.2 Customer destination verification
Ask CS/customer to verify objects are landing in the destination prefix. Expected naming pattern:
- `org=<ORG_ID>/region=<REGION>/dt=YYYY-MM-DD/hr=HH/*.jsonl.gz`

### 4.3 Event schema spot-check
Download one object and confirm:
- `event_id` present
- `source_service` present
- no prompt/completion fields

## 5) Document the enablement
Update the Jira ticket with:
- exact destination identifiers
- auth mode and role/binding used
- validation results (dashboard screenshot link or metric note)
- time export was enabled

# Rollback / Disable
Use when:
- repeated 403/permission errors
- customer requests pause
- suspected data boundary issue

Commands:
```bash
rdw-admin audit-export disable --org-id <ORG_ID>
```
If needed, remove destination:
```bash
rdw-admin audit-export destination delete --org-id <ORG_ID>
```

# Troubleshooting
## Common errors
- `AccessDenied` / `403`: customer role trust policy or bucket policy incorrect. Loop in Security and CS.
- `SlowDown` / throttling: increase connector backoff; ask customer to review destination limits.
- High delivery lag: verify connector capacity in region; check incident channel for broader issues.

# Related pages
- Security controls and approval gates
- Audit log export architecture
- Support intake SOP

records.title: Mixed-priority cgroup and soft-quota playbook for multi-tenant inference
records.text:
Mixed-priority cgroup and soft-quota playbook for multi-tenant inference

Summary

This playbook defines a pragmatic, deployable policy and reference implementation pattern for enforcing mixed-priority resource controls on Redwood inference nodes. It combines OS-level cgroups, a soft-quota crediting algorithm, and scheduler-level hints to guarantee tenant fairness for bursty traffic while protecting latency-sensitive SLAs. The goal is predictable SLOs with controlled cost and graceful degradation under contention.

Scope

- Applies to dedicated GPU hosts and shared GPU slice deployments used for multi-tenant inference.
- Covers CPU, GPU memory residency, NVLink and PCIe bandwidth gating, and host-level network egress shaping where supported.
- Does NOT replace cloud provider-side hard quotas or hypervisor limits; this is an infra-layer policy implemented inside Redwood-managed nodes.

Definitions and terminology

- Soft-quota: a rate-style allocation enforced by token/credit accounting rather than hard kernel-level denial. Gives tenants temporary burst capacity until credits are exhausted.
- Cgroup profile: named resource envelope mapped to a tenant route or model variant (e.g., low-priority-batch, standard-realtime, realtime-guaranteed).
- Preemptible slot: runtime slot eligible for preemption when higher-priority work arrives. Clients may receive a retryable 429 with retry-after hints.
- Credit refill window: interval on which soft-quota credit balances are replenished.

Principles

1) Prioritize latency SLOs for realtime-guaranteed tenants; starvation-avoidance for all others.
2) Make policies observable and auditable: every decision must emit events and metrics.
3) Prefer non-destructive throttling before eviction.
4) Provide transparent billing signals: exhausted credits should generate usage traces and billing-affecting tags.

Service model and mapping

- Map inbound request classes to cgroup profiles at the edge ingress (edge-proxy or inference gateway) based on API token, route, or customer contract.
- Example profile names: realtime-guaranteed, standard, burstable, spot-preemptible.

Resource profile table (reference)

Profile | GPU share | CPU share | Burst credits per minute | Preemptible
---|---:|---:|---:|---:
realtime-guaranteed | 60% | 4 CPUs | 0 | false
standard | 25% | 2 CPUs | 100 credits | true
burstable | 10% | 1 CPU | 1000 credits | true
spot-preemptible | 5% | 0.5 CPU | 5000 credits | true

Operational invariants

- P95 latency for realtime-guaranteed must remain under 80 ms for 2kB prompt workloads under nominal load.
- P99 latency degradation must be limited to 3x baseline under accepted degraded mode.
- No tenant should consume >2x its configured long-term average without exhausting burst credits.

Soft-quota algorithm (summary)

1) Each profile has a token bucket: capacity (burst cap) and rate (sustained).
2) Requests consume tokens proportional to an estimate of per-request GPU time (token_cost = base_cost + size_factor).
3) When tokens are available, allow request and deduct tokens. When depleted, attempt polite throttling: apply queueing/backoff first (retry-after 150–500 ms depending on queue depth), then reject with 429 when queue > max_queue_len.
4) Credits are replenished on a 1s tick with leaky-bucket refill semantics; windows can be tuned per workload.

Cgroup & kernel-level controls (implementation notes)

- Use systemd.slice + unified cgroup v2 where available. For GPU residency/visibility we use Nvidia MIG or runtime-controlled CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES mapping. For non-MIG GPUs, rely on process-level CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES combined with per-process niceness and CPU bandwidth controls.
- Example cgroup layout (text description): root/rdw/guaranteed.slice, root/rdw/standard.slice, root/rdw/burstable.slice, root/rdw/spot.slice.
- CPU bandwidth values set with systemd CPUQuota= and MemoryMax= where applicable.

Example cgroup profile YAML (to be consumed by node agent)

profile_name: standard
labels: ["multi-tenant", "standard"]
cpu_quota_percent: "25%"
gpu_share_percent: "25%"
burst_capacity_tokens: "1000"
refill_rate_tokens_per_s: "16"

(node-agent will translate to systemd + token-bucket state on startup)

Preemption and eviction policy

- Soft preemption: first step is to stop accepting new requests for preemptible profiles and burn down queues. Provide clients with a Retry-After header. Emit PreemptionWarning event to tracing.
- Hard eviction: only when soft preemption fails for longer than 30s AND SLOs for realtime-guaranteed are violated by >10% over a rolling 1m window. Evicted sessions are checkpointed if runtime supports incremental KV-cache persistence; otherwise return structured error with model-invocation-id for audit.

Telemetry and SLI set (required metrics to emit)

- profile.request_rate (per-profile, r/s)
- profile.token_balance (gauge)
- profile.rejects_429 (counter)
- node.gpu_utilization (gauge)
- node.preemption_events (counter with reason label)
- request.latency_p50/p95/p99 (per-profile)

Alerting thresholds (recommended)

- SLO breach alert: realtime-guaranteed.p99 > 120 ms for 2 consecutive 1m windows -> page SRE oncall.
- Exhaustion alert: profile.token_balance < 1% of capacity for 5m -> create sustained-throttling ticket.
- Preemption storm: node.preemption_events > 10 in 1m -> create incident and auto-scale farm capacity.

Testing and validation

- Synthetic load: use the perf-harness tool with a mixed-profile manifest. Example CLI:
  rdw-perf start --manifest tests/manifests/mixed-bursty-50-30-20.yaml --duration 10m --trace=on
- Chaos test: inject CPU throttling (stress-ng) and GPU memory pressure (cuda-memtest) during a 30m soak; verify token balances and preemption events are emitted and SLOs respected.
- Contract tests: run end-to-end convergence tests in staging where billing tags, traces, and token accounting are validated.

Rollout plan (canary -> gradual -> global)

1) Implement node-agent feature flag behind runtime.flag.soft_quota_v2. Deploy to 2 canary nodes in staging.
2) Run mixed synthetic load for 24h and validate metrics/alerts.
3) Canary in production: enable on 5 nodes serving non-critical tenants for 48h with increased sampling.
4) Gradual rollout: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% of nodes, with 6h observation between steps.
4a) If preemption storm or SLO regressions are observed, auto-rollback to previous flag state.

Operational runbook (summary)

- Detect: Alert for realtime-guaranteed.p99 and node.preemption_events.
- Mitigate: Increase node pool capacity (scale up dedicated nodes) or temporarily reduce burst refill rates via platform API: POST /admin/quota/adjust {"profile":"burstable","refill_rate":4}.
- Recover: If hard eviction triggered, restart affected runtime with persisted KV-cache, and run postmortem with request ids (attach trace ids to incident).

Ownership and change control

- Primary owner: infra-scheduling@redwood.com (team: eng-infra).
- Secondary owner: serving-runtime@redwood.com for runtime integration.
- Any config changes to default profiles must go through CHANGE-FEATURE ticket and be approved by owners; large profile changes require a 1-week staged rollout and telemetry gating.

Security and privacy considerations

- Token accounting and audit logs must not include PII. Traces related to billing or chargebacks should be stored in restricted retention with RBAC.
- Ensure GPU-side libraries are up-to-date to avoid kernel CVEs that could allow cross-tenant leakage.

Appendix: Example node-agent CLI and YAML patch

# Apply a new profile
rdw-agent apply-profile --file profiles/burstable.yaml

# Query balances
rdw-agent profile-status --profile burstable --format json

YAML (profiles/burstable.yaml)
profile_name: burstable
cpu_quota_percent: "10%"
gpu_share_percent: "10%"
burst_capacity_tokens: 5000
refill_rate_tokens_per_s: 80
queue_max_len: 64
preemptible: true

Related docs and references

- See GPU fleet soft-quota eviction policy (eng-infra) for cross-reference.
- See ADR: adaptive-priority-fairness for bursting for background rationale.

Change log

- 2025-10-12: Draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2025-11-03: Added refill tuning guidance after staging tests.
- 2026-03-01: Published after canary verification and reviewer sign-off.

Contact

For questions or rollout coordination, contact infra-scheduling@redwood.com or open a ticket in #infra-scheduling on Slack.

records.title: per-route function-call telemetry and JSONL output tagging
records.text:
per-route function-call telemetry and JSONL output tagging

description:
Motivation: customers using function/tool-calling and structured output have limited ability to correlate tool calls to per-route metrics, and streaming JSONL outputs lack stable tags for downstream log processors. This PR attaches per-route metric tags to function-call events, enriches JSONL streaming output with consistent telemetry headers, and adds trace propagation across the OpenAI-compat adapter layer. Changes aim to improve observability without changing public API semantics. Summary of changes: 1) Add per-route "route.tags" metadata to function-call events emitted by the gateway and runtime; 2) Emit a compact telemetry header ("rwid, srv, route, call_idx") at the start of streaming JSONL chunks to enable log reassembly; 3) Propagate distributed trace context and span IDs into function-call instrumentation and structured logs; 4) Update openai-compat adapter to translate OpenAI-style "request_id" into rwid and include route tags for compatibility; 5) Add unit and integration tests covering streaming reassembly and metric label cardinality limits; 6) Add doc comments and console notes for admins about limiting custom route tags. Checklist: - [x] Add telemetry header and tests - [x] Preserve streaming shape for openai-compat clients - [x] Ensure route tag cardinality cap (100) enforced - [x] Add end-to-end smoke test against mock tool runner - [x] Update docs and changelog Impact: no user-facing API change; observability improvements are additive. Rollout plan: feature gated behind experiment flag "obs.route_tags_tool_calls" for three days in canary, then staged rollout to 25% traffic, then full rollout assuming no regressions. Monitoring: added alerts for spike in unique route tags and increased rate of incomplete streams.

review_comments:
Jon Liu: Can you confirm the added telemetry header is at most 256 bytes to avoid proxy truncation?
Maya Patel: Confirmed, header is compacted and base64-encoded; tests include a 256-byte boundary case.
Sofia Ramirez: We should cap unique per-route tags to avoid high-cardinality metrics - where is that enforced?
Maya Patel: Cap enforced in runtime/instrumentation/serializer.go with a hard limit of 100 tags and metrics emitted when limit hit.
Evan Brooks: Integration tests flaked once on CI due to a timing window in the mock tool runner, please add retry/wait up to 500ms.
Maya Patel: Added small retry and fixed race; CI rerun included below.
Sofia Ramirez: Approving pending a short note in docs about tag cardinality and cost implications.
Sofia Ramirez: Approved after doc update.
Release-Manager (auto): No conflicts with main; merge allowed.

release_notes:
Add per-route telemetry tags for function/tool calls and compact streaming JSONL telemetry header (rwid, srv, route, call_idx). This improves ability to correlate tool calls with per-endpoint metrics and enables downstream log reassembly. Feature rolled out behind experiment flag obs.route_tags_tool_calls.

records.title: Customer-managed audit log export: security controls and approval gates
records.text:
Customer-managed audit log export: security controls and approval gates

# Purpose
This page defines the **mandatory security controls** and **approval gates** for enabling **customer-managed audit log export** from Redwood Inference to customer-controlled cloud storage (e.g., S3/GCS/Azure Blob) across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

This is a control surface that touches: customer data boundaries, identity and access, encryption, and retention. **Do not enable export** without satisfying the requirements below.

# Scope
In scope:
- Export of **platform audit logs** (auth events, RBAC changes, API key lifecycle, console/admin actions, private control-plane actions).
- Delivery to a **customer-owned destination**.

Out of scope:
- Model inference payload logging (prompt/completion content). That remains disabled by default and requires a separate data logging exception.

# Definitions
- **Audit log**: event records emitted by Redwood control plane and selected data-plane components.
- **Customer-managed export**: Redwood pushes logs to an endpoint owned/controlled by the customer; the customer sets retention and access.
- **Export Connector**: Redwood-managed service that ships logs (see architecture page for details).

# Control requirements (must pass)
## 1) Data classification
- Audit logs are classified as **Customer-Sensitive Metadata**.
- Audit logs may include: user identifiers, IPs, org IDs, resource IDs, timestamps, and administrative actions.
- Audit logs must **not** include request bodies or model outputs.

## 2) Encryption
- In transit: TLS 1.2+ is required for any HTTPS endpoints.
- At rest: the customer destination must be configured with server-side encryption.
  - S3: SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS (customer preference).
  - GCS: Google-managed keys or CMEK.
  - Azure: Microsoft-managed keys or CMK.
- Redwood-side staging (if used by the connector) must be encrypted at rest using Redwood-managed KMS.

## 3) Least privilege access
- Hosted and Dedicated exports must use **assume-role / workload identity** patterns; no long-lived customer keys stored in Redwood.
- The role/policy must only permit:
  - write/put to a specific bucket/container prefix
  - list only if required by the connector health checks
- Policies must be reviewed by Security for correctness.

## 4) Network & destination allowlisting
- The destination must be customer-owned and reside in an allowed provider account/subscription/project per the contract.
- For Private deployments, outbound egress must be constrained by the customer (preferred) or by Redwood (if Redwood-managed networking is in scope).
- Public endpoints are allowed only if authenticated and protected with least-privilege credentials; **PrivateLink / private endpoints are preferred** when available.

## 5) Retention and deletion
- Default recommended destination retention: **90 days** (unless the customer requires more).
- If the customer requests retention < 30 days, note it in the request but it is allowed.
- If the customer requests retention > 1 year, Customer Success must confirm contract language supports it and that the customer understands storage cost/ownership.

## 6) Logging about logging (auditability of export)
- The platform must emit events for:
  - export enabled/disabled
  - destination changes (bucket/container/prefix)
  - auth/role changes used by the connector
  - delivery failures and retries
- These events must be visible in Redwood internal dashboards and retrievable for incident response.

# Approval gates (required)
## Gate A: Customer request validation (Customer Success + Support)
Required before Security review:
- customer company + deployment mode (Hosted / Dedicated / Private)
- target cloud + region
- desired log categories (standard only unless exception)
- retention intent
- contact for incident notifications

## Gate B: Security review (required for all modes)
Security must approve before any production enablement:
- destination configuration meets encryption and least privilege requirements
- no inference payload logging is included
- any cross-region delivery is evaluated (see Cross-region constraints)

Approval artifact:
- Jira internal-support ticket must include a Security comment: **“Approved for enablement”** with reviewer name + date.

## Gate C: Privacy/Legal check (conditional)
Required if any of the following are true:
- customer requests cross-region export that changes data residency guarantees
- customer requests inclusion of user email addresses or other PII fields beyond standard audit schema
- customer contract includes bespoke audit log clauses

# Cross-region constraints
- Default rule: **export must stay within the customer’s chosen region** that matches the deployment region.
- Cross-region export is allowed only when:
  1) Legal confirms it does not violate contractual residency terms
  2) Security confirms threat model is acceptable
  3) Customer acknowledges increased failure modes and latency

# Security exception process
If the customer cannot satisfy the above controls (e.g., insists on long-lived keys), file a Security exception under `security-and-compliance/risk-and-exceptions` and link it in the enablement ticket.

# Required evidence (attach/link in the Jira ticket)
- Destination policy snippet (IAM policy / role trust policy / workload identity binding)
- Confirmation of encryption at rest on destination
- Proof of ownership (account/subscription/project identifiers)
- For Private: network diagram or egress policy statement

# Related pages
- Audit log export architecture (Observability Standards)
- Hosted enablement runbook (Eng Platform)
- Dedicated customer setup runbook (Eng Infra)
- Private configuration guide (Eng Private Deployments)
- Support intake process (Customer Success & Support)

records.title: Northpeak Analytics - procurement via AWS Marketplace (security + next steps)
records.text:
Northpeak Analytics - procurement via AWS Marketplace (security + next steps)

summary:
Northpeak Analytics wants to purchase Redwood Inference through AWS Marketplace (preferably via private offer) so spend can count toward their AWS commitments. They asked detailed security questionnaire items (SOC 2 posture, encryption/KMS, retention, audit logs, data residency, incident response, SSO/RBAC) and clarified shared responsibility for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Redwood outlined marketplace subscription → entitlement → Redwood org provisioning flow and noted typical entitlement propagation delays. Next steps include sending the marketplace security packet, confirming which SKU matches their target deployment (Hosted initially; Dedicated later), and starting an AWS private offer request with required buyer details.

topics:
Why AWS Marketplace purchase path (EDP / committed spend) and private offer vs public offer
SKU fit: Hosted API now, Dedicated capacity later; what is and isn't supported via Marketplace
Metering and billing dimensions: tokens/requests, reporting cadence, invoice visibility
Security questionnaire: SOC 2 / ISO alignment, encryption in transit/at rest, KMS options, audit logs, retention controls, data residency
Onboarding: subscription → entitlement validation → org linking → first API key → first call
Support & escalation: SLA expectations for enterprise + marketplace customers
Timeline: internal approvals, legal/security review, and target pilot start

action_items:
Redwood (Stephanie): Email AWS Marketplace private offer intake checklist (buyer AWS account ID(s), preferred region(s), start date, term, committed spend) by 2026-01-23

next_steps:

Book technical deep dive focused on audit logging, retention controls, and AWS Marketplace entitlement troubleshooting
Follow-up call to confirm pilot scope (models, expected TPM, latency targets) and pick Hosted vs Dedicated SKU

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-22
Time: 11:00am - 11:52am PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Title: Northpeak Analytics - procurement via AWS Marketplace (security + next steps)

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Stephanie Nguyen (AE), Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Naomi Feldman (Security/Compliance)
Northpeak Analytics: Dana Willis (Procurement), Ravi Deshpande (Security), Megan Cho (Platform Eng), Tom Alvarez (FinOps)

Auto-summary (generated)
- Customer prefers AWS Marketplace purchasing to simplify vendor onboarding and apply spend to AWS commitments.
- Customer asked for SOC 2 status, encryption/KMS, audit logs, retention, residency, and SSO/RBAC details.
- Redwood described Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment options and shared responsibility boundaries.
- Redwood described onboarding flow and noted entitlement propagation delays can be a few minutes.

Questions captured
- Do you support customer-managed KMS keys for Hosted, or only for Private/VPC?
- What is retained from prompts/outputs by default and can we set retention to 0?
- What audit log events are available and can they be exported to Splunk?
- Can we constrain processing to us-east-1 only?
- How does metering show up in AWS Marketplace billing (dimensions, timing)?

Transcript
[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, looks like we’re at time. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Stephanie from Redwood Inference. Markus is on with me as well, and Naomi from our security team may hop in—she’s here now actually.
[00:12] Dana Willis: Hi. Dana, procurement. Thanks.
[00:14] Megan Cho: Hey, Megan, platform engineering.
[00:16] Ravi Deshpande: Ravi, security and risk.
[00:18] Tom Alvarez: Tom, FinOps.
[00:21] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Goal today is pretty specific: you all want to buy through AWS Marketplace, and we want to make sure the listing, the SKU, and the security packet lines up with what your procurement and security review expects.

[00:38] Dana Willis: Yep. We have a policy basically—if it can go through Marketplace, it should. Otherwise it’s like, months.
[00:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. And is that primarily because you want it to count toward an EDP, or it’s just the vendor onboarding workflow?
[00:56] Tom Alvarez: Both. The spend counting is the big one. We also like the consolidated invoicing.

[01:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Makes sense. For AWS Marketplace there’s generally public offers and private offers. For enterprise we usually do a private offer so we can align to term, committed spend, and any guardrails. But we can do pay-as-you-go too, depending.
[01:20] Dana Willis: We’d prefer private offer. It’s simpler on our side. Also our legal team likes to see something with an order form.

[01:30] Markus Klein: And from the technical side it doesn’t change your integration—same API endpoints, same org in our console. Marketplace is basically procurement + entitlement + metering.

[01:41] Megan Cho: Can we talk through that entitlement thing? We had a not-great experience with another vendor where the subscription didn’t provision anything for like two days.
[01:51] Markus Klein: Yep, totally. So the flow is: you subscribe in AWS Marketplace, AWS sends an entitlement signal to our entitlement service, we validate it, then you either create a new Redwood org or link to an existing org. From there you generate an API key and you’re off.
[02:09] Markus Klein: There can be propagation delays—usually minutes, not days. We also have a manual fallback where support can verify the subscription ID and force a sync if needed.
[02:21] Dana Willis: So if it’s delayed, who do we contact? AWS or you?
[02:26] Stephanie Nguyen: Start with us. We can tell if we’ve received the entitlement. If we haven’t, we can advise on AWS steps, but typically we can resolve faster on our side.

[02:39] Ravi Deshpande: Before we go too deep, I have a list of security questions. Some are standard. I’m going to rattle them off.
[02:46] Stephanie Nguyen: Please do. Naomi is here to help as well.

[02:51] Ravi Deshpande: First: do you have SOC 2 Type II and can you provide the report under NDA, or via a portal?
[02:59] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We’re SOC 2 Type II. We share the full report through our trust portal with access control. For Marketplace reviews we also provide a security overview packet that references the relevant controls without oversharing.
[03:14] Ravi Deshpande: Okay. Next: ISO 27001?
[03:17] Naomi Feldman: We’re aligned to ISO 27001 controls; we can provide our statement and program overview. If you need a specific certificate, we can clarify what’s current in the packet. But SOC 2 is the main attestation we provide today.

[03:33] Ravi Deshpande: Encryption: in transit and at rest. TLS versions.
[03:37] Naomi Feldman: In transit: TLS 1.2+ for API and console. At rest: encryption on our storage layers. For Hosted, we manage keys via our cloud KMS. For Private deployments in your VPC and for certain Dedicated configurations, we can support customer-managed keys depending on architecture.
[03:56] Megan Cho: So Hosted can’t do BYOK? Like customer KMS key?
[04:01] Naomi Feldman: For the standard Hosted multi-tenant control plane, it’s provider-managed KMS keys. If customer-managed key is a hard requirement, we usually recommend Private (VPC) where key management and network boundaries are customer-controlled.

[04:17] Ravi Deshpande: Data retention: do you store prompts and completions? If yes, default retention and can we set it to zero.
[04:26] Naomi Feldman: Great question. By default we retain limited request metadata for operational purposes and abuse prevention, and we do not use customer data to train models. For content retention—prompts/outputs—we have configuration knobs depending on the product mode. We can support reduced retention and in some cases “no storage” modes with logging disabled except what’s required for billing and security.
[04:49] Ravi Deshpande: “In some cases” worries me.
[04:52] Naomi Feldman: Totally fair. Let’s make it concrete: for Hosted, there’s a baseline operational logging layer. We can configure content logging off for enterprise tenants, and we can scope retention windows. For Private, you can set retention policies more strictly since data paths are under your control plane. We’ll follow up with the specific retention matrix and what is configurable today.
[05:16] Stephanie Nguyen: We have a marketplace-facing “data handling and retention” doc we can send after the call. It spells out defaults and options.

[05:28] Tom Alvarez: From FinOps: what data is required for billing? Are you measuring tokens? requests? Both?
[05:34] Markus Klein: Metering is by usage dimensions that map to tokens for generation and embeddings units, depending on SKU. In AWS Marketplace it shows up as dimensions—like “tokens” or “1k tokens” style—then AWS bills you. Internally we reconcile to your org usage so your console usage report matches the invoice.
[05:57] Tom Alvarez: How quickly does it show in AWS cost explorer?
[06:00] Markus Klein: It’s not real-time. Typically you’ll see the line item and usage with some delay—hours-ish. We’ll confirm the exact cadence but it’s the standard Marketplace metering behavior.

[06:13] Dana Willis: And SKUs—are we buying Hosted, Dedicated, Private? I saw three things in the deck.
[06:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Right now what we’re proposing is: start with Hosted API via Marketplace for the pilot, and if you need predictable throughput or isolation, we can move you to Dedicated capacity. Private is VPC/on-prem and is usually a bigger procurement and architecture step.
[06:36] Megan Cho: We likely want Dedicated eventually. For the pilot, Hosted is okay, but we’ll need to pin a model version and have some fallback. Also region restriction.
[06:46] Markus Klein: Hosted supports pinned model versions and rollout policies. Region-wise, we can route you to a region. We’ll check which regions are available for your target compliance needs.

[07:02] Ravi Deshpande: Data residency: we have workloads that must stay US. Sometimes specifically us-east-1.
[07:09] Naomi Feldman: For Hosted, we can support regional processing commitments within available regions. If you require strict single-region, we can set policy to keep requests in that region and not fail over cross-region unless you explicitly enable it. For Private in your VPC, it’s inherently in your chosen region.
[07:30] Ravi Deshpande: We need that in writing.
[07:32] Naomi Feldman: Understood. We can include it in the order form / private offer exhibits and reference the data handling doc.

[07:42] Megan Cho: Another question: do you do SSO? SAML? RBAC?
[07:47] Markus Klein: Yes. SSO/SAML for enterprise orgs, role-based access control for the console, API keys scoped by org and project. Naomi can speak to audit controls.
[07:58] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We have audit logging for admin actions—like user invites, role changes, API key creation, model deployments, and policy changes. We also log auth events. Export options include API export; we also have patterns to ship into SIEM like Splunk via your pipeline.
[08:21] Ravi Deshpande: Is audit log immutable? Like WORM storage.
[08:26] Naomi Feldman: We maintain integrity controls; for WORM/immutable retention, the cleanest approach is exporting to your SIEM / log archive where you enforce immutability. We can help with the integration guidance.

[08:42] Tom Alvarez: Sorry, going back—if we buy Hosted via Marketplace, do we get a committed spend discount, or is it always on-demand pricing?
[08:50] Stephanie Nguyen: With private offer we can do a committed spend construct even for usage-based. AWS supports that via contract terms, and we map it to your usage in Redwood. The details depend on your target monthly/annual commit.
[09:06] Dana Willis: We’ll need term options, 12 months standard.
[09:09] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep.

[09:12] Megan Cho: Can you compare to Bedrock? We’re getting pressure to “just use Bedrock.”
[09:18] Markus Klein: Totally. Bedrock is convenient if you want managed access to certain models. Where Redwood tends to win is when you care about serving economics—latency, throughput, routing, and more control over model versions and performance tuning. Also we support Dedicated and Private where you want isolation or VPC control. But we can keep that more for the technical deep dive.

[09:41] Ravi Deshpande: Incident response: breach notification timelines?
[09:45] Naomi Feldman: We have an incident response program with defined severity and notification processes. Specific timelines are typically handled contractually. We can align to your requirements and include those in the enterprise terms.
[09:58] Ravi Deshpande: Subprocessors—do you have a list?
[10:01] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We maintain a subprocessor list and can provide it. For Hosted, we operate the service; we also have standard cloud infrastructure providers. For Private, your infrastructure reduces the scope of subprocessors.

[10:16] Dana Willis: Legal terms—do we sign your paper or AWS paper?
[10:21] Stephanie Nguyen: Marketplace uses AWS terms as the transaction backbone, but we typically attach our EULA / service terms and any data processing terms as part of the private offer or accompanying exhibits. We can also do a separate DPA if needed.

[10:39] Tom Alvarez: Can Marketplace spend roll up into our EDP? That’s the whole reason.
[10:44] Dana Willis: It should, if it’s an eligible private offer.
[10:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Generally yes, but the exact eligibility is your AWS agreement. We’ll structure it in the standard way. If needed, we can loop in our AWS partner manager to confirm mechanics.

[11:03] Megan Cho: Switching gears: what’s the actual onboarding steps? Like if I subscribe today, what do I do next.
[11:10] Markus Klein: After subscribe, you go to Redwood console. There’s a marketplace entry point. It asks you to connect your subscription—sometimes it’s automatic, sometimes you paste a subscription identifier. Then you either create a new org or link to your existing org. Then create an API key. Then do a test call. We have a quickstart app and docs.
[11:33] Megan Cho: And if we already have a Redwood org from a prior trial?
[11:36] Markus Klein: You can link it. That’s one of the edge cases. The UI will ask “use existing org” and verify you have admin rights.

[11:49] Ravi Deshpande: And multi-subscription? Like different business units.
[11:52] Markus Klein: Supported, but we need to decide if you want multiple subscriptions tied to one org or separate orgs. Finance reporting tends to be simpler with one org and tags/projects; procurement sometimes wants separation. We can advise.

[12:08] Stephanie Nguyen: Dana, can I ask: what’s your target timeline for approval and pilot start?
[12:14] Dana Willis: If we can get the security review done in two weeks, we could do a pilot in February. But it depends on Ravi.
[12:22] Ravi Deshpande: Yeah, I need the packet and ideally the SOC 2 report access, plus answers on retention and residency.

[12:31] Naomi Feldman: We can get you the marketplace security packet immediately, and we’ll start the trust portal access process for the full report. Usually that’s same day once we have the right contacts.
[12:44] Ravi Deshpande: Ok.

[12:46] Tom Alvarez: Also need pricing dimensions. If it’s tokens, we need to map that to budgets.
[12:52] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll include in the private offer: the dimension names and what they correspond to, plus an example usage scenario.

[13:01] Megan Cho: One technical risk: we need to ensure prompts aren’t used for training. I know you said it, but we need it contractually.
[13:07] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We do not train on customer data. That commitment is in our terms, and we can highlight it.

[13:16] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) And do you log the prompts for debugging?
[13:19] Naomi Feldman: Not by default for enterprise configurations; we can disable content logging. There may be minimal transient processing in memory to serve the request, but that’s not persisted as “training data.”
[13:34] Megan Cho: Sorry, just to be clear, “transient in memory” is fine. We care about storage and later human access.
[13:41] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. And access controls—least privilege, audit trails, and we can explain our internal access policy.

[13:56] Ravi Deshpande: Okay, continuing questionnaire: Do you support customer-owned VPC endpoints, PrivateLink.
[14:03] Markus Klein: For Private deployments in your VPC, yes. For Hosted, we can discuss private connectivity options; typically Hosted is over public internet with TLS, but for strict requirements, Private is the route.
[14:18] Megan Cho: That probably means Private is in scope later.
[14:21] Markus Klein: Yep, we can phase it. Pilot on Hosted; then if you need VPC-only, we do Private.

[14:30] Dana Willis: If we start Hosted through Marketplace, can we later move to Private through Marketplace too?
[14:35] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, we can structure it as an additional SKU or an expansion. Sometimes Private is better as a separate contract depending on complexity, but we can do Marketplace if that’s your policy.

[14:49] Tom Alvarez: Another question: support levels. Do we get an SLA if purchased via Marketplace?
[14:55] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. Support and SLA are based on the plan/SKU, not the procurement channel. Marketplace customers get the same enterprise support terms.

[15:05] (brief silence)

[15:07] Stephanie Nguyen: Maybe it’s useful if we summarize SKU options in plain English.
[15:11] Markus Klein: Hosted: shared infrastructure, fastest start, usage based. Dedicated: reserved GPU pool, predictable throughput, isolation. Private: control plane in your network, customer-managed networking and optionally keys, strongest residency/control.
[15:28] Megan Cho: For our pilot, Hosted. For prod, likely Dedicated, and for regulated workloads maybe Private.

[15:38] Ravi Deshpande: And audit logs for Hosted—are those included or add-on.
[15:43] Markus Klein: Baseline audit logs are included for enterprise orgs; advanced retention/export may be tied to an add-on. We’ll confirm what’s standard vs add-on.
[15:54] Naomi Feldman: Regardless, we can ensure the events you need are captured. The question is retention period and export mechanism.

[16:06] Dana Willis: Okay, so next steps: we need a private offer draft and the security packet.
[16:11] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. To draft a private offer we’ll need: your AWS account ID(s) that will accept the offer, desired start date, term length, any committed spend target, and the region constraints. Also who signs.
[16:28] Dana Willis: I can send the account ID. Tom can send spend targets.
[16:32] Tom Alvarez: Yeah, I’ll send a ballpark. We’re thinking low six figures annual for pilot-to-prod, but I need to validate.

[16:42] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s helpful. We can propose a structure: initial committed spend with overage at list, or a tiered discount. We’ll align with how AWS wants it expressed.

[16:56] Megan Cho: Can we schedule the technical deep dive? I want to see the console onboarding and error states, because that’s where vendors fall over.
[17:05] Markus Klein: Yes. I’ll send a couple times. We can show the marketplace entry point, entitlement check, and what happens if it’s not found.

[17:16] Ravi Deshpande: I’d also like to see the audit log events list.
[17:19] Naomi Feldman: We can cover that. We have a doc that enumerates event types. We’ll include it in the packet.

[17:27] Stephanie Nguyen: Anything else on procurement mechanics?
[17:30] Dana Willis: Not right now. But one caution: our legal will ask about data processing terms. Please include DPA options.
[17:37] Stephanie Nguyen: Will do.

[17:40] (topic shift)

[17:42] Megan Cho: Random question: do you support function calling / tools? Some providers call it “tool use.”
[17:48] Markus Klein: Yes, we support tool calling patterns and structured output. Model-dependent, but the API supports it.

[17:57] Tom Alvarez: And usage analytics—do we get per-project breakdown?
[18:01] Markus Klein: Yes, the console has usage by org/project, model, route, latency, token breakdown. That’s part of why reconciliation with Marketplace invoices is easier.

[18:15] Ravi Deshpande: Okay I think I have what I need. Send the packet and we’ll review.

[18:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Before we drop, quick recap:
[18:26] Stephanie Nguyen: 1) We’ll send the AWS private offer intake checklist and start drafting an offer. 2) Naomi will send the marketplace security documentation pack and start SOC 2 report access via trust portal. 3) Markus will schedule a technical deep dive to walk through audit logs, retention controls, and the Marketplace onboarding flow.
[18:47] Stephanie Nguyen: From your side, Dana/Tom will send AWS account IDs and procurement timeline, Ravi/Megan will send the questionnaire and any must-have clauses.

[18:58] Dana Willis: Sounds right.
[19:00] Ravi Deshpande: Yep.
[19:01] Megan Cho: Works.
[19:03] Tom Alvarez: Good.

[19:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up by end of day tomorrow with the links and next steps.

(Transcript continues with light scheduling chatter; recording ends.)

support

Dev Patel: Escalation: marketplace buyer stuck in provisioning ("Waiting for entitlement"). They subscribed via AWS Marketplace ~2+ hrs ago and still can’t create an org / API key. Customer is Northpeak Analytics (enterprise trial via marketplace).

Dev Patel: Jira: SUP-4821 https://jira.redwoodinference.com/browse/SUP-4821

Dev Patel: Symptoms per ticket:
- Console onboarding -> "We couldn’t verify your marketplace entitlement yet" (retry loop)
- They can sign in, but the marketplace entrypoint never links subscription -> org
- AE/SE is on the call and customer’s procurement is watching :grimacing:

Rachel Kim: Ugh. Do we have their org already created or net-new?

Dev Patel: Net-new as far as I can tell. No existing org in console.

Markus Klein: I’m on the Zoom. They subscribed from AWS account ending in 9041 (per screenshot). They have the subscription confirmation in AWS Marketplace.

Chloe Martin: That error is specifically when `/marketplace/entitlements/verify` returns `NOT_FOUND` (or `PENDING`) for AWS. If it’s been 2h, we should check the sync job + the raw entitlement lookup.

Ethan Park: Can someone paste the subscription identifier / customerIdentifier from AWS side? Without that we’re guessing.

Markus Klein: They don’t see a "customerIdentifier" in the UI, but they can download the subscription agreement. I asked them to grab the "Entitlement" page screenshot too.

Dev Patel: In SUP-4821 I added the screenshot they sent. It includes Product Code `redwood-inference-prod-aws` and the AWS account ID, but not the customerIdentifier.

Jira Cloud: SUP-4821 updated by Dev Patel: "Added customer screenshots + confirmed AWS acct ending 9041; still pending after 2h."

Priya Natarajan: If AWS is delayed we can do the manual mitigation: create org, temporarily grant a Hosted entitlement (time-boxed), then reconcile once entitlement lands. But we need to be careful on metering.

Nadia Rahman: +1. Also want to capture telemetry for this case (entitlement lookup latency + retry counts). If someone can share the request_id from console, I can trace.

Chloe Martin: Console shows request_id in the error modal if you click "Details". Markus can ask for it.

Markus Klein: Got it. Asking now.

Ethan Park: Meanwhile I’ll check entitlement sync logs for AWS around now. What region is their org trying to provision in? (console defaults us-east-1)

Dev Patel: They’re in us-east-1. They didn’t change anything.

Ethan Park: Checking… I see repeated retries for AWS entitlement sync with `AccessDeniedException` for `ResolveCustomer` starting ~30 min ago. That would explain NOT_FOUND everywhere.

Priya Natarajan: That’s bad. Is this the IAM/webhook config regression from last week?

Ethan Park: Possibly. It’s coming from the marketplace sync service role. I’ll page Platform on-call after I confirm.

Dev Patel: For customer comms: can I tell them we’re seeing an internal entitlement sync issue and we’re working it? Need an ETA.

Chloe Martin: Yes, but offer workaround: we can provision them manually so they can start testing today.

Priya Natarajan: Approved. Dev, proceed with manual provision + temp Hosted access (24h) to unblock. Note in SUP ticket and tag Billing for later reconciliation.

Dev Patel: OK. Manual mitigation steps I’ll follow:
1) Create Redwood org for Northpeak (name: Northpeak Analytics)
2) Link user to org
3) Apply temporary Hosted SKU entitlement (24h) + conservative rate limits
4) Send them API key creation steps + marketplace linking page for later

Dev Patel: Chloe/Ethan, anything special to avoid breaking later linking when AWS entitlement is fixed?

Chloe Martin: Yes: don’t mark it as marketplace-linked in the org metadata. Just grant a normal Hosted entitlement. Once entitlement sync is healthy, they can go through marketplace linking and we’ll attach subscription -> org (we have a "link existing org" path).

Ethan Park: +1. Also note: once the AWS entitlement lands, the org should attach to the correct subscription. If they create a second org accidentally, it becomes a mess.

Rachel Kim: Markus, make sure they DO NOT keep clicking create/retry and accidentally start multiple flows. Tell them we’re provisioning and they’ll get an email.

Markus Klein: Copy. Also got request_id from console: `mp_onboard_req_7f3d2a91c6b8`. Sharing here.

Nadia Rahman: Traced. That request maps to entitlement verify returning `AWS_RESOLVE_CUSTOMER_ACCESS_DENIED`. So root cause is definitely IAM permission on sync service.

Ethan Park: I’m paging Platform on-call now and linking SUP-4821. We should also open an internal incident if this affects multiple customers.

Dev Patel: I’ll update SUP-4821 with mitigation + request_id + suspected root cause.

Jira Cloud: SUP-4821 updated by Dev Patel: "Workaround approved: manual org provision + temp Hosted entitlement (24h). Root cause suspected: AWS ResolveCustomer AccessDenied in entitlement sync. Console request_id mp_onboard_req_7f3d2a91c6b8."

Priya Natarajan: Once Platform has the IAM fix, let’s add a postmortem note: why did this not alert earlier? Nadia, can we add an alert on `AWS_RESOLVE_CUSTOMER_ACCESS_DENIED` > threshold.

Nadia Rahman: Yes. I’ll create a follow-up (ENG) after this thread. For now I’ll set a temporary dashboard alert.

Dev Patel: Manual org created + user invited. Markus, I DM’d you the org slug and the steps to get them an API key.

Markus Klein: Confirmed on call: they’re in, API key created, first request succeeded. Procurement is happy again :thumbsup:

Chloe Martin: Great. Please remind them to come back and complete marketplace linking once we resolve entitlement sync, otherwise billing won’t route through AWS Marketplace.

Dev Patel: Will do. Leaving SUP-4821 open until entitlement sync is healthy and we’ve confirmed marketplace linking works end-to-end.

Ethan Park: Platform on-call acknowledged. They’re rolling back the IAM policy change and will redeploy entitlement sync. I’ll post once we see ResolveCustomer succeed.

Ethan Park: Update: ResolveCustomer calls are succeeding again. Entitlement sync is catching up. Expect AWS entitlements to appear within ~15-30 min.

Dev Patel: Noted. I’ll follow up with Northpeak tomorrow to link subscription -> existing org and close SUP-4821.

records.title: Private Deployments: Upgrade Go/No-Go Checklist (Enterprise)
records.text:
Private Deployments: Upgrade Go/No-Go Checklist (Enterprise)

## Purpose
This checklist is the required go/no-go gate for upgrading an *enterprise* Redwood Private deployment (VPC or on-prem). It defines the minimum validations, evidence, and sign-offs required before starting the maintenance window, and the stop/rollback criteria during execution.

## Scope
Applies to any customer production Private environment upgrade of: (a) control plane components (operator, controller, API gateway), (b) serving runtime/data plane images, (c) cluster dependencies shipped by Redwood (ingress, cert-manager bundles, logging agents), or (d) installer/upgrade tooling.

> Policy dependencies: This page is the operational gate, but approvals/comms requirements are defined in the Change Management Policy and Planned Maintenance Comms SOP. Security-specific sign-off requirements are defined in Secure SDLC: Security Sign-off for Customer Deployments. SLO/error budget checks are defined in Planned Change SLO / Error Budget Review Requirements.

---

## Pre-window requirements (must be complete 24h before window)
### A) Change record + ownership
1. Create a change request ticket using the Private Upgrade Change Request template (Jira internal-support).
2. Name a single *Change Owner* (usually Private Deployments on-call or the assigned Solutions/Delivery engineer).
3. Confirm customer-side *Change Approver* and *Operator* contacts (who will be present in the window).

### B) Version + compatibility
1. Record current versions: installer, operator/controller, runtime images, chart versions.
2. Confirm target versions and the exact upgrade path (no skipping major versions unless explicitly supported).
3. Confirm model/runtime compatibility notes for the customer’s pinned models.

### C) Backups + rollback readiness
1. Confirm backups exist and are recent for:
   - Control plane config state (values files, helm releases, operator CRs)
   - Any Redwood-managed persistent volumes (if present)
   - Customer-provided external dependencies are documented (DB, SSO, KMS)
2. Validate rollback artifacts are available locally: previous installer bundle, previous image tags, and prior values files.
3. Ensure a rollback decision point is explicitly called out in the window plan (see “In-window gates”).

### D) Preflight validations (attach evidence)
Run the standard preflight and attach the output to the change ticket:
- Cluster capacity and node readiness checks
- Storage class/PV health
- DNS and egress reachability (if images are pulled during window)
- TLS/certificate expiration checks
- Required Kubernetes API versions present (no deprecated APIs that will break charts)

### E) Observability readiness
1. Confirm dashboards/alerts are visible to Redwood during the window (temporary access granted if needed).
2. Confirm the following signals are available:
   - Control plane API error rate
   - Inference request error rate (5xx)
   - P95 latency for primary routes
   - GPU utilization and OOM/restart rates

---

## Go/No-Go gate (must be completed at window start)
The Change Owner must explicitly record “GO” in the change ticket after confirming all items below.

### 1) Required sign-offs (links required)
- Change Management approvals completed (see policy for approvers by risk level).
- SRE SLO/error budget review completed (or documented risk acceptance).
- Security sign-off completed if triggered (auth/RBAC/audit/TLS/dependency changes).
- Customer Success owner acknowledges comms plan and customer readiness.

### 2) Customer communications ready
- Maintenance notice sent according to comms SOP (timing + channel).
- During-window escalation path confirmed (Redwood + customer).
- “All clear” message drafted for post-window.

### 3) Final technical readiness
- Preflight output has no *red* blockers; any *yellow* warnings have an owner and mitigation.
- No open P0/P1 incidents on Redwood side that would reduce ability to respond/rollback.
- If a change freeze is active, an exception is approved and linked.

---

## In-window gates (stop points)
### Gate A: Post-control-plane upgrade health
Proceed only if all are true within 10 minutes:
- Operator/controller pods Ready
- Control plane API healthy (no sustained 5xx)
- No unexpected restart loops

### Gate B: Post-data-plane rollout health
Proceed only if all are true within 15 minutes:
- Runtime pods Ready and stable (no crashloops)
- Can complete a synthetic inference request on each region/cluster segment
- Customer confirms application-level smoke test passes

### Gate C: Verification window
Hold for 30 minutes of steady state with alerting enabled and monitored.

---

## Rollback criteria (immediate NO-GO / trigger rollback)
Rollback should be initiated if any of the following occurs and cannot be resolved quickly:
- Sustained inference 5xx above customer’s baseline +5% for >5 minutes
- P95 latency regression >30% for >10 minutes on the primary routes
- Authentication failures (SSO/JWT validation) or RBAC denial spikes
- Audit log pipeline breaks (if contractual requirement)
- Control plane cannot reconcile/upgrade further

---

## Evidence to attach to the change record
- Preflight output
- Version matrix (from/to)
- Rollback plan (commands + expected time)
- Links to SLO/error budget check and any risk acceptance
- Security sign-off (or “not required” rationale)
- Copy of customer comms and confirmation of receipt

## Ownership
Primary: Private Deployments
Consulted: SRE, Security & Compliance, Customer Success

records.title: Operator fallback experiment matrix and cost penalty catalog
records.text:
Operator fallback experiment matrix and cost penalty catalog

Overview
========

This document captures a reproducible experiment matrix for operator-driven fallback strategies and an associated cost-penalty catalog used to evaluate trade-offs between SLO preservation and unit economics across regional surges. It is intended for platform operators, SREs, and product engineers running controlled degradation experiments or designing automatic fallback policies.

Why this exists
---------------
- Fallbacks are a major lever for preserving SLOs during capacity scarcity or model regressions, but they have measurable cost and quality impacts.
- Operators need a concise experiment plan with metrics, dashboard queries, and a cost penalty model to compare candidate strategies.
- This doc standardizes experiment telemetry, rollout/rollback steps, and decision criteria for productionizing fallbacks.

Goals and scope
---------------
- Goal: Provide a repeatable experiment matrix that yields quantitative comparisons of: latency SLO retention, token-cost delta, quality regressions (evaluations), and operator intervention effort.
- Scope: Multiregion inference surface (hosted + dedicated), model variant fallbacks (quantized, smaller model families), and routing degradations (regional drain, tenant throttling).
- Out of scope: Model training/data pipelines, legal/customer contract negotiation.

Definitions and abbreviations
---------------------------
- Fallback variant: Any alternative response path (e.g., model C => model B, or cached response) used when the primary path is unavailable or overloaded.
- Cost penalty: Unit cost increase or revenue impact metric associated with using a fallback (e.g., tokens * $/token diff, or additional infra cost).
- SLO preservation: Fraction of requests meeting 95th percentile latency target and error-rate SLO.

Experiment matrix (canonical)
---------------------------
Columns: experiment_id | description | fallback_type | trigger | primary-metric | cost-metric | quality-metric | run-length | owner

Example rows (use these as templates):
1) EXP-001 | Model-variant degrade (Llama-70B -> Llama-13B-int8) | model_variant | queue-depth > 100 OR p95 latency > 600ms | p95 latency, error-rate | token-cost-delta-per-hour | eval-regression@20 prompts | 2h | operator-team
2) EXP-002 | Regional drain to peer region (eu-west -> us-east) | regional-routing | region capacity throttle 80% | p99 tail latency cross-region | egress-cost-delta | user-visible-quality (latency jump) | 4h | platform-network
3) EXP-003 | Prefetch cache fallback (serve from prefix cache) | cache_prefetch | cold-start rate > 30 req/min | mean latency | compute-cost-savings | correctness mismatch ratio | 3h | runtime-team
4) EXP-004 | Token-budgeted throttling for low-priority tenants | quota_throttle | burst credits exhausted | 95th latency of high-priority | revenue-at-risk | customer-error-annotations | 6h | platform-ops

Telemetry and dashboarding recipe
--------------------------------
Create a dedicated experimental dashboard with following panels per experiment run:
- SLO heatmap: p50/p95/p99 latency over time (per region, per tenant priority). Query examples:
  - latency_p95{experiment_id="EXP-001"} (PromQL)
  - request_duration_bucket_sum by (le, region)
- Cost delta stream: rolling token-cost-per-minute and infra-cost-surge.
  - token_cost_rate{fallback_variant!=""}
- Quality regression signal: evaluation pass-rate across a held promptset (20-50 prompts) run every 15 minutes.
  - eval_pass_rate{promptset="fallback-20"}
- Operator interventions: number and duration of manual rollbacks, with links to runbook tickets.
  - operator_rollbacks_total{experiment_id="EXP-001"}
- Composite KPI panel: cost-penalty vs. SLO-preservation scatter plot for each variant.

Minimum instrumentation checklist
--------------------------------
1) Annotate requests with experiment_id and fallback_variant in trace metadata.
2) Emit fallback_reason counter in request pipeline.
3) Record per-request token accounting and model_version label.
4) Attach prompt-set id for synthetic eval traffic.
5) Ensure operator actions log into the incident system with experiment_id tag.

Cost penalty catalog (examples and formulae)
-------------------------------------------
Catalog rows: fallback_variant | per-token-diff | expected-throughput | hourly-cost-delta | rollback-cost-estimate | notes
Example entries:
- L70B -> L13B-int8 | +0.002 $/token (lower cost) | 2k tokens/s | -$14.4 / hour per 1000 rps | negligible | reduced quality on long-form completion
- cross-region-eu->us | +$0.05 / 1k tokens (egress) | 1k tokens/s | +$180 / hour at 1000 rps | potential SLA credits | watch cold-start p95
- cached_prefix_response | -$0.001 $/token (savings) | N/A | -$3.6 / hour per 1000 rps | risk of stale content | requires invalidation policy
- quota-throttle-low | revenue-at-risk estimate (see calc) | depends on tenant mix | - | revenue-impact = average-MRR-per-req * blocked-reqs | requires customer comms plan

Cost calculations (short formulas)
- token_cost_delta_hourly = sum_over_requests(token_count * (cost_primary - cost_fallback)) per hour
- egress_delta_hourly = egress_bytes * egress_rate
- revenue_at_risk = blocked_requests * avg_revenue_per_request
Include these calculations in the dashboard as derived timeseries.

Experiment run playbook (step-by-step)
-------------------------------------
1) Planning (2–4 days)
   a) Define hypotheses: e.g., "model-variant fallback preserves p95 latency with <5% quality regression and cost delta < $200/hr"
   b) Pick held promptset (20–50 prompts) and synthetic traffic profile matching customer mix.
   c) Create experiment_id, add telemetry tags and dashboard.
2) Preflight (1 day)
   a) Run synthetic traffic against fallback in staging and collect baseline metrics.
   b) Validate eval pass-rate and trace annotation.
   c) Pre-commit rollback playbook and test it in canary.
3) Execution (2–6 hours normally, up to 24 hours for long-run metrics)
   a) Apply experiment on a small cohort (1% of traffic or single region).
   b) Monitor SLO panels and operator intervention panel.
   c) Escalate to oncall if p99 > target * 2 or error-rate increases > 2x baseline.
4) Ramp or rollback (decision gates)
   a) If cost-savings or SLO-preservation meet hypothesis -> ramp to 10% then 50% using pre-defined step intervals.
   b) If quality regression > threshold or operator rollbacks > 1 -> rollback immediately, file incident.
5) Post-run analysis (within 48 hours)
   a) Populate experiment report template (see artifacts).
   b) Archive synthetic trace samples and evaluation results.

Rollback quick commands (examples)
--------------------------------
- Immediate global rollback: CLI helper
  - redwoodctl rollout cancel --experiment EXP-001 --force
- Regional undo (eu-west):
  - redwoodctl routing set-region-weight --region eu-west --weight 1.0 --experiment EXP-001
- Re-enable primary model:
  - redwoodctl model set-default --model redwood/llama-70b --variant baseline --experiment EXP-001
Include these command snippets in runbook templates and verify operator RBAC before using.

Decision criteria matrix (accept/ramp/abandon)
--------------------------------------------
- Accept: p95 latency maintained within 10% of baseline AND eval regression <= 3% AND hourly cost delta within budgeted threshold.
- Ramp: p95 within 20% and eval regression <= 7% with operator acceptance.
- Abandon: p95 > 20% degradation OR eval regression > 10% OR unexpected customer errors in the error-tracking system.
Document reasons in experiment report.

Artifacts to capture and store
----------------------------
- Experiment report (.md) with: hypothesis, traffic profile, duration, metrics before/after, cost calculations, operator notes.
- Trace bundle (link to S3) and synthetic eval outputs (json).
- Dashboard snapshot and Prometheus queries used.
- Postmortem if rollback occurred.

Operational responsibilities and ownership
----------------------------------------
- Owner: platform-ops (primary contact: oncall@platform) for run coordination.
- Instrumentation: runtime-team for trace and metric changes.
- Cost modeling: finance-eng liaison for hourly cost validation.
- Security review: security-team if any customer data is used in synthetic prompts.

Safety and customer communication
--------------------------------
- For tenant-facing throttles or degradations that materially impact customer SLAs, coordinate with Customer Success for banner messaging and QBR notes.
- For enterprise customers with Dedicated/Private deployments, require explicit sign-off per the customer SLAs before ramping.

Retrospective template (post-experiment)
--------------------------------------
1) Summary: one-paragraph outcome
2) Metrics: baseline vs. experiment (latency, error-rate, cost, eval pass-rate)
3) What went well
4) What failed / surprises
5) Action items (owner + due date)
6) Decision: accept/ramp/abandon

Appendices
----------
A. Sample PromQL snippets
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference",experiment_id=~"EXP-.*"}[5m])) by (le, region))
- fallback rate: sum(rate(fallback_reason_total[1m])) by (fallback_variant)

B. Template experiment report checklist (copy into new experiment ticket)
- Experiment ID: 
- Owner: 
- Hypothesis: 
- Synthetic promptset id: 
- Baseline run links: 
- Dashboard link: 
- Rollback commands verified: Y/N
- Customer communication required: Y/N

C. Related runbooks and pages
- emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation (runbook)
- platform-operator-handbook-degraded-kv-prefix-cache (operator runbook)

D. Change log
- 2025-11-12: Document created by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-12-08: Added cost-penalty formulas and cross-region egress example (review: Miguel Torres).
- 2026-01-18: Finalized decision criteria and PromQL snippets (review: Dana Li).

Contact and follow-up
--------------------
For questions or to schedule a live walk-through of the experiment templates, ping #platform-ops or email aisha.patel@redwood.ai.

records.title: Audit log export (customer-managed destinations): architecture and operational model
records.text:
Audit log export (customer-managed destinations): architecture and operational model

# Overview
Redwood Inference supports **customer-managed audit log export** so customers can ingest Redwood audit events into their SIEM (Splunk, Datadog, Chronicle, Sentinel, etc.) from a destination they control.

This page describes the reference architecture used across deployment modes (Hosted, Dedicated, Private) and how responsibilities are split between Redwood and the customer.

# Goals
- Provide near-real-time delivery of **platform audit logs** to customer storage.
- Ensure exports are secure (least privilege + encryption) and observable (failure detection + retry).
- Keep a consistent schema across modes and regions.

# Non-goals
- Exporting inference payloads (prompt/completion).
- Providing customer-specific transformations beyond supported formats.

# Components
## 1) Audit Event Producers
Sources of events (examples):
- `control-plane-auth` (SSO, API key lifecycle, token exchange)
- `rbac-service` (role bindings, policy updates)
- `console-actions` (admin actions)
- `private-control-plane` (cluster admin actions for Private)

## 2) Audit Event Bus
- Internally, producers emit to a regional audit bus (`audit-bus-*`).
- The bus provides buffering and ordering guarantees per partition.

## 3) Export Connector
A Redwood-managed service that:
- consumes from the audit bus
- batches and compresses records
- writes to the customer destination
- tracks delivery offsets/checkpoints
- emits its own audit/health events

Service name: `audit-export-connector`

## 4) Customer Destination
Supported sinks (customer-managed):
- AWS S3 (preferred for AWS-native customers)
- Google Cloud Storage
- Azure Blob Storage

Formats:
- JSON Lines (`.jsonl.gz`)
- Optional: Parquet (`.parquet`) for select customers (requires feature flag)

# Data model (high level)
Each record includes:
- `event_id`, `event_time`
- `org_id`, `project_id`
- `actor_type`, `actor_id`
- `action`, `resource_type`, `resource_id`
- `source_service`, `region`
- `ip`, `user_agent` (when available)

Redaction rules:
- No request bodies
- No model outputs
- Token strings are never logged

# Delivery semantics
- At-least-once delivery. Customers must deduplicate by `event_id`.
- Typical delivery lag: 1–5 minutes.
- Backpressure: connector will increase batch size up to a safe limit; if the sink is failing, it will retry with exponential backoff.

# Multi-region behavior
- Exports are **regional** by default.
- If a customer operates in multiple regions, a separate destination prefix per region is recommended.
- Cross-region export is not enabled by default and requires Security + Legal signoff.

# Failure modes & detection
Common issues:
- IAM permission errors (403)
- destination throttling
- private endpoint DNS/TLS failures (Private)
- customer rotates role/trust without notifying Redwood

Detection:
- `audit-export-connector.delivery_success_rate`
- `audit-export-connector.delivery_lag_seconds`
- `audit-export-connector.write_errors_total`

Pager policy:
- Dedicated/Private enterprise customers: page on sustained delivery failure > 30 min
- Hosted self-serve: alert (non-paging) unless multiple tenants impacted

# Responsibility matrix (RACI)
| Activity | Hosted | Dedicated | Private | Customer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Create destination bucket/container | C | C | C | R |
| Configure encryption/retention | C | C | C | R |
| Provide role/workload identity | C | C | C | R |
| Enable connector + routing | R | R | C | I |
| Validate delivery | R | R | R | C |
| Ongoing monitoring of sink cost | I | I | I | R |

Legend: R=Responsible, C=Consulted, I=Informed

# References
- Security controls and approval gates: `security-and-compliance/audit-logging/customer-managed-audit-log-export-controls`
- Hosted enablement runbook: `eng-platform/runbooks/hosted-audit-log-export-enablement`
- Dedicated setup runbook: `eng-infra/runbooks/dedicated-audit-log-export-customer-setup`
- Private configuration guide: `eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-audit-log-export-configuration`

records.title: rbac policy 'not_in' operator fallthrough grants unexpected access when claim missing in private deployment
records.text:
rbac policy 'not_in' operator fallthrough grants unexpected access when claim missing in private deployment

description:
Issue summary: Atlas Retail observed that several service accounts and a subset of human users were granted admin-level routes in their private VPC deployment despite RBAC policies that should exclude them via a 'not_in' expression. Impact: Incorrectly permissive access to admin/config APIs for a small number of identities, risk of configuration changes. Environment: Private deployment (customer-managed control plane), prod-us-east region, customer using SSO via their IdP with claims delivered as JWT to the identity-proxy. Observation window: 2026-03-12 22:30 - 2026-03-13 03:00 UTC. Steps to reproduce: 1) Customer provided a minimal policy that allows action if user.entitlements not_in ["admin", "superuser"] 2) Send request with JWT that omits the 'entitlements' claim altogether 3) Call to /admin/config returns 200 and allowed instead of denied. Expected behavior: Missing claim should be treated as empty set and 'not_in' should evaluate to true for empty set only if semantics intended; policy author expected deny when admin exclusion is required. Observed behavior: Policy evaluator treats missing claim in 'not_in' as a non-match that bypasses exclusion, resulting in grant. Customer impact: Two internal teams escalated (SRE and Platform) and temporarily halted config pushes. No data exfiltration detected.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Customer defines policy: allow if user.entitlements not_in ["admin", "superuser"]
2) Acquire JWT from IdP that omits entitlements claim (token valid for authN)
3) Call admin API route through identity-proxy and observe 200 OK
4) Inspect policy-evaluator logs and request trace (trace_id: trace-20260313-34b9)

logs:
2026-03-13T00:11:45Z authz-eval INFO allow user=svc-ordering token_kid=abcd1234 trace=trace-20260313-34b9 expr='user.entitlements not_in [\"admin\",\"superuser\"]' claim=ABSENT
2026-03-13T00:11:45Z proxy INFO request forwarded route=/admin/config status=200 trace=trace-20260313-34b9
JWT payload (redacted): {"sub":"svc-ordering@atlas", "email":"svc-ordering@atlas.example", /* entitlements claim not present */ }

comments:
Leah Park (Support): Initial report received from Atlas Retail. They included traces and a minimal policy example. Blocking their ability to push config; asked for escalation.
Diego Morales (SRE): Reproduced locally with a mock token. Policy evaluator returned ALLOW when entitlements absent. Created local debug build with extra logging. Tagging eng-authz.
Priya Nair (AuthZ Eng): Looking into boolean ops and value coercion in the policy evaluator. Hypothesis: not_in implementation does a string-contains check and treats absent as empty string which short-circuits differently than spec.
Atlas Retail (Customer): Confirmed workaround of explicitly setting entitlements claim to [] for service accounts mitigates. Requested timeline for patch and whether rollback/mitigation will be supported in their private control plane.
Diego Morales (SRE): Opened INT-4456 to track rollout/patch automation for private deployments. Requested canary rollout to dedicated infra before pushing to private updater.

investigation:
Summary: AuthZ engine's expression runtime performs 'not_in' by iterating subject values and checking membership against target list; when claim is absent the evaluator treats subject as a single empty string value leading to membership checks that return false and overall expression evaluating to true. Repro steps run in a dev harness mirrored customer config. Reproduced with token missing 'entitlements'. Additional tests: - token with entitlements: ['readonly'] -> correctly allowed - token with entitlements: ['admin'] -> correctly denied - token with absent entitlements -> incorrectly allowed. Root cause hypothesis: backward-compatible change in the policy-eval library (v2.14.0) introduced value coercion for absent claims. Related PR suspected: https://github.com/redwood-inference/authorization/commit/5f7e2b3. Impact surface: Private deployments that rely on omission semantics for exclusion policies. Risk: Moderate-high for private customers using exclusion-based RBAC.

resolution:
Workaround: Advise Atlas Retail to set entitlements claim to empty array for service accounts and short-lived tokens; this required a small IdP mapping change. Temporary policy recommendation provided: add explicit exists(user.entitlements) and deny if not exists. Fix: AuthZ team prepared fix to treat absent claims as empty set in 'not_in' semantics and to avoid coercing absent -> empty string. Patch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/authorization/pull/869. Deployment plan: canary merge to staging on 2026-03-15, rolling release to hosted and a patch bundle for private control plane customers on 2026-03-18. Follow-ups: document 'missing-claim' semantics in policy language reference; add unit tests for absent-claim cases. Customer communication: emailed timeline and temporary mitigation steps; customer accepted workaround and asked for confirmation post-rollout.

notes:
AuthZ eng to add regression tests for all membership operators: in, not_in, any_of, all_of
Add monitoring alert for unusual increases in admin-route allows per tenant
Prepare KB article for private customers about claim absence semantics and policy patterns
