records.title: introduce-invocation-context-fingerprinter-and-alert-squelch-fabric
records.text:
introduce-invocation-context-fingerprinter-and-alert-squelch-fabric

description:
Motivation: noisy per-tenant SLO alerts and expensive wide-context joins were making incident triage slow for teams that operate multi-tenant workloads. This PR introduces an Invocation Context Fingerprinter (ICF) and a lightweight Alert Squelch Fabric (ASF) to reduce alert churn and enable low-latency correlation of token-cost/latency signals across anonymized tenants. Design summary: the ICF computes a stable, privacy-preserving 128-bit fingerprint for each invocation by hashing a compact context vector (route id, prompt-shape hash, first-2-token-signature, kernel-path-id) and a locality-sensitive sketch of the first N token embeddings to capture structural similarity without retaining raw PII. Fingerprints are stored as 64-bit hex in ClickHouse column invocation_fingerprint with a TTL and approximate cardinality rollup. The ASF consults a cohort registry that groups fingerprints by entropy and recent error-rate similarity, and applies time-decayed suppression rules to transient alert spikes for cohorts that have high within-group homogeneity. Implementation highlights: - New package telemetry/icf implementing LSH + XXHash-based stable folding, with deterministic tests. - ClickHouse migration: add invocation_fingerprint, cohort_id, and a per-invocation token_cost_histogram (compact 8-bucket time-decayed histogram) for fast per-route rollups. - Observability API: new endpoint GET /v1/observability/fingerprints/{route} to retrieve recent cohort summaries and representative fingerprints. - Console: Dashboard panels added to Observability Console: Invocation Fingerprint Matrix, Cohort Token-Cost Heatmap, and Alert Squelch Monitor. - CLI: redwoodctl observability enable-fingerprinter --route <route> and redwoodctl observability cohort-dump. - Runtime integration: the runtime attaches the fingerprint to existing traces as trace tag fingerprint.hex and to spans as marginal tag icf.bucket. - Backwards compatibility: feature gated via env REDWOOD_ICF_ENABLED and per-tenant opt-in toggle; if disabled, nothing is written to ClickHouse and traces include a placeholder tag. Testing: unit tests cover LSH stability across seeds and simulated embedding noise, ClickHouse migration tested in staging with a compact dataset, e2e smoke validates that enabling ICF does not materially change per-request latency (median overhead measured at +0.6ms on p3.2xlarge). Load test: cohort rollups were exercised with a 10k rps synthetic workload in perf-lab and show 0.4% increase in storage read traffic thanks to compact histograms. Observability: added prometheus metrics telemetry_icf_processed_total, telemetry_icf_sketch_entropy, and asf_suppressed_alerts_total with labels (route, cohort). Alert tuning: new alert policy ASF-FLAP-01 suppresses repeated high-latency alerts for cohorts that meet suppression criteria (min_invocations=50 in window, entropy<0.25, no error-rate increase). Rollout plan: gate on REDWOOD_ICF_ENABLED, enable for internal tenants for 48h, monitor telemetry_icf_sketch_entropy and asf_suppressed_alerts_total, then progressive enable for external beta tenants.

Review conversation:
Miguel Torres: Nice design, the LSH sketch looks compact. Question: how deterministic is the fingerprint across different embedding implementations?
Aisha Khan: We use an L2-normalized float16 sketch with deterministic seed folding; tests include fuzzed embedding variants to validate stability within acceptable epsilon.
Samir Patel: Concern: adding columns to ClickHouse could increase query complexity for high-cardinality tenants. Suggest adding a TTL and sampled materialized view for costly joins.
Aisha Khan: Added TTL (30d) and a sampled materialized view in migration; updated the console panels to query the MV for heatmap generation.
Claire Zhang: Please add an opt-out at tenant-level and ensure KMS keys are not used to derive fingerprints (do not store raw user identifiers).
Aisha Khan: Confirmed tenant opt-out flag implemented and fingerprint is one-way hashed from non-PII features only.
Miguel Torres: CI failure on first run (go vet + staticcheck) — some unused imports in sketch_test.go
Aisha Khan: Fixed unused imports and rebased; CI passed on rerun.
Samir Patel: Approved pending small docs tweak to explain suppression hysteresis
Claire Zhang: Approved — merging when green.

Release notes:
Adds Invocation Context Fingerprinter (ICF) and Alert Squelch Fabric (ASF). ICF provides a compact, privacy-preserving fingerprint for invocations enabling cohort-level rollups and faster cross-invocation correlation. ASF reduces noisy alert churn by suppressing transient spikes for homogenous cohorts. New dashboards, CLI commands, and metrics included. Feature is opt-in and disabled by default.

Additional notes:
migration includes a light-weight materialized view to avoid scanning raw events and a staged backfill strategy that writes fingerprints for a 7d sliding window initially. Operational playbook added to docs/observability/fingerprinter_playbook.md with runbook steps for unmuting suppressed cohorts and diagnosing false suppression.

maria: Heads-up — since last night's driver rollout to 546.1 on eu-west GPUs we're seeing a small but sustained bump in Xid errors and NCCL watchdog timeouts in a subset of pods. Not a full outage yet but noisy.
raj: saw that alert at 01:12, investigating. Which clusters specifically?
maria: eu-west-prod-gpu and eu-west-batch-1. Mostly p3/p4 pools, tail latencies up ~2-3x on some jobs.
cheng: deploy-bot shows the driver rollout completed at 00:45 across eu-west.
deploy-bot: driver-rollout: version=546.1 region=eu-west status=successful started=1787999500 finished=1788000300
sre-oncall: jumping in. I pulled nvml logs from one affected node, there are repeated Xid 31 and Xid 43 messages around 00:50-01:05.
leo: Xid 31 is memory access fault, Xid 43 is illegal instruction in some driver paths. Could be a kernel+driver ABI mismatch on a handful of hosts.
raj: can we correlate with kernel versions? I remember the kernel bump last week on eu-west-hosts-2.
maria: yes — eu-west-hosts-2 have kernel 6.3.4-rt, other hosts at 6.2.x. The driver rollback test on a host with 6.2 didn't reproduce.
cheng: that suggests a compatibility regression with kernel 6.3.4-rt + 546.1. We should update runbook to include kernel check for Xid spikes.
sre-oncall: Quick mitigation: cordon affected nodes, drain GPU pods onto nodes still on 6.2, and create a canary pool that pins driver to 545.3 for kernel 6.3 hosts.
leo: I can prepare a short kube job to evict pods and move batch jobs — want to avoid preempting inference traffic.
raj: Please add/patch an alert: increase sensitivity for "nvidia.xid.rate" so we get per-node spikes (not only global). Current rule is global > 50/min which hides small clusters of failures.
maria: agreed. Proposed alert:
```
- alert: NvidiaXIDNodeSpike
  expr: rate(nvidia_gpu_nvml_xid_total[1m]) > 0.5
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "XID spike on node {{ $labels.instance }}"
```
cheng: I recommend we scope by driver_version and kernel_version labels so we can auto-assign to infra owners: severity=critical if driver==546.1 and kernel>=6.3
sre-oncall: adding checklist to thread (short playbook):
 1) Identify nodes with Xid > 5 in 5m (promql below).
 2) Check kernel_version and driver_version via inventory service.
 3) If driver==546.1 && kernel>=6.3 -> cordon + drain, pin to 545.3; else cordon + restart nvidia-dcgm + kubelet.
 4) If tasks are latency-sensitive, route traffic to fallback region (eu-central) using traffic-router.
 5) If drain fails due to unschedulable pods, fallback: restart driver on node and monitor for 10m.
PromQL example to find nodes:
```
sum by(node, driver_version, kernel_version) (increase(nvidia_gpu_nvml_xid_total[5m]))
```
maria: nice. Also add a dashboard panel for "NCCL watchdog timeouts" using metric nccl_watchdog_timeouts_total so we can spot correlation.
leo: I'll add a Grafana panel and a runbook section to link to the node inventory + kernel tag.
raj: action items: leo to add dashboard and alert patch (ETA 2h), cheng to prepare a pinning daemonset image (545.3) and a rollback playbook (ETA 3h), maria to update runbook text and incident doc (ETA 1h). I'm on-call to coordinate.
cheng: I'll also add a smoke test job that runs a small NCCL all-reduce across a canary node after driver change. Automate it into our rollout pipeline.
sre-oncall: temporary pager-rule: escalate Xid spike alerts if >10 nodes affected across a region. For now keep as warning to avoid noisy pages.
maria: thanks — one more: add a quick command snippet to runbook for manual repro on node:
```
# on node
sudo systemctl stop kubelet
sudo modprobe -r nvidia_uvm nvidia
sudo modprobe nvidia
sudo systemctl start kubelet
# run tiny NCCL job from infra tools
infra-nccl-run --gpus 2 --iters 20
```
raj: good. Capture outputs to /var/log/nvidia-repro.log and include a parsing helper in the runbook.
leo: I'll drop the updated runbook link here once uploaded.
maria: great work — this should keep us ahead of noisy regressions during driver rollouts. We'll revisit after the dashboard + alert changes. :thumbsup:

Anika (Vendor Ops): Heads-up: Saffron AI (India) sent invoice INV-2026 for fine-tuning work. They charged 18% GST and asked us to gross-up for 10% Indian withholding (TDS) — says clause 7.4 in SOW requires net payment. They want Redwood to pay the tax on their behalf.

Jo (Finance): Do we have a gross-up clause in the SOW? If so we might be contractually bound. If not, default is payer deducts TDS where required by Indian law.

Anika (Vendor Ops): Clause 7.4 is vague. It mentions "taxes and withholdings as required by law" but also a supplier indemnity paragraph. Not an explicit gross-up.

Ravi (Tax APAC): Quick checklist: 1) Is the supplier Indian tax resident? (likely yes). 2) If Indian resident, TDS rules apply on payments for technical services, but payer deducts and remits; gross-up only if contract requires. 3) If they claim non-resident status or treaty relief, they need Indian TRC (Tax Residency Certificate), Form 10F, and a withholding tax exemption certificate from Indian tax authorities.

Hannah (Payments): From payments side: if we don't gross-up, we deduct 10% at source, remit to Indian govt and provide TDS certificate (Form 16A) to vendor. We need vendor PAN to remit correctly.

Anika (Vendor Ops): Vendor emailed saying: "We're registered Indian company (GSTIN: 29AAXCM1234M1Z5), want Redwood to gross-up as our AP team says it's Redwood policy to gross-up for foreign tech buyers. Please confirm or we'll hold the invoice." They attached an invoice PDF and a scanned PAN.

Jo (Finance): Don't let them hold payment as a negotiation tactic. We need to respond with what we need.

Ravi (Tax APAC): Draft reply below 12 please review and shorten if needed:

```
Hi Saffron AI team,

Thanks for the invoice. A few items required to process payment:
1) Confirm whether Saffron AI is an Indian tax resident (PAN attached suggests yes).
2) Provide GSTIN and confirm the GST classification on the invoice (you have 18%).
3) Provide the SOW/contract clause that you rely on for gross-up. Absent an explicit gross-up clause we are required by Indian law (section 195/194J as applicable) to deduct withholding and remit to the Indian government.
4) If you claim any treaty relief or exemption, please provide your Indian Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) and Form 10F and any Indian withholding certificate permitting lower/no withholding.

If we do not receive a contractual gross-up obligation or official exemption, Redwood will deduct the applicable TDS (10%) and remit on your behalf. We will issue the TDS certificate post-remittance. If you prefer Redwood to remit a higher grossed-up amount, please provide a signed contract amendment referencing the gross-up obligation.

Please upload documents to the secure vendor portal so AP can proceed.

Best,
Ravi (Tax APAC)
```

Hannah (Payments): Add: "Please confirm the exact remittance name that matches your GST/PAN." Also mention timeline: upload within 5 business days or we will withhold.

Anika (Vendor Ops): Sent that to vendor. Vendor replied: "We are Indian resident. We cannot accept TDS deduction because it impacts our cashflow. We have a clause in SOW that says 'full payment without reduction' - see attached signed SOW pg3." They attached SOW excerpt.

Jo (Finance): If they have a signed gross-up clause, we need legal review and management sign-off. Can you attach SOW and highlight clause?

Ravi (Tax APAC): I'll review the SOW. Contractual gross-up would mean Redwood pays additional amount so vendor receives invoice amount net of tax. We'll need CFO approval. Also confirm whether the SOW references gross-up for "taxes imposed by law" vs specifically withholding — wording matters.

Anika (Vendor Ops): Uploaded SOW and invoice to shared drive, highlighted clause. Also asked vendor for their monthly TDS certificate history (they offered but didn't attach).

Ravi (Tax APAC): If we agree to gross-up, AP workflow: calculate gross-up amount using formula: gross_payment = net_amount / (1 - withholding_rate). Example: net 100 -> gross = 100 / 0.9 = 111.11, with 11.11 paid as additional to cover 10% withholding. We must also ensure VAT/GST treatment still correct on grossed-up number.

Jo (Finance): I don't love setting precedent. Let's loop in Legal and CFO. For this invoice amount (INR ~1,800,000) the gross-up delta is material. But if contract requires it, we should comply.

Hannah (Payments): Meanwhile I'll hold disbursement and flag for Legal review. If Legal ok with gross-up, tell AP to compute gross payment and route to treasury for funding in INR.

Saffron AI Pvt Ltd: Vendor: Thanks. We'll send a signed amendment if needed but prefer quick payment. Can Redwood provide a one-time netting or issue a PO amendment?

Ravi (Tax APAC): Reply to vendor: we can expedite if you sign contract amendment accepting Redwood's calculation and provide PAN/GST/TDS history. Otherwise Redwood will deduct TDS and remit.

Anika (Vendor Ops): Sent message. Legal pinged me, wants to review clause and vendor's proposed amendment. I'll schedule a quick call with vendor and Legal. Closing notes: request vendor docs up front during onboarding to avoid this next time. :spiral_calendar:

records.title: Access Containment and Evidence Archive Playbook (Cross-Control Incident Guide)
records.text:
Access Containment and Evidence Archive Playbook (Cross-Control Incident Guide)

Summary:
This playbook defines a single, cross-control procedure for containing access-related incidents, collecting audit evidence, and archiving artifacts in a manner that satisfies data residency and retention requirements. It is intended for security responders, SRE, platform engineers, and product owners responsible for model-serving and tenant isolation.

Purpose:
- Reduce time-to-contain for authorization and access incidents (target: contain within 30 minutes for high-severity).
- Produce a forensically sound evidence bundle that meets audit and regulatory requirements across regions.
- Ensure remediation and SDLC gates are applied before re-enabling affected services or entitlements.

Scope:
- Applies to incidents involving: RBAC/entitlement abuse, service account compromise, tenant cross-talk, audit log tampering, suspicious model or artifact access, and confirmed data exfiltration affecting Redwood-hosted inference.
- Not for pure availability incidents without access impact (see eng-sre runbooks for availability-only).

Definitions:
- Entitlement: Any identity (human or service) permission that allows access to a resource (API keys, roles, groups).
- Evidence bundle: The packaged set of logs, manifests, artifacts, and provenance proof used for audits and investigations.
- Chainproof: Signed manifest that links artifacts to the collection operation (who/when/how).

Owners and primary contacts:
- Incident Lead (security): oncall-security@redwood.com (PagerDuty, P0 routing)
- SRE runbook owner: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com
- Platform engineering (artifact/archive): platform-ops@redwood.com
- Evidence custodian (for archive and legal): legal-evidence@redwood.com

Incident classification and triage (high level):
1) Initial intake: identify observable symptom(s), affected principal(s), and suspected resource set. Create an incident in the IR tracker and tag scope as: ACCESS-LOCAL, ACCESS-CROSS-REGION, or ENTITLEMENT-ESCALATION.
2) Severity determination: use the matrix below (example):
   - Sev 1 (Critical): confirmed data exfiltration of customer PII, or active lateral movement across tenants.
   - Sev 2 (High): confirmed privilege escalation or long-lived credential compromise affecting production services.
   - Sev 3 (Medium): suspicious access pattern with no confirmed data access.
   - Sev 4 (Low): non-production or anecdotal events.
3) Assign containment and evidence zones (see containment playbooks).

Containment playbooks (select by incident type):
A) Compromised human or service credential (immediate):
   - Revoke affected tokens/keys: rotate API keys, disable sessions, and revoke refresh tokens.
   - Apply temporary attribute-based deny rule on identity provider for the principal (JIT block) with ttl=4h.
   - If the principal is a service account used in jobs, suspend job scheduler entries and attach a dry-run flag.
   - Record change in the incident timeline with who/what/why.
Evidence to collect (A):
   - Authentication logs (OIDC/SAML) for the principal: timestamp range +/- 60 min.
   - Service audit trail: which routes, resource IDs, and tokens used.
   - Host/session capture (if interactive): ps/top dumps, process command lines.

B) Privilege escalation or role-binding change (immediate):
   - Revoke the newly created/modified role binding and quarantine role definition (mark as "suspended").
   - Snapshot role-binding repository and export IAM graph for affected org/tenant.
   - Create a read-only clone of the affected RBAC datastore for forensic queries.
Evidence to collect (B):
   - RBAC change logs and approval records; git history if IaC-managed.
   - API server audit logs showing the binding event.

C) Suspected data exfiltration (priority):
   - Block egress routes for implicated hosts/pods, or move affected tenants to restricted egress proxy.
   - Snapshot storage containers/blobs and lock writes to affected datasets (write-once snapshot).
   - Notify legal and customer-success (for PII/regulated data).
Evidence to collect (C):
   - Storage access logs (object read events), network egress flows, and model-inference request traces.
   - Token usage correlation (which token requested which object).

Audit logging and evidence requirements (collection and minimal schema):
- Minimum log fields to collect for evidence:
  - timestamp (ISO 8601), principal_id, principal_type (user/service), action, resource_type, resource_id, request_id, src_ip, dest_ip, user_agent, outcome (allow/deny), audit_version
- Retention by severity and region:
  - Critical incidents: preserve full raw logs for 7 years in the incident evidence archive (region-bound; see Residency mapping).
  - High: preserve 2 years.
  - Medium/Low: retain standard retention (90 days) unless legal hold applied.
- Example Elasticsearch/Kusto query snippets to collect session span (append to incident ticket):
  - ES: POST /_search?q=principal_id:PRINCIPAL & body {"range": {"@timestamp": {"gte":"2026-11-15T00:00:00Z","lte":"2026-11-15T01:00:00Z"}}}
  - Kusto: AuditLogs | where PrincipalId == "PRINCIPAL" | where TimeGenerated between (start..end) | order by TimeGenerated asc

Data residency and retention mapping (decision table):
- Rule 1: If the affected tenant has residency required in EU, evidence copies must remain in the EU evidence vault.
- Rule 2: For cross-border incidents, keep a regional manifest with pointers to each region's evidence; do not consolidate raw logs to another jurisdiction unless legal approves export.
- Example mapping snippet:
  - Tenant.region == "eu-west-1" -> evidence-vault-eu-west-1 (S3/GCS bucket with SSE-KMS in EU key)
  - Tenant.region == "us-central1" -> evidence-vault-us-central1 (SSE-KMS in US)
  - Cross-region: create manifest in secure-control-plane with redacted pointers (no raw payload) linked to regional vault entries.

Evidence packaging and archival workflow (forensic-grade):
1) Collection: collect raw logs, config snapshots, RBAC export, and any binary artifacts (model checksums, docker image refs).
2) Hashing and chainproof: compute SHA256 of each collected artifact and write an audit manifest (manifest.json) that includes collector identity and timestamp. Sign manifest with the incident-collector key.
3) Packaging: create a directory structure: /evidence/IR-<INCIDENT-ID>/raw, /evidence/IR-<INCIDENT-ID>/manifests, /evidence/IR-<INCIDENT-ID>/analysis.
4) Storage: write artifacts to the regional evidence vault with naming convention: <region>/IR-<INCIDENT-ID>/artifact-type/<artifact>-<sha256>.gz.
5) Locking: apply object-level legal-hold and set retention metadata (retention-until) on the vault object.
6) Notification: automatically create a sealed incident package entry in the evidence catalogue and notify legal-evidence@redwood.com and the incident lead.

Sample manifest.json (example snippet included as reference):
{
  "incident_id": "IR-2027-00042",
  "collected_by": "anita.rao@redwood.com",
  "collected_at": "2027-02-03T18:34:22Z",
  "artifacts": [
    {"path": "raw/authn-logs/2027-02-03-authn.ndjson.gz", "sha256": "<sha256-hex>"},
    {"path": "rbac-snapshots/rbac-graph-2027-02-03.json.gz", "sha256": "<sha256-hex>"}
  ],
  "manifest_signature": "<base64-signature>"
}

Secure SDLC remediation gates (must be followed before re-enable):
- Gate 1 (engineering patch): patch branch created with PR referencing IR-<ID>. Security reviewer assigned and automated tests added for the exploit vector.
- Gate 2 (staging validation): run the incident regression suite (see applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness) and deploy to canary for 24 hours of telemetry with strict authz guards.
- Gate 3 (postmortem and legal signoff): require a security postmortem drafted and legal-evidence signoff for any data exposure before customer notifications and re-enable.

Risk and exceptions process (timebound):
- If an operational exception is requested (e.g., temporary cross-region debug access), submit the exception request via the Exception Board form with: incident id, justification, duration (max 72 hours), mitigations, and approver list.
- Approvals required: security lead + legal for cross-border, or security lead + product for internal-only dev access.
- All exceptions must be logged and auditable; the evidence manifest must record the exception and who executed it.

Escalation matrix and SLAs:
- Within 5 minutes: oncall-security paged for Sev 1/2 incidents.
- Within 30 minutes: containment actions in place for Sev 1.
- Within 4 hours: evidence package initial snapshot uploaded to regional vault.
- Contact list (examples):
  - Security Oncall: +1 555-0101 (PagerDuty)
  - SRE Lead: sre-lead@redwood.com
  - Legal evidence: legal-evidence@redwood.com
  - Product security liaison: product-security@redwood.com

Appendix A — Command and query references (copy into incident tickets):
- Rotate API key (CLI): redwood iam keys rotate --principal PRINCIPAL_ID --key KEY_ID --reason "IR-<ID> containment"
- Snapshot RBAC graph (example): curl -H \"Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN\" \"https://rbac.redwood.internal/v1/graph?tenant=TENANT_ID\" > rbac-graph.json && gzip rbac-graph.json
- Export audit slice to S3 (example): 
  aws es query --query-file es-slice.json | gzip > authn-slice.ndjson.gz && aws s3 cp authn-slice.ndjson.gz s3://evidence-vault-eu-west-1/IR-<ID>/raw/

Appendix B — Evidence retention quick rules:
- Never delete evidence under legal hold.
- Do not move raw logs out of region without explicit legal approval.
- When redacting for cross-team troubleshooting, produce redacted copies and keep originals sealed and access-controlled.

Appendix C — Post-incident deliverables:
- Postmortem (security template) with root cause, timeline, remediation, and preventative actions.
- Regression test cases merged to the eval-harness repo.
- Evidence closure notice with vault entries and retention-until dates recorded in IR ticket.

Related references and links:
- RBAC entitlement provenance (internal): /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/entitlement-provenance-and-retention-framework-2026
- Audit schema and contract: /confluence/security-and-compliance/audit-logging/event-schema-contract-and-retention-runbook-2025
- Data residency standards: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/inference-data-flow-deidentification-and-audit-correlation-standards-2026

Revision history:
- 2026-11-15: created (initial playbook draft).
- 2027-02-03: updated regional evidence vault naming and added SDLC gate requirements.

marina: looks like split-tunnel behavior — traffic to 10.25.0.0/16 should go over utun1 (vpn). a quick test: `ping 10.25.10.5` (staging-api internal ip) and `ssh -v carol@bastion.redwood.internal` to get verbose ssh logs. if ping fails, run `traceroute 10.25.10.5` to see where packets go.

carol: `ping 10.25.10.5` -> `connect: Network is unreachable`. traceroute shows first hop as 192.168.1.1 (my home router). so seems split tunnel is sending internal traffic over local network.

it-support: yep that's the symptom. For Pulse on mac there's a setting 'Route all traffic through VPN' — enable that if your profile allows it. If not, you can add a temporary route on mac: `sudo route -n add -net 10.25.0.0/16 10.8.0.1` (replace `10.8.0.1` with your utun gateway). After that `ping`/`ssh` should go via the VPN.

marina: also check bastion ACLs — we only allow ssh from the internal-access security group and specific sources. carol, can you confirm your SSH public key is uploaded to your profile? if not, do `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub carol@bastion.redwood.internal` (if allowed) or paste the key into the onboarding form. i'll check the SG and add you if needed.

it-support: opened ticket IT-2026 to add carol to `internal-access` and verify bastion ACLs: https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/IT-2026 — ETA ~30m.

carol: added the route as advised (`sudo route -n add -net 10.25.0.0/16 10.8.0.1` with my utun ip) — ping works and `ssh carol@bastion.redwood.internal` connects now. thanks!! :raised_hands:

marina: awesome, welcome again :slightly_smiling_face: i'll update the onboarding VPN doc (docs/onboarding/vpn.md) with Pulse screenshots and the split-tunnel troubleshooting steps. if you hit authorization errors after the ticket, i'll follow up. ping us anytime.

support

katie-support: FYI customer (acct: redwood-acme) opened a billing escalation — they say the Usage -> Tokens chart is showing higher totals than the raw API metrics. They selected region=eu-west-1 but totals look global. ticket: https://redwood.support/t/2345
mike-frontend: can you paste the tenant id and exact filters they used? also screenshot if available
katie-support: tenant_id: tenant_58b7
filters: region=eu-west-1, model=redwood-small-v2, version=2025-11-02
screenshot attached in ticket
james-backend: quick sanity check from metrics API (should be authoritative):
```
curl -s "https://api.redwood.com/metrics?tenant=tenant_58b7&region=eu-west-1&model=redwood-small-v2&from=2026-03-10&to=2026-03-11"
```
Returns counts scoped to eu-west-1. So likely a dashboard/frontend or aggregator cache mismatch, not the core metrics store.
olivia-sre: is this tenant the only reporter? any dashboard renderer errors around spike time?
katie-support: only this tenant reported so far. They said the console charts were slow and then showed inflated totals after a traffic spike.
lee-analytics: heads-up — we rolled out a small change yesterday that normalizes region keys in the analytics ingest layer (maps short keys like `eu` -> `eu-west-1`). If the dashboard client is still sometimes sending `eu` shorthand then aggregator cache keys will differ.
mike-frontend: pls paste the network payload when they clicked EU. I want to confirm whether UI sent full key or shorthand.
katie-support: customer devtools: `GET /dashboard/usage?tenant=tenant_58b7&region=eu&model=redwood-small-v2&from=...` — UI sent `region=eu` (shorthand) not the canonical name.
james-backend: that explains it. Aggregator caches use normalized `eu-west-1` keys (rollout-2026-03-16). When ui uses `eu`, cache lookup misses and code falls back to global precomputed buckets after a short timeout, resulting in inflated totals.
lee-analytics: reproducer I ran locally:
1) enable feature flag `region-normalization=v2` on analytics-service
2) dashboard requests with `region=eu`
3) aggregator normalizes internally but cache lookup ordering caused a miss then fallback to `*` global bucket after ~30s
Logs:
```
[2026-03-16T21:42:01Z] cache_lookup key=tenant_58b7|eu-west-1|redwood-small-v2 miss
[2026-03-16T21:42:01Z] fallback_to_global=TRUE
```
olivia-sre: fallback path should be conservative. Looks like a race: normalization happening in one place but cache key computed earlier in the flow in another shard. Could be rollout ordering inconsistency.
mike-frontend: mitigation options: 1) quick client patch to always send normalized region name, 2) rollback the analytics normalization flag, 3) patch aggregator lookup to normalize earlier. Which is least risky short-term?
lee-analytics: immediate step: roll back the normalization flag (low blast radius) and push a tiny frontend patch to normalize on the client. Rollback stops future misses but won't repair already-cached global aggregates.
james-backend: long term: ensure canonicalization at ingress for both UI and telemetry, and add a backfill re-aggregation job for affected tenant/region windows. I'll prepare a one-off backfill plan.
katie-support: customer reports ~12% higher token usage in the console for that day and asking for billing adjustment if backfill reduces counts. They want ETA.
olivia-sre: action items (owners):
- [P1] rollback analytics region-normalization flag (lee-analytics)
- [P2] frontend client quick patch to normalize region param (mike-frontend)
- [P2] one-off backfill/re-aggregation for tenant_58b7 and other hit tenants (james-backend)
- support: keep customer updated and collect any other impacted tenants (katie-support)
mike-frontend: opened tiny PR to normalize region on client and guard against shorthand: https://github.com/redwood-inference/frontend/pull/3921
lee-analytics: rollback in progress
deploy-bot: rollback triggered by lee-analytics on analytics-service @ 2026-03-17T02:14:22Z
lee-analytics: rollback completed, analytics-service back to previous behavior. Posting follow-up logs to #eng-ml.
james-backend: started backfill for tenant_58b7 for window 2026-03-10..2026-03-11, initial estimate ~12m, will update when done.
katie-support: told customer we patched rollback and will follow up within 24h with backfill/billing outcome. Keeping ticket open.
support-bot: Escalation created: ESC-8742 | severity P1. linked ticket: https://redwood.support/t/2345
mike-frontend: note for postmortem: root cause = asymmetric normalization during staggered rollout + cache fallback path too eager. Suggested fixes: canonicalize filters at ingress, make cache fallback conservative, and sequence rollouts to avoid asymmetric states.
lee-analytics: will collect logs and write a short postmortem in #postmortems after backfill confirms counts.
katie-support: tagging @account-team for potential billing outreach if backfill reduces billed tokens.

records.title: Kernel Hint Propagation Profiling Pipeline
records.text:
Kernel Hint Propagation Profiling Pipeline

Summary:

This document specifies the Kernel Hint Propagation Profiling Pipeline (KHPPP) — an end-to-end process used by the serving runtime team to capture, synthesize, and propagate lightweight kernel hints from production traces to the kernel selection and scheduler subsystems. The pipeline is optimized for low-overhead sampling, deterministic replay for hypothesis testing, and safe automated rollout of hint-driven kernel recommendations to the runtime.

Goals:
- Reduce unexpected kernel regressions by surfacing causal correlations between request shape and kernel latency.
- Provide repeatable profiling artifacts usable by scheduler and kernel teams for autotune jobs.
- Automate a canary rollout path for kernel hint changes with observable safety gates.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: inference request-level sampling -> trace enrichment -> hint extraction -> validation replay -> recommendation artifact -> canary rollout.
- Non-goals: full-model-level retraining or kernel code changes (those are handled by kernel engineering RFCs).

Owner and runbook contact:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime / Kernel Signals team (oncall: @kernel-signals).
- Secondary: eng-platform / Scheduler (oncall: @scheduler-op).
- On-call escalation ladder: pager -> lead kernel engineer -> runtime SRE.

Architecture overview:
1) In-proxy lightweight sampler (service: trace-sampler): attaches to request ingress and emits a sampled event with the following fields: request_id, model_id, route, token_len, prefix_hash, routing_decision, upstream_kernel_hint (if present). Sampling rate is configurable per-service (default 0.1%).

2) Enrichment & correlation (service: hint-enricher): enriches sampled events with kernel telemetry pulled from kernel-telemetry-store (per-GPU kernel latency percentiles, occupancy, kernel version). Correlation computes the candidate hint map for (model_id, sequence_bucket, route).

3) Hint extractor (service: hint-extractor): runs a lightweight causal check (Granger-inspired) to output a candidate hint: {hint_id, model_family, sequence_bucket, suggested_kernel_profile, confidence_score, sample_count, top_covariates}. Output written to artifact-store as a JSONL stream with TTL 90 days.

4) Replay & validation (service: hint-replay): replays a bounded subset of the original sampled traces in the internal replay lab (sandbox runtime) to validate latency delta, regression rate, and resource delta. Replay uses the same scheduler and kernel loader versions as production canary.

5) Recommendation and canary (service: hint-orchestrator): packages validated hints into a signed recommendation manifest and drives a staged canary rollout through the runtime configuration service (route-level config).

SLOs and thresholds (applies to the pipeline):
- End-to-end artifact availability: 99% within 15 minutes of sample capture.
- False-positive detection: target false-positive rate for deployed hints <= 2% measured over 7-day window.
- Canary safety: any canary that increases p99 latency for a route by > 3% or absolute +40ms must auto-abort.
- Resource delta: kernel profile must not increase GPU memory usage by > 6% without manual signoff.

Sampling configuration table (example):

| service | default-sampling | max-sampling | notes |
|---------|------------------:|-------------:|-------|
| public-api | 0.1% | 1% | Route override by SLA tier |
| internal-batch | 0.05% | 0.5% | High-throughput, low-latency sensitivity |
| dedicated-gpu | 0.2% | 2% | More signal for deterministic workloads |

Data retention and PII notes:
- Sampled traces omit prompt payloads by default. The pipeline stores prompt hashes and token counts only. Full payload capture is gated behind an explicit customer opt-in and legal review.

Trace enrichment schema (sample line):

{
  "request_id": "r_123abc",
  "model_id": "open-llama-13b",
  "route": "/v1/chat/completions",
  "sequence_bucket": "0-64",
  "kernel_versions": ["kv1.3.2"],
  "observed_p50_ms": "12.4",
  "observed_p99_ms": "73.1"
}

(Above is an example logged by hint-enricher; fields are stored as strings in artifact JSONL to simplify downstream joins.)

Validation replay checks (ordered step-by-step):
1) Replay subset selection: choose top 500 traces per candidate hint (or all if sample_count < 500).
2) Run replay with baseline kernel profile and with suggested kernel profile.
3) Capture metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU memory, kernel occupancy, and error rate.
4) Apply decision rules (see decision matrix).

Decision matrix (simplified):
- Accept if: p99 improves by >= 4% AND resource delta <= 3% AND confidence_score >= 0.75.
- Tentative if: p99 improves 1–4% AND resource delta <= 6% -> schedule extended evaluation (72h).
- Reject if: p99 regresses > 0% OR error_rate increases > 0.1% OR resource delta > 10%.

Canary rollout procedure (operational checklist):
1) Create signed manifest via hint-orchestrator, include: hint_id, target_routes, advisory_notes, rollback_conditions.
2) Deploy to 1% of traffic in canary region (region: us-west2 by default).
3) Monitor canary dashboard for 30 minutes baseline, then 6-hour extended observation window.
4) Automated gates: if p99 delta > 3% or error_count delta > 0.05% -> immediate rollback. If any kernel panics or GPU OOMs -> immediate rollback and page oncall.
5) If canary passes extended window, increase to 10% for 24 hours, then 50% for 6 hours, then global rollout.

CLI and artifact examples:
- Inspect recent candidate hints:
```
$ rlctl hints list --since 2026-02-01 --filter model_family=open-llama-13b --min-confidence 0.6
ID        MODEL       SEQ_BUCKET  CONF  SAMPLES  STATUS
ht-8a2c   open-llama  0-64        0.78  1,240    validated
```

- Manifest sample (YAML):
```
hint_id: ht-8a2c
model_family: open-llama
sequence_bucket: 0-64
suggested_kernel_profile: wave-compact-v2
confidence_score: 0.78
validation:
  p99_delta_pct: -6.1
  resource_delta_pct: 1.8
  replay_samples: 500
canary_policy:
  initial_traffic_pct: 1
  region: us-west2
  abort_conditions:
    p99_delta_pct_gt: 3
    error_rate_delta_pct_gt: 0.05
```

Observability and dashboards:
- Dashboard: KHPPP / Candidate Hints Overview (service: grafana-khppp) shows candidate hint throughput, validation pass/fail rate, avg confidence, and top failing routes.
- Alerting rules:
  - khppp-artifact-delay-high: fires if >1% of artifacts are older than 15 minutes (SEV3).
  - khppp-canary-p99-abort: fires if any canary violates p99 delta > 3% (SEV2).
  - khppp-replay-failure-spike: fires if hint-replay job failure rate > 0.5% over 10m (SEV2).

Developer guidelines for writing kernel hints:
- Keep hints scoped: prefer sequence_bucket granularity (0-64, 65-256, 257-1024).
- Annotate top_covariates (e.g., prefix_hash, prompt_type) to help scheduler isolation policies.
- Provide a manual test plan in the artifact when confidence_score < 0.8.

Safety and rollback patterns:
- All manifests carry a 24h automatic rollback window if no explicit promotion is run.
- Rollbacks must be recorded in the audit log with cause and mitigation notes.
- For routes with strict SLOs (enterprise-tier), the pipeline is opt-in; hints will not be applied unless the customer has agreed to canary policy.

Troubleshooting playbook (quick steps):
1) Missing artifacts: check trace-sampler logs -> hint-enricher -> artifact-store. Rehydrate by running: `rlctl hints backfill --from 2026-02-10 --to 2026-02-11 --service public-api`
2) Replay failures: check sandbox runtime container logs (service: hint-replay) and kernel-telemetry-store ACLs. Common causes: missing kernel image or incompatible kernel loader.
3) Unexpected p99 regression in canary: immediate rollback via `rlctl canary abort --manifest-id <id>` and run `rlctl hints debug --id <hint_id>` to fetch top failing traces.

Runbook: immediate incident steps for kernel hint-induced outage:
1) Page kernel-signals and scheduler-op.
2) Abort running canaries and set global kernel manifest to baseline.
3) Capture traces for affected time window, escalate to kernel engineering.
4) Open postmortem and tag hint as rejected with root-cause.

Metric catalog (important signals):
- khppp.candidate.count (counter)
- khppp.validation.pass_rate (gauge, %)
- khppp.replay.latency_ms.p95
- khppp.canary.p99_delta_pct
- khppp.artifact.queue_time_seconds.p90

Related pages:
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026

Appendix: example decision rule JSON (flattened for automation):
```
{"rule_id":"dr-2026-11","min_confidence":"0.75","p99_improve_pct":"4","max_resource_delta_pct":"3","action":"promote"}
```

Notes and future work:
- Integrate KV-cache prefix signals to make hints prefix-aware rather than only sequence-length aware.
- Add a privacy-preserving differential sampling mode for regulated customers.
- Expose an internal UI for kernel engineers to triage top_covariates and request ad-hoc replays.

References:
- artifact-store schema: s3://redwood-artifacts/khppp/schema-v1.md
- scheduler contracts: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026

Owner signoff:
- Jordan Patel (Kernel Signals)
- Priya Rao (Runtime SRE)

vivian_csm: I'll message the customer with the canary plan and expected rollback criteria. Scheduling full rollout for 9am PST tomorrow if canary passes. @marta_cs I'll capture their feedback in the enablement notes. :white_check_mark:

marta_cs: Thanks team. After canary completes let's export the eval run (automated) + manual notes. If everything looks good we'll request cost estimate for a permanent routing policy and suggest enabling caching on their production route.

divyesh_re: Canary completed at 11:05 PST. Automated eval: relative quality delta = -0.3% (within threshold). Cost sim: ~36% savings estimated. Marking canary as PASS.

marta_cs: Awesome — I'll log this in the onboarding tracker and notify renewal owner that we have an ops playbook to reduce unit cost while improving latency. Closing out here and will post a short enablement deck to the customer. :rocket:

records.title: support
records.text:
support

maria: FYI incoming from customer (ticket #5839). They report SSE stream stops abruptly ~1 token before the end, the JSON payload is left open and there's no finish_reason. Repro steps attached.
alex: Can you paste the raw stream capture? browser SDK or server-side?
maria: Customer ran curl from their backend. Here's the trimmed capture they sent (sanitized):\n\n```\nevent: response\ndata: {"choices":[{"text":"...final sentence starts but gets cut", "index":0, "logprobs":null},\n\n// connection closes here, no closing ] or }, no finish_reason\n```\n\nmaria: They also said this happened right after a billing plan change in their account, and they saw a 200 then silent EOF on the TCP socket.
tony: Hm. Two immediate hypotheses: 1) auth/billing state change triggered a proxy to reset the connection, 2) client reconnect resume header mismatch left an open kvcache state so server didn't emit final flusher. Can you confirm if they were doing resume (client provided resume headers)?
maria: Customer says they were NOT intentionally resuming — just a single long-stream generation. Token was rotated ~30s before the request (they use short-lived tokens).
alex: Ok. Please ask customer to re-run with this exact curl to collect raw bytes and Response headers (we need to see any intermediate 1xx/302/401):\n\n```bash\ncurl -v -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \\\n  -o - https://api.redwood-inference.example/v1/streams/generate\n```\n\nalex: When they run, ask them to pipe output into a file and attach it (binary-safe). Also grab tcpdump/pcap if possible around the time.
maria: I've asked the customer for the raw file and pcap. They provided these hints:\n- socket closed client-side, no HTTP error code seen in app logs\n- server logs show request accepted and tokens consumed, but no explicit close event on the runtime side\n- they saw a spike in latency ~120s before the closure\n\ntony: Could be a proxy idle/billing reassign job (our cloud partner sometimes rebinds resources during plan swaps). Those jobs sometimes issue a TCP FIN without propagating a final SSE event. Engineering should check whether the runtime emits an explicit final object (finish_reason) before socket close, and whether we flush the trailing sentinel synchronously on plan-change hooks.
alex: I'll add an ingest-bot trace to the thread. @ingest-bot can you pull the runtime trace for request id the customer sent? (we got their request-id header in logs: r-9a7c3b)
ingest-bot: Collected traces for r-9a7c3b: request accepted -> batching -> dispatched to model shard -> token emission started -> last emitted token at t+18s -> NO final flusher invocation logged -> connection closed at t+19s (TCP FIN) -> no finish_reason event recorded.

alex: That lines up with the "final flusher not called" theory. Next steps:
1) SRE: check if any proxy (ingress) recorded a close reason or RST around t+19s. Look for HTTP/2 RST or 499 from nginx equivalent.
2) Runtime: add defensive flush on connection termination path to emit a minimal final object if possible (e.g., {"finish_reason": "connection_closed", "partial": true}).
3) DevEx: advise customers to enable keepalive and to capture raw SSE output on their side to avoid client-level truncation masking.
maria: Customer asked if this is a billing-related outage. Can we confirm whether billing changes trigger mid-request terminate? We should avoid saying yes/no until SRE confirms.
alex: Agreed. I'm triaging with SRE now. Also ask the customer to try one quick repro: run the same long prompt but include header `X-No-Plan-Swap: true` (we'll honor as a debug-only bypass for control plane jobs) so we can see if stream survives the windows around plan-change. If they can't, ask them to repro during an off-peak window and attach pcap.
tony: Also request their SDK version and whether any intermediate API gateway (CloudFront/CF) is present. Some gateways buffer and then drop trailing bytes on backend handoffs.
maria: Customer returned a raw file — there's an extra trailing comma just before the connection cut in one sample. I'll upload to the ticket.
alex: Trailing comma suggests server serialized an array but didn't close it. Could be our serializer crashed after emitting comma, or the process was killed by the orchestration agent during a rebind. SRE: check host-level OOM/eviction events around that timestamp.
mar ia: (typo) oops meant maria :eyes: the customer is running node 18 SDK with built-in reconnect. They reported the reconnect attempted and then created a second session which got a full response. So it's intermittent but reproducible when plan changes happen.
alex: Great actionable items. I'll file an internal incident note and assign to eng-runtime and eng-sre. Please keep ticket #5839 updated with raw files and pcap. Until we have fix, recommend customers use shorter streams or explicit final sentinel in the payload and client-side JSON repair (defensive parsing) as a workaround.
maria: Will do. Customer appreciated the quick triage. Closing loop when SRE/Runtime has root cause.

records.title: eng-runtime
records.text:
eng-runtime

anya: Quick check-in — after the dma-buf export/import path landed I hit a divergence where imported buffers sometimes show stale page refcounts when we tear down pinned-host-backing. Repro: run a tenant stress test that flips between export/import and local host-pinned reuse.

sam: ugh, seen similar. is this the one where the importer doesn't call the release callback in the fastpath?

anya: maybe. I captured a minimal trace:
```
trace: tenantA -> export(fd) -> import(fd) -> mmap -> munmap -> importer never calls dma_buf_put() in the async detach path
```

jorge: can you paste the diff of the new export path? my guess is ordering: we do an attach, then we hand a raw page pointer to the allocator, but the allocator's free path assumes it owns the pin and calls dma_buf_detach first. race on detach vs exporter unref could leave pages resident with >0 refcnt but inaccessible.

anya: attaching the logs: I see attach, mmap, allocator_free, dma_buf_detach, then exporter_put. but sometimes exporter_put arrives before the allocator_free completes due to work-queue reordering.

ellie: that sounds like a visibility/order problem across our worker threads. we probably need an explicit ownership transfer handshake instead of relying on refcounts alone. refcounts are racy across async teardown ordering.

sam: idea: introduce an allocator flag ALLOC_DMABUF_EXPLICIT_HANDOFF. when set, allocator_free will queue an ownership-release task and wait for a completion event (or mark transient state) before issuing dma_buf_detach. exporter_put must observe that state and call a complement API to finalize. keeps ordering deterministic.

jorge: i like the explicit handoff notion but be careful about blocking in free on hot paths. need a nonblocking protocol: state machine transitions (ACTIVE -> HANDOFF_PENDING -> RELEASED) and a fastpath that can steal ownership if the other side is in HANDOFF_PENDING for >X ms.

anya: agreed. how about: allocator_free sets HANDOFF_PENDING and emits an async completion token (opaque 64-bit). exporter_put must call handoff_complete(token) or the token times out and a compensating reclaim path runs. we can emit metrics: dma_handoff_wait_ms, handoff_timeouts, stolen_handoffs.

ellie: also need to address memory visibility: after handoff_complete we must ensure any writes to page metadata are published. add an smp_wmb() equivalent or use atomic ops for the state transition. otherwise importer may see RELEASING page metadata stale.

sam: good call. use atomic_exchange to move state, and pair with acquire/release semantics on the token handshake. that keeps kernel vs user-space ordering sane.

jorge: another angle: ensure dma-buf export path returns a signed export cookie that encodes the allocator version and a small nonce. importer validates cookie against current allocator ABI (so forward/backwards mismatches fail early).

anya: that will help debugging. I also want a debug-build option to assert that no exported fd is closed while HANDOFF_PENDING counters > 0. panic in dev.

ellie: API surface proposal (sketch):
- dma_buf_export_with_handoff(fd, flags) -> {cookie, token}
- allocator_handoff_claim(token) -> ok|retry
- allocator_handoff_complete(token) -> finalizes detach
- allocator_handoff_force(token) -> admin path to steal after timeout

sam: keep names short. also we need to document invariants: who may call handoff_claim (only importer or allocator?), whether token is single-use, and what happens on process crash. add kernel-level leak detector to scan HANDOFF_PENDING tokens older than 5m and emit a metric and optional reclamation.

anya: process-crash recovery is critical: if importer dies after import but before handoff_complete, pages could be pinned forever. force reclaim via netlink admin or evictor. evictor-bot: note: scheduling reclaim task for orphaned handoffs.

evictor-bot: auto-note: enqueued reclaim job for orphaned-handoff-scanner every 1h. telemetry labels: orphaned_handoffs, orphaned_handoff_age_max_ms.

jorge: minor perf thought: for hot small allocations used by model KV caches, the extra handshake may add latency. we should make ALLOC_DMABUF_HOT_ALLOWED that keeps the old refcounted fastpath but enables periodic validator that flips any leaking pins to handed-off after a threshold. i.e., hybrid mode.

ellie: test plan:
- unit tests for state transitions + token lifecycle
- end-to-end stress that toggles export/import under heavy mem churn
- fuzz: random delay between exporter_put and allocator_free
- integration: verify no pinned pages survive tenant shutdown (leak detector)

anya: ok. next steps: I'll open an RFC PR with the state-machine diagram, token encoding, and proposed kernel APIs. sam, can you prototype the user-space importer changes (handshake calls)? jorge, can you draft the evictor reclamation flow and metrics? ellie, please list memory visibility asserts and kernel atomic ordering notes for the RFC.

sam: on it. i'll add a small shim in the importer library and run the tenant stress harness.

jorge: will sketch the evictor reclamation with backoff and admin override.

ellie: I'll write the ordering notes and a checklist for kernel audits. also add pointer to a small litmus test we can run under tsan/lockdep.

anya: thanks all :thumbsup: let's aim to have the RFC PR up by EOD Friday so we can iterate before next week's sprint.

sam: quick question — do we want to expose handoff telemetry per-tenant or per-device? per-tenant probably better for billing and debugging.

anya: per-tenant + per-device labels. done.

ellie: one more: log format for reclaim events should include token, age_ms, originating_pid, tenant_id, and allocator_gen so postmortems are easier.

anya: noted. will include examples in the RFC.

jorge: ping me once the PR exists and i'll run the fuzz harness.

anya: will do. thanks everyone.

records.title: marketing
records.text:
marketing

jo_marketing: @leo_runtime marketing needs a concise benchmark focused on sudden single-shot spikes for the launch blog. Can eng/runtime run a reproducible calibration and hand over artifacts + a one-slide summary by Monday noon?

leo_runtime: Sure. Define the spike shape, model variants, and what constitutes 'artifact' for you. Also region?

jo_marketing: Spike shape: idle 45m, then a 90s spike ramping to peak concurrency 48, then idle. Also include a repeatable micro-burst test: ten 15s spikes spaced 2m apart. Models: flagship float32, int8 quant, distilled small. Region: us-west1 primary, single sanity in eu-west1.

devan_analytics: Include tokenization.csv, 30 paired outputs per bucket for quality checks, and raw timing traces (request and per-token). We'll compute percentiles.

anya_infra: We can attach run traces; enabling GPU telemetry adds ~8% overhead. Skip unless needed for root-cause.

leo_runtime: Plan: greedy decode for latency, concurrency sweep [1,8,24,48], token buckets small/med/large (1-16, 40-120, 400-800) with 50/35/15 split, seed=777 for determinism. Measure 3m steady-state after 20s ramp for each point. KV cache: persist during bursts, flush after idle. Batching: off and micro-batching (10ms window).

jo_marketing: Good. Artifacts: run-config.json, sample-payloads.jsonl (3 per bucket), tokenization.csv, outputs_paired.tar.gz, csv summaries with P50/P95/P99, throughput curves, and a 1-slide markdown. Also include cost-per-1M-tokens calc using hosted rate X and dedicated estimate Y.

leo_runtime: We'll lock tokenizer to v2-bytepair and include tokenizer_version in metadata. Artifact prefix: s3://redwood-bench/launch/3141592653/{variant}/{run-id}/. ETA: minimal smoke pack ~5h, full calibrated sweep ~26h.

runtime-bot: bench-run-3141592670 queued by leo_runtime  variants: float32|quant|distilled; spike: single-90s|micro-repeat; concurrency: [1,8,24,48]; batching: off|micro; region: us-west1.

records.title: Post-demo: Time-to-first-token targets & streaming cadence (Atlas Labs)
records.text:
Post-demo: Time-to-first-token targets & streaming cadence (Atlas Labs)

From: Michael Grant <michael@redwood.com>
To: Priya Sharma <priya@atlaslabs.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 16 May 2026 14:08:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo: Time-to-first-token targets & streaming cadence (Atlas Labs)

Hi Priya — thanks for the time today. Quick recap from our call and the asks we heard so we have a clean handoff to engineering: 

- Primary perf goal: Time-to-first-token (TTFT) for short prompts (1–20 tokens) <= 250 ms P50, <= 450 ms P95 under steady-state.
- Burst/scale: baseline concurrency 60 req/s for web clients, ability to sustain short bursts to 180 req/s for <2 minutes.
- Streaming: web clients prefer SSE; mobile app will likely use WebSocket as a fallback. We should support both and auto-fallback if SSE handshake fails.
- Chunk cadence: target chunk emission every 200–300 ms for typical responses, with a maximum chunk size of ~256 tokens to avoid large blocking latencies.
- Acceptance telemetry: per-token latency, P50/P95/P99 of first byte and first token, tracing id in headers, and token counts in response.

I've attached Atlas' sample prompt set and our initial TTFT probe plan. Next steps we proposed on the call:
1) Tech spike to validate SSE handshake and chunk cadence under representative load (owner: Karthik).
2) Pilot environment: dedicated pilot capacity for 48 hours with your sample prompts and synthetic concurrency to validate SLOs.
3) Telemetry contract: agree on the minimal telemetry fields and sample rates (we suggested 1% full trace + 10% condensed).

Can you confirm these priorities and give us the name/email of the engineer who will join the spike? Also let us know if the TTFT targets above are firm or negotiable — we can tune tradeoffs (quantization, batching) once we know the strict target.

Thanks — Michael
Michael Grant
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
michael@redwood.com

---

From: Priya Sharma <priya@atlaslabs.com>
To: Michael Grant <michael@redwood.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 17 May 2026 09:14:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-demo: Time-to-first-token targets & streaming cadence (Atlas Labs)

Hi Michael — thanks for the clear recap. Confirming priorities and adding a couple clarifications from our side: 

- TTFT target: we need <= 250 ms P50 for short prompts and <= 500 ms P95 for production traffic. P99 is less critical for now but should be tracked.
- Concurrency: baseline 60 req/s (global), but our peak traffic windows can spike to 180 req/s for ~90–120s. We want graceful degradation (e.g., degrade chunk cadence before dropping requests).
- Streaming modes: web clients should use SSE. Mobile SDK will default to WebSocket; fallback to non-streaming if connection is flaky.
- Chunk cadence goal: 200 ms ideal, acceptable range 150–350 ms depending on network and model load. We care more about consistent cadence than absolute minimum latency for later tokens.

We're happy to provide an internal engineer for the spike — please loop in Sahil (sahil@atlaslabs.com). For the pilot, we can spin up a staging API key and share a short-lived test token.

A couple asks from our infra/security team:
- We need a list of what telemetry is captured and whether PII appears in traces (we'll redact as needed).
- Does Redwood support IP allowlisting for the pilot endpoints?

I'll confirm Sahil's availability for a spike on Tuesday/Wednesday next week.

Best,
Priya
Head of Product, Atlas Labs
priya@atlaslabs.com

---

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>
To: Priya Sharma <priya@atlaslabs.com>, Michael Grant <michael@redwood.com>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 18 May 2026 07:45:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-demo: Time-to-first-token targets & streaming cadence (Atlas Labs)

Thanks — good notes. Technical thoughts / feasibility and proposed test plan: 

1) Feasibility: the targets (<=250ms P50, <=500ms P95) are achievable with a few levers: warm resident workers, KV prefix caching for repeated prompts, and modest quantization (int8) on the model we propose. Batching helps throughput but increases TTFT; we'll avoid batch delays for the first token by prioritizing fast path execution for single-request emits.

2) Streaming implementation: Redwood supports SSE and WebSocket simultaneously. We'll prefer SSE for browser clients (smaller handshake) and route mobile-origin traffic to WS. We already have auto-fallback policies that detect handshake failure and fall back to polling/non-streaming if streaming can't be established.

3) Chunk cadence: we can target 200–250 ms cadence on average by tuning the emitter cadence and limiting chunk token size to ~64 tokens typical (~256 hard max). We'll instrument per-emit timestamps to measure cadence drift.

4) Concurrency and burst: for pilot, propose a 4x-GPU dedicated pool (NVIDIA A10G or equivalent) with autoscale headroom. With the above config we can hit 60 steady req/s with 180 short bursts for the 2-minute window. We'll validate with load tests.

5) Acceptance criteria (suggested): run 48-hour pilot, run templated workload from atlas-sample-prompt-set.csv with realistic jitter: if TTFT P50 <= 250ms and P95 <= 500ms for >95% of test windows and chunk cadence median within 200–300ms, consider acceptance. We will surface per-request traces and aggregate histograms.

6) Security/ops: we support IP allowlisting for pilot endpoints and can redact PII in traces if you mark sample prompts. We'll send a short telemetry schema doc prior to the spike.

Action items: 
- Karthik to own the tech spike (this week).
- Priya to provide Sahil's contact and confirm staging token.
- Michael to schedule the spike kickoff and provide the probe harness link.

I'll prepare a short test harness (link below) and a runbook for the pilot.

Runbook (draft): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ExampleTTFTProbe
Test harness: https://internal-tools.redwood.com/ttft-harness/DL-8792

--
Karthik Iyer
Senior Engineer, Serving Runtime
karthik@redwood.com

---

From: Michael Grant <michael@redwood.com>
To: Priya Sharma <priya@atlaslabs.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 18 May 2026 09:22:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-demo: Time-to-first-token targets & streaming cadence (Atlas Labs)

Perfect — summary and next steps (short):
- Tech spike: Karthik leads; target window Tue/Wed (please confirm Sahil availability).
- Pilot: 48-hour dedicated pool run once spike validates handshake/cadence.
- Security: we'll send telemetry schema and IP allowlist instructions; Neha will own that thread.
- Deliverables before spike: Atlas to share staging token + prompt set (received), Redwood to share probe runbook and sample dashboards.

I'll schedule a 30-min kickoff and loop Sahil in when you confirm — proposed: Tue 10am PT. If that works, I'll send the calendar invite and attach the preliminary probe plan (ttft-probe-plan.pdf).

Thanks all — Michael
Michael Grant
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

records.title: eng-runtime
records.text:
eng-runtime

samir: FYI I've got a perf regression after switching the default KV layout to interleaved for paging experiments. Short-context workloads (seq=64/128) are slower.

leah: ugh. numbers?

samir: microbench (fused_flash path):
```
# before (separate-kv): mean token latency = 3.2 ms
# after  (interleaved-kv): mean token latency = 3.6 ms  <-- ~12.5% worse
# throughput (seq=128,batch=8): 310 tok/s -> 273 tok/s
```
nvprof snapshot shows increased uncoalesced loads + L1/TEX miss up ~18%.

anya: is this only for fp16 or bf16 too?

samir: repro with fp16 and bf16: fp16 shows the regression, bf16 is noisier but also worse in several runs. float32 (debug) not measurable due to compute-bound dominance.

max: can you paste the perf command you used?

samir: perf command and env:
```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python perf/bench.py --model llama-13b \
  --dtype=float16 --kv-layout=interleaved --seq-len=128 --batch-size=8 --mode=generate
```
also profiler: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt -o /tmp/nsys_interleaved`

ci-bot: perf-run finished: job 2024-03-11_11:05 (link: https://ci.internal/perf/1856789012) :white_check_mark:

leah: my quick hypothesis: interleaved layout changed stride/alignment so the fused FlashAttention kernel's vector loads are no longer 128-byte aligned -> warp fragmentation -> higher L2 and more global loads. Could also expose a bug in the strided index math for page boundaries.

anya: any sign of TLB misses or page-split counters?

samir: yes nvprof shows ctx: pt_miss and TLB miss counters spiked when crossing 64KB page boundaries in the interleaved layout. Also saw more `ld.global.ca` and fewer `ld.shared` coalesced operations in the kernel.

max: Does the fused kernel assume contiguous per-head KV layout? The interleaved layout packs heads across pages which can produce non-unit strides for head dim accesses.

leah: correct — fused kernels expect head-major contiguous K/V per beam to use vector loads. If stride != 16 or misaligned to 128 bytes they fall back to scalar codepaths or produce unaligned memaccesses.

samir: quick patch idea: add alignment pad to interleaved allocation to 128 bytes and ensure head_stride % 16 == 0, then re-run. If that fixes perf we still need a kernel-selector guard.

anya: also try forcing `--kv-layout=interleaved-chunked` where we chunk per-page so strides stay small (e.g., chunk size = 64). Might keep paging benefits while preserving contiguous small strides for kernels.

samir: ran two experiments:
```
1) interleaved + 128B pad -> token latency: 3.25 ms (almost back to baseline)
2) interleaved-chunked (chunk=64) -> token latency: 3.28 ms
```
both reduce L2 / TLB anomalies in profiler traces.

max: great. So the underlying issue is alignment/stride semantics, not the paging idea itself.

leah: action items:
- (samir) add allocator path that returns 128-byte aligned KV buffer for interleaved layout and add unit microbench.
- (anya) update kernel selector heuristic: prefer fused_flash when (dtype==fp16) AND (head_stride_bytes % 128 == 0) AND (seq_len <= 1024?) — otherwise pick paged/fallback kernel.
- (max) add diagnostic counters exposed to Console: per-request chosen-kernel, head_stride_bytes, alignment_pad_bytes, page-splits.

anya: one more nuance: bf16 path currently performs a cast -> fp16 on some devices in the runtime; ensure the cast doesn't re-pack into an unaligned buffer. We saw a case where cast created a temporary with natural alignment 16B, not 128B.

samir: noted. I'll also add an assert in debug builds when we pick fused_flash: check (uintptr_t(buffer) % 128 == 0) and head_stride alignment. That will catch CI regressions.

leah: do we want a fast rollback plan for Dedicated clusters? If this selector misfires we could regress many customers.

max: rollback = set default KV layout to separate-kv for all prod pools via runtime flag and bump rollout to canary until selector is in. Also add perf Canary: seq lenses 32/64/128 synthetic traffic.

anya: I'll prototype selector diff and post a PR with tests that simulate misaligned buffers.

samir: I'll push the allocator change and run the end-to-end perf suite. If green I'll attach nsys flame and updated numbers to the PR.

leah: thanks. small ask: include a microbench that toggles batch sizes/batching heuristics because some batching heuristics amplify the regression (small batch + many short sequences hit the slow path more).

samir: good call — adding batch sweep (1,2,4,8,16) to the bench.

ci-bot: deploy plan checklist added to perf ticket: https://issues.internal/PROD-6421 :white_check_mark:

max: ok. keep updates here. If someone spots a regression on CI tag me. :+1:

samir: will follow up with PR link and nsys captures in ~2 hours.

records.title: customer-success

records.title: SLO runbook & cost levers — Nimbus Health discovery follow-up
records.text:
SLO runbook & cost levers — Nimbus Health discovery follow-up

["From: Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwood.ai>
To: Marian Lopez <marian.lopez@nimbushealth.com>, CloudOps Team <ops@nimbushealth.com>
Cc: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.ai>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 22 Oct 2026 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: SLO runbook & cost levers — Nimbus Health discovery follow-up

Hi Marian / CloudOps,

Thanks again for taking time today — good conversation. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can narrow pilot scope: 

Summary of your SLO targets (call notes):
- Latency: p95 <= 250ms for single-turn clinical-assist prompts (~512 tokens); p50 <= 120ms.
- Throughput: sustained 250 reqs/min during business hours, spiky bursts to 800 reqs/min for campaign windows.
- Concurrency: typical concurrent streams 8–12, peak concurrency target 36.
- Streaming: token-level streaming required for the assistant UI (low startup latency).

Primary constraints: PHI-sensitive data (on-prem VPC first), and tight latency targets for the in-clinic assistant.

Immediate asks / proposed next steps:
1) We'll run a focused perf qualification: 72-hour pilot in your staging VPC to exercise 3 representative prompts (clinical summary, triage, coding assist).
2) Action: please share a short suite of 6–10 prompt examples and the expected token lengths (or we can use the samples you uploaded).
3) We will provide a runbook with cost/perf levers and an expected cost range (baseline + optimized).
4) Tentative owners: Redwood SE (Sean) will run the load tests; Vivek will coordinate quantization profiles and model variants; Ava will own the commercial proposal.

Attachment: I attached an initial SLO matrix with assumptions we discussed. [attachment: slo_matrix.csv (CSV, 12KB)]

A few initial notes on levers so you have context before our qualification run:
- Continuous batching: valuable at steady throughput to reduce per-token overhead, but must be tuned carefully for streaming to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- KV/prefix caching: for episodic prompts (patient context), caching will reduce model work for repeated prefixes and improve tail latency.
- Quantization profiles: 4-bit q4_0 and mixed-precision for some model families can cut inference compute ~2–3x with modest quality loss; we’ll evaluate on your prompts.
- Model variants: propose evaluating a latency-optimized distilled variant for in-clinic fast-path and a higher-quality base variant for overnight batch jobs.

Proposed dates: pilot kickoff on Mon 2026-10-26; load window Wed/Thu; results and cost runbook by Fri 2026-10-30.

Please reply with prompt samples and any mandatory security checklist items we should know about before VPC access.

Thanks,
Ava Chen
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
ava.chen@redwood.ai | (415) 555-0142

", 'From: Marian Lopez <marian.lopez@nimbushealth.com>
To: Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwood.ai>
Cc: CloudOps Team <ops@nimbushealth.com>, Procurement <procurement@nimbushealth.com>
Date: Fri, 22 Oct 2026 17:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SLO runbook & cost levers — Nimbus Health discovery follow-up

Thanks, Ava — this is helpful. A couple clarifications from CloudOps: 

- Streaming requirement: we need first-byte streaming within 80–120ms for the “patient readout” flow; if batching would push that above 120ms we can accept a hybrid where critical prompts go to the latency-optimized model with minimal batching.
- Concurrency: the 36 peak is for clinic peak hours across 4 regions; we can allocate traffic regionally but need consistent SLOs.
- Compliance: VPC peering is preferred; we cannot move PHI out of our subnet. We’ll provide a short allowlist and an infra contact to coordinate.

Prompt samples: I uploaded 8 anonymized prompts to the shared drive link you provided (they’re short — 40–300 tokens).

Procurement note: we’ll need a one-page description of the pilot scope and success criteria to raise the staging change ticket. Can you send that?

—Marian
Director, Clinical Products | Nimbus Health
marian.lopez@nimbushealth.com

', "From: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.ai>
To: Marian Lopez <marian.lopez@nimbushealth.com>, Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwood.ai>
Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 26 Oct 2026 09:16:00 -0700
Subject: RE: SLO runbook & cost levers — Nimbus Health discovery follow-up

Marian — quick technical recap and a first-pass cost/latency sketch based on the 8 prompts you dropped. Details in the attached perf profile PDF. [attachment: redwood_perf_profile.pdf (PDF, 420KB)]

Key assumptions used for estimates:
- Model family: LlamaX-13B equivalent; baseline float16, opt-quant q4_0 and a distilled 7B fast variant for latency path.
- Sequence: avg request 512 tokens; streaming enabled for first 64 tokens to hit interactive feel.
- HW: A100-class for baseline; T4 for cheapest quantized path in Dedicated pockets.

Preliminary numbers (ballpark):
- Baseline (no quant): p95 ~ 300ms per prompt on A100 at 1 concurrent stream; cost ~= $0.010 per prompt.
- Quantized + batching (q4_0, continuous batching tuned): p95 ~ 180–230ms; cost ~= $0.004–$0.006 per prompt.
- Distilled 7B variant (latency path): p95 ~ 90–130ms; cost ~= $0.002–$0.003 per prompt.

Trade-offs and recommended runbook steps: 
1) Hybrid routing: route critical UI prompts to the distilled 7B under an A/B policy; route other requests to quantized 13B with prefix caching. This hits the 80–120ms streaming requirement for first-byte while keeping quality high for complex cases.
2) Streaming + batching config: use micro-batches with max_hold_ms = 12 and token-based batching threshold to avoid adding >40ms headroom to first-byte. We'll test these in the pilot.
3) KV/prefix caching: results show up to 40% token reduction for repeated patient-context prompts on our sample — big win for tail latency.
4) Autoscaling buffers: reserve burst slots (Dedicated capacity) to handle 3x baseline peaks; Redwood Dedicated can pre-warm pools for clinical hours.

Open items we need from Nimbus:
- Representative latency probe (a single TCP ping + 1 warm request) from your clinic VM to our staging endpoint.
- Confirmation which 2 prompts must always go to the latency path vs. candidate pool.

I’ll schedule the first load window for Wed 10/28 02:00–06:00 PT unless you prefer a different window.

Thanks,
Sean Gallagher
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
sean.gallagher@redwood.ai

", 'From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.ai>
To: Marian Lopez <marian.lopez@nimbushealth.com>, Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwood.ai>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 09:28:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SLO runbook & cost levers — Nimbus Health discovery follow-up

Appreciate the clear plan. Marian — once you confirm the 2 critical prompts and the allowlist items, we’ll cut a short pilot statement of work (SOW) outlining success criteria: p95 <= 250ms for targeted prompts, sustained 250 reqs/min, successful VPC peering and audit log access.

Commercial next steps:
- Ava: please draft the one-page pilot scope + expected cost band and attach DocuSign for a pilot acceptance form.
- Procurement: we can offer a 30-day pilot credit to speed approval; terms TBD after pilot.

Marian — happy to join the kickoff call if helpful.

Cheers,
Lauren Bishop
Head of Sales Operations | Redwood Inference
lauren.bishop@redwood.ai

records.text:
eng-runtime

Maria G.: FYI, I'm prototyping headroom signaling + preemptive shuffle for interactive tenants to tame p99 spikes. want quick feedback on correctness/tradeoffs
Sam L.: Nice. can you sketch the flow? is this in the online scheduler or a separate controller?
Maria G.: In the online scheduler. idea: each tenant has a dynamic headroom credit. when queue depth grows, scheduler signals 'need-headroom'. idle lanes can preemptively pull one op from low-priority queues (swap) into a spare GPU slot before the backpressure fully fires. aim: avoid long-lived tail due to cold contention.
Kevin H.: Two immediate tradeoffs: a) preemption increases complexity (KV cache churn), b) swapping reduces throughput if done aggressively. how do you measure/cap churn?
Maria G.: Good Q. plan: limit swaps per-second per-device, and only swap if estimated improvement > swap_cost. estimate swap_cost ~ kv_miss_penalty + context_switch_ms. keep a max_swap_rate and a cooldown per-tenant.
Anika R.: We should also consider instability: headroom oscillation can cause thrashing. add a dampening factor and hysteresis. metrics: headroom_allocations, swap_count, queue_age_histogram, p99_latency.
Priya V.: Also worry about fairness across bursty tenants. If we allow preemptive shuffles, rich tenants might hog spare slots. need a weight floor or token bucket per-tenant.
Sam L.: Any config prototype?
Maria G.: quick draft:
```yaml
scheduler:
  headroom:
    initial: 2
    max: 8
    alpha: 0.2  # dampening
    max_swap_rate: 5/s
  swap:
    min_benefit_ms: 20
    cooldown_ms: 500
    per_device_limit: 10
```
Kevin H.: Looks reasonable. I'd add `kv_warmth_threshold` to avoid swapping in ops that will miss cache. and `fallback_policy: 'defer' | 'preempt'` to control rollback.
Maria G.: Agree. also thinking about a 'soft-reservation' window: small reserved slots per-tenant that cannot be stolen below X to guarantee progress.
Anika R.: How about instrumentation? we need time-series and lightweight traces. Events: headroom_signal({tenant, delta}), swap_decision({device, from_tenant, to_tenant, reason}), swap_outcome({latency_delta}).
Priya V.: Simulation request: can someone run a 4-tenant mixed workload with bursty arrivals and KV hit/miss model? we need p50/p95/p99 and throughput across policies.
Sam L.: I can run a quick sim later today. quick question: how do we compute expected benefit? analytic or learned?
Maria G.: Start analytic: benefit ~= queued_wait_ms - expected_swap_penalty. later we can train a lightweight model with historical traces.
deploy-bot: deploy scheduled: scheduler/headroom-experiment -> canary at 2 nodes (by Maria G.) :rocket:
