records.title: Walled node hardening intake - OmniHealth Systems
records.text:
Walled node hardening intake - OmniHealth Systems

summary:
Intro discovery to map requirements for a strictly walled (no egress) private deployment. Customer has existing rack-level GPU assets, strict quarterly patch windows, and signed firmware policy. Key topics: offline update process, signed bundles, KMS/HSM constraints, model-size/quantization tradeoffs for VRAM-limited cards, and acceptance testing/benchmarking. Agreed next steps: share security pack, run onsite hardware audit, and schedule a 2-week pilot with a 2-node cluster in their lab environment.

transcript:
Meeting header
09:22 PST — 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Ramos (CTO, OmniHealth), Jenna Holt (Head InfoSec), Marcus Li (Infra Lead), Samir Bhatt (Regulatory)

Summary: quick intro and then deep into offline update mechanics, HW mapping, and acceptance tests.

00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, Alex from Redwood - thanks for carving out time. we'll keep this focused, want to understand the walled environment constraints.
00:18 Dr. Elena: Hi, thanks. We run patient-facing inference in our own colo and cannot allow outbound calls to public control planes. basically airwalled.
00:28 Jenna: Right, and compliance needs signed updates only. no USB, no manual installs unless checksums signed by our HSM.
00:40 Priya: Okay, that's helpful. Our Redwood Private supports a private control plane pattern; there are offline bundle workflows where we produce signed update artifacts you can verify with your KMS. How are you currently doing signed firmware or software rollouts?
01:02 Marcus: Today we use vendor-signed firmware and an internal tool that validates signatures against our HSM. patch windows are quarterly; emergency patches are very gated. Also some of our older racks have A10s and older Ampere 80GB cards but a few nodes are 32GB A100s only.
01:27 Alex: Good — so we need to consider models and memory footprint. for nodes with 32GB VRAM we might want int8 quant or smaller model variants. Priya, can you walk through the offline bundle process?
01:40 Priya: Sure. High level: we build a deploy bundle that contains the runtime, model artifacts (optional delta for model weights), and orchestration metadata. the bundle can be signed by Redwood and then re-signed or re-keyed by your HSM for final acceptance. Bundle verification runs at install time and the node refuses to apply anything not signed by your key.
02:05 Jenna: That fits our policy. question: does bundle verification require any outbound key check? we can't allow any egress.
02:14 Priya: No — verification is local. the node has a verification agent that validates the signature chain and checks certificate revocation lists that you can provide as part of the offline package. we also support a policy where you mlock the key material into an HSM and only import transient verification keys for the upgrade window.
02:35 Samir: And for audit — do you provide install-time provenance logs? we need tamper-evident records for regulators.
02:42 Priya: yes, we emit audit logs that can be written to an append-only store. we can format them to meet your retention window and include the signed bundle hash, installer identity, and step-by-step exit codes. If you prefer, we can route logs to an on-prem SIEM via a push during your maintenance window.
03:03 Dr. Elena: On the model side, we have two main workloads: clinical summarization (batch, large contexts) and real-time triage (low-latency, single-request). Triage needs <150ms p99 ideally but we know tradeoffs.
03:20 Alex: For p99 in a walled setup you'll likely choose Dedicated-like reserved capacity but private. With limited VRAM older cards, batching and quantization will be the main levers. Priya — thoughts on caching?
03:33 Priya: We have prefix/KV caching and continuous batching in the runtime. On small cards, we recommend offloading KV cache to NVMe-backed local cache or use model sharding so the hot KV is resident. also reduce context window if possible for triage.
03:50 Marcus: NVMe cache is OK. we can't do model sharding across nodes due to our network isolation?
03:58 Priya: Node-local sharding is possible; cross-node inference requires network and we avoid that for airgapped. we'll size models per node.
04:10 Jenna: What about key management? our policy mandates HSM for any master keys and we cannot have Redwood hold keys.
04:17 Alex: That's supported. Redwood Private can be configured to use customer-managed KMS/HSM; only signed tokens are used by the runtime and we never persist plaintext keys in our control plane. In fully offline cases the control plane runs behind your VPC or on a physically separated manager that you operate.
04:36 Samir: Any certification matrix? we need to know what parts of your stack are SOC2 and what components are simply engineering controls.
04:45 Alex: We'll provide a security pack with SOC2 Type II, ISO artifacts, pen test summaries, and a private deployment checklist that indicates which responsibilities remain with OmniHealth vs Redwood.
04:58 Marcus: Thermal and power are concerns. Some of our racks are older; can you advise on operational overhead for continuous inference?
05:07 Priya: We'll bring a sizing guide. For steady low-latency triage at p99 150ms, with 32GB cards you might only manage smaller models like 7B quantized. For large-context summarization we recommend dedicated 80GB nodes or burst policies to a different cluster. If 80GB aren't available, we can run summarization as batch jobs overnight.
05:29 Dr. Elena: Sounds pragmatic. What about rollback? if a bundle causes regressions we need a fast path to revert.
05:37 Priya: Bundles are versioned and we keep the previous install on node until a successful health-check window completes. rollback is a local operation that doesn't require egress; the orchestration can be triggered by a local operator or via Redwood's private control plane if you enable it.
05:57 Jenna: For acceptance test, what metrics do you recommend we capture during pilot?
06:02 Priya: Latency p50/p95/p99, token cost, model output tokenization diffs vs baseline, memory pressure, and cold-start times. We'll provide the test harness to replay a canonical set of prompts.
06:18 Marcus: We'll need CPU/IO numbers too since NVMe caching will hit drives.
06:22 Priya: Absolutely. the harness captures IO and CPU counters.
06:27 Alex: Okay, near-term next steps: I'll send the security artifacts and network diagram template. Priya will draft the pilot plan and test harness. Marcus will share HW inventory.
06:36 Dr. Elena: Target pilot window late Feb is good. Also, can you provide rough pricing for a 2-node pilot and for ongoing support?
06:45 Alex: We'll include a pilot quote and options for annual reserved pricing if you need dedicated capacity. We'll also include a line for professional services to run the initial on-site install.
06:55 Jenna: One more item — our compliance team insists on signed firmware images for GPUs. do you coordinate firmware upgrades?
07:02 Priya: We don't push vendor firmware; we provide orchestration hooks. you retain final control and must apply vendor-signed firmware. our installer honors firmware baselines and will refuse to run if firmware deviates from approved list.
07:18 Dr. Elena: Great. that's it from us. thanks.
07:22 Alex: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invites for the lab day.
07:28 Meeting end.

Notes: transcription contains speaker turns and occasional mis-recognitions (Speaker 6 label used). Some technical terms have been simplified in transcript (e.g., K-V cash vs KV cache).

records.title: architecture
records.text:
architecture

maya: Quick thought — propose a "pilot slit-fence" rollout pattern: slice traffic by tenant, ramp inside each slice, and have an automatic hard fallback that sends a tenant back to the previous variant on either latency or error spikes. Keeps blast radius small and avoids global flapping.

ajay: sounds promising. main worry is KV cache warmup + session affinity. if we flip mid-session we could get bad tail latency because caches miss.

sam: can we do session affinity with a TTL so active sessions aren't moved during the ramp? e.g. session-affinity: 10m.

liz: also need signal smoothing. raw 1-min P95 bounce will cause churn. debounce and evaluation windows matter. i'd lean toward p95 over 5m + error rate over 5m and a 2m debounce.

nora: where do we evaluate the thresholds? router-level (fast) or central controller (global signal)? tradeoffs: router is low-latency but sees only local load; controller sees global but slower.

ajay: hybrid — router enforces immediate hard SLO (if local p95 > threshold then short-circuit) and controller reconciles aggregate metrics and does the official slice flip. router flip should be reversible quickly, controller flip persists policy.

maya: agreed. sample config sketch:
```yaml
pilot:
  slices: 128
  slice_policy: "tenant_id % slices"
  rollout:
    initial_pct: 1
    max_pct: 25
    step_sec: 900
  session_affinity_ttl_sec: 600
  fallback:
    latency_p95_ms: 300
    error_rate_pct: 1.5
    evaluation_window_sec: 300
    debounce_sec: 120
  router_guard:
    local_latency_p95_ms: 450
    local_error_rate_pct: 5.0
```


liz: nice. one more: quotas and golden traffic. we should keep a reserved pool (2-5%) that never goes to the pilot variant so we have a clean baseline to compare.

sam: yes — golden traffic helps differential signals and regression detection. also thought: if cache warmup is a problem, mark slices as "warmup-required" and only increase traffic after a successful warmup probe.

maya: warmup probe idea is good. define a probe path that exercises KV access pattern and short sequences. probe success => slice marked warm.

nora: need to handle multi-variant sessions where a single user request fans out to multiple model variants (reranking + generator). the router should tag requests so replay/trace can attribute to variants.

ajay: implementation note: avoid storing per-tenant state in router; use token in header for affinity + a small LRU for recent flips. router should be mostly stateless. controller writes target percentages to config store; routers poll.

maya: quick ops commands for emergencies: `/pilot pause <pilot-id>` to freeze, `/pilot rollback <pilot-id>` to force revert slices to previous variant, `/pilot promote <pilot-id>` to promote and drain old variant. add audit log.

deploy-bot: deployment maya/pilot-slitfence -> model-v6 started: slices=128 initial=1% :rocket:

liz: runbook note — when router-local guard trips for >3 consecutive windows, ops pager. add rate-limited alerts to avoid alert storms.

sam: test plan: unit tests for router decision logic, integration tests with fake latency/error injection, e2e with staged warmups and golden traffic checks.

maya: follow-up: i'll draft an RFC with the config shape, router vs controller responsibilities, metrics to collect (per-slice p95, error_rate, cache_miss_rate, probe_success), and a runbook. owner: maya. deadline: next Tue.

nora: +1, cc @platform for rollout automation hooks.

ajay: one more micro concern — telemetry cardinality. per-slice per-tenant metrics could explode. suggest rollup: emit per-slice aggregates and sample per-tenant traces only when anomalous.

liz: agreed. keep metrics light but keep linkable traces.

maya: ok — onboarding checklist: 1) RFC, 2) router guard PR, 3) controller reconcile PR, 4) runbook, 5) canary job. i'll ping infra and observability.

maya: thanks all — quick sync next week to finalize thresholds. :thumbsup:

Mutual action plan: performance validation & streaming TTFT (initial plan)

["From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
To: Elena Martin <elena@asterlabs.io>, Tom Wu <tom.wu@asterlabs.io>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>, Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 15:05:00 -0700
Subject: Mutual action plan: performance validation & streaming TTFT (initial plan)

Hi Elena / Tom,

Thanks again for the product demo last week — excited to move towards a performance gate as part of the MAP so your team can feel confident running live chat at scale. Attached is a concise plan (map-performance-plan.xlsx) that outlines the test phases, acceptance criteria, and proposed close timeline. High level: 

- Kickoff: 09/16 — align infra, signal test windows
- Eval sprint: 09/17-09/18 — run streaming TTFT and concurrency sweeps (warm + cold cache)
- Canary & rollout: 09/20-09/24 — 10% canary, monitor regressions, then ramp
- Target close: 10/05 (final sign-off + SOW)

Acceptance asks (proposed):
- TTFT (time-to-first-token) streaming p95 <= 500ms, p99 <= 900ms under expected concurrency profile
- Sustained throughput: 4–6k tokens/sec aggregate for your expected peak concurrency pattern
- No functional regressions on the sample prompt set (we'll run your 120 prompt eval set)

We'll run tests from a Redwood dedicated cluster (us-west-2, A100-40GB). Test harness will be the same harness we used in the demo, with both cold-start and warm-KV cache passes — we'll provide raw traces and packet-level timings. Please confirm the acceptance targets above or flag any changes before EOD 09/15 so we can lock the MAP and schedule runs.

Attachments: map-performance-plan.xlsx (spreadsheet), test-harness-spec.md (link in map)

Best,
Jordan Blake
Account Executive — Redwood Inference
(jordan_blake@redwood.com)

", "From: Elena Martin <elena@asterlabs.io>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
Cc: Tom Wu <tom.wu@asterlabs.io>
Date: Wed, 15 Sep 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Mutual action plan: performance validation & streaming TTFT (initial plan)

Jordan — thanks for the clear plan and timeline. A couple clarifications from our side before you run the eval: 

1) Our primary concern is tail TTFT for newly opened chats under load. We are hoping p99 stays under ~1s for 30 concurrent agents (each agent ~1 chat stream). If you can show both p95 and p99 with cold-start and warm cache, that'll be ideal.
2) For throughput, our peak expected burst is roughly 3k tokens/sec sustained for ~5 minutes and 6k tokens/sec as a short burst. Can you confirm your throughput measurement methodology (tokens/sec aggregated vs per-worker)?
3) Do you require any firewall or IP allowlist changes for you to run tests against our staging environment?

Also, can you confirm when we'll get the raw trace files? We want to run a quick internal comparison to our telemetry.

Elena Martin
Head of Product — Aster Labs
elena@asterlabs.io

", "From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
To: Elena Martin <elena@asterlabs.io>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>, Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 15 Sep 2026 11:48:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Mutual action plan: performance validation & streaming TTFT (initial plan)

Elena — great questions, quick answers: 

- Tail focus: we'll report TTFT p50/p95/p99 for both cold and warm runs. Cold run is no KV cache and cold backend process; warm run will be after a 5-minute priming period.
- Throughput: our CSVs report both per-worker tokens/sec and an aggregated tokens/sec across the serving pool; we'll highlight the aggregate in the summary and include per-worker breakdown for reproducibility.
- Network: no inbound to your staging required — we can run from Redwood's test harness pointing at a staging endpoint if you provide an allowlist IP range; alternatively we can run from our cluster and replay recorded client patterns if allowlist isn't possible.
- Traces: raw trace bundles (latency CSV + per-request trace.jsonl) will be uploaded within 24 hours after the sprint completes.

We're holding a short sync tomorrow (09/16) at 10:00 PT to finalize test windows — joining this call will help us lock the MAP. Invite sent separately.

Cheers,
Jordan

", "From: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>
Cc: Elena Martin <elena@asterlabs.io>, Tom Wu <tom.wu@asterlabs.io>
Date: Fri, 17 Sep 2026 08:44:00 -0700
Subject: RE: Mutual action plan: performance validation & streaming TTFT (initial plan) — eval results

Elena / team — we completed the eval sprint on 09/17. Summary below; raw CSV attached (latency-results-09-17.csv) and trace bundles uploaded to the Drive link in the MAP. Tests run from Redwood dedicated cluster (us-west-2, 4 x A100-40GB), model variant: redwood-stream-13b-q4-optim, sequence: 512 tokens typical. We ran three passes: cold-start, warm-start, and concurrency sweep.

Quick summary (aggregated across the serving pool):
- Cold-start TTFT (first request after cold boot): p50 420ms, p95 1,180ms, p99 2,040ms
- Warm-start TTFT (after 5-minute priming): p50 150ms, p95 430ms, p99 780ms
- Subsequent-token streaming latency (warm): p50 28ms, p95 75ms, p99 160ms
- Concurrency sweep (ramp to 50 concurrent streaming clients): sustained aggregate tokens/sec: 5,100 tps for a 5-minute steady window; peak short-burst 6,300 tps observed for 90s

Mapping to acceptance:
- Your requested p99 under ~1s at 30 concurrent agents (estimated ~2.4k aggregate tps) — warm-start p99 measured at 780ms (PASS).
- Throughput: we observed sustained aggregate >3k tps in the 30-concurrency slice; we comfortably hit your burst expectations in the cluster used for the test.

Notes & caveats:
- Cold-start p99 exceeds 1s (2s+) — this is expected for cold infra. Production mitigations: keep worker pool warm, use steady keepalive priming, and client-side retry/backoff.
- Numbers will vary slightly by model variant and sequence length; we'll include guidance in the MAP spreadsheet for recommended capacity to meet SLOs with 20% headroom.

Attachments: latency-results-09-17.csv (raw), summary-traces.tar.gz (uploaded)

Next steps: if these numbers match your expectations, we propose to move to the canary window starting 09/20. Sergio will propose a canary playbook.

Thanks,
Neha Kapoor
Sr. Performance Engineer — Redwood Inference

", "From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>
To: Elena Martin <elena@asterlabs.io>, Tom Wu <tom.wu@asterlabs.io>
Cc: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 18 Sep 2026 10:02:00 -0700
Subject: RE: Mutual action plan: performance validation & streaming TTFT (initial plan) — canary proposal

Elena — following Neha's results, here is a short canary proposal we want to include in the MAP (attached: canary-playbook.md):

- Canary window: 09/20 00:00 PT -> 09/23 23:59 PT (72 hours)
- Traffic split: 10% of production chat traffic directed to Redwood serving pool; monitor costs and p95/p99 every 10 minutes
- SLOs during canary: warm-start p95 <= 500ms, warm p99 <= 900ms; if either metric exceeds thresholds for >3 consecutive 10m windows, automatic rollback to previous model routing
- Rollback plan: immediate 100% failover to fallback model (redwood-stream-13b-safe) + incident playbook; CS and SRE on call for first 24 hours
- Acceptance gating for full ramp: 72h canary with no SLA breaches and no more than 2 regressions requiring operator intervention

records.title: adaptive tool hedging and result coalescing to improve multi-tool ergonomics and streaming stability
records.text:
adaptive tool hedging and result coalescing to improve multi-tool ergonomics and streaming stability

description:
Motivation: multi-tool and parallel tool-call patterns were exposing two frequent pain points: 1) wasted duplicate work when multiple upstream planners (or speculative hedges) invoked equivalent tools in flight, and 2) streaming clients observed inconsistent marker points when tool results were injected out-of-order. This PR introduces an adaptive hedging/hedge-coalescer in the runtime and ergonomic surface updates in the API layer to: (a) deduplicate in-flight tool invocations across a request scope, (b) allow controlled parallelism with per-tool retry windows and jittered retry backoff, and (c) coalesce results deterministically for structured output and streaming consumers. Key design points: - In-flight idempotency tokens: tool invocations now carry a scoped idempotency key (derived from model request id + normalized tool signature) so workers can detect duplicate intent and avoid duplicate external calls. - Hedging controller: at runtime we run a short speculative hedging policy for latency-sensitive calls (configurable per-route). Hedged calls are registered with the coalescer rather than executed as independent outputs. - Result coalescer: worker-level component collects first-success responses and merges secondary responses into metadata (latency info, fallback reasons) instead of double-injecting content. This preserves streaming handshake semantics and keeps the final structured output deterministic. - OpenAI compat layer: updated function-calling adapter to respect the new idempotency semantics and to map merged results into a single function_call entry (with a tool_call_history array in metadata). - SDK ergonomics: TypeScript and Python SDKs expose an optional callHint to opt-in to hedging/coalesce behavior and surface a stable injection ordering promise for streaming clients. Checklist: - [x] Runtime: implement hedging controller + coalescer (server/runtime/tool_coalescer.py) - [x] API: add callHint + callToken to OpenAI-compat function call payloads (api/openai_compat/func_call_adapter.py, sdk/ts/src/tool/call.ts, sdk/python/redwood/tooling.py) - [x] Tests: unit tests for dedupe logic, coalescer, and streaming markers - [x] Docs: describe behavior and configuration (docs/observability/tool-hedging.md) - [x] Backwards compat verification against existing function-calling tests Summary of changes (high level): - server/runtime/tool_coalescer.py: new coalescer and hedging flow, small internal state machine for lifecycle of hedged calls. - api/openai_compat/func_call_adapter.py: serialize callToken/callHint, map coalesced responses to function_call with call_history metadata. - sdk/ts/src/tool/call.ts: add optional callHint param, promise-based injection ordering helper for streaming clients. - sdk/python/redwood/tooling.py: mirror ergonomics and provide convenience wrapper for idempotency token generation. - docs/observability/tool-hedging.md: short explainer and diagrams for typical flows. Commits: - 7f4b2d3: introduce tool_coalescer + hedging controller (core runtime) - c102b9a: openai compat adapter changes, map call_history into function_call metadata - 9a8d01f: ts & py sdk ergonomics + tests - 11b2e6a: add unit tests for dedupe and coalescer, CI tweaks - 5b7c0f2: docs and release notes Draft testing notes: initial canary against internal perf-canary showed median P95 token latency improvement of 8% for poly-tool workloads and a 25% reduction in duplicate external API calls for hedged routes. CI summary: first run had a flaky test in streaming-marker.t — fixed by adding a small sync barrier in the coalescer; final CI run: all checks passing. Backwards compatibility: default behavior off; existing routes unchanged unless callHint is provided or route-level hedging is enabled in config. Migration notes: enabling hedging on highly stateful external tools is discouraged until tool implementations are idempotent or the caller supplies a dedupe key. Related Linear tickets: ENG-1427 (tool hedging prototype), ENG-1534 (streaming marker stability). Links: (internal) Linear ENG-1427, ENG-1534.

Liam O'Connor (reviewer): Can you add an integration smoke test that simulates a streaming client receiving the streaming markers and final injection? The guardrail in streaming-marker.t fixed the flake but want an explicit scenario.

- Temporarily applied conservative rate limit for Solara's IP range to reduce retry amplification
- Forced warm KV cache for affected model family and pre-warmed two additional inference pools in us-west-2
- Enabled a circuit-breaker to shed excess requests and return fast failures to avoid queue pileups

records.text:
support

Lina (Support): FYI ticket H-3241 from Helios Health. They ran the usage CSV export after our manual backfill and see an extra day (2025-11-09) showing 0 tokens in the CSV, but the invoice shows ~548k tokens for that day. Customer is asking why CSV != invoice. Can someone triage?

Sophie (Support): attaching the snippet they pasted into the portal. They said the portal dashboard and invoice both show tokens for 2025-11-09, only the export is missing the rows.

Sophie (Support): ```
date,customer_id,model,tokens
2025-11-08,helios-001,gpt-xx,42123
2025-11-09,helios-001,gpt-xx,0
2025-11-10,helios-001,gpt-xx,50234
```

Michael (Billing): I see invoice line: 2025-11-09 -> 548,173 tokens billed (charged). Our daily ledger aggregate also shows 548,173 for that customer/day. So the billing pipeline has the tokens, export is missing them. Could be backfill export dedupe or a filter.

Ashish (Infra): looking at backfill job logs (s3://redwood-backfills/helios/2025-11-09/run-7/logs). Quick grep: ``write_row(customer=helios-001,date=2025-11-09): SKIPPED duplicate_key collision shard=4 key="helios-001|2025-11-09|gpt-xx|<hash>"``

backfill-bot: Backfill job run-7 completed 2025-11-10T04:12Z - status=completed warnings=2 skipped_writes=1

Tara (Eng): That log line suggests the backfill write path is deduping on a key that can collide across replay runs. For manual backfills we replay raw ledger rows but don't set a stable ingestion_run_id, so dedupe_key collapsed multiple sets into one and the export worker filters out rows marked as 'replay_skipped'.

Tara (Eng): repro plan: 1) run the ledger query to count raw rows for 2025-11-09 2) run the export tool in dry-run to see which rows are filtered 3) inspect dedupe ids for collisions.

Sophie (Support): ledger query the billing folks suggested: ```
SELECT customer_id, sum(tokens) as tokens_sum FROM raw_usage
WHERE customer_id='helios-001' AND date='2025-11-09' GROUP BY customer_id;
```

Michael (Billing): Running that against ledger-analytics returns tokens_sum = 548173 (matches invoice). So raw data exists. Export pipeline must be dropping them during export.

Ashish (Infra): digging deeper - export worker marks rows with header `write_status` and sets `write_status=skipped_replay_collision` when dedupe_key already exists. Sample from export worker debug: ```
{row_id: "r-xxxxx", customer: "helios-001", date: "2025-11-09", tokens: 548173, write_status: "skipped_replay_collision"}
```

Tara (Eng): Root cause hypothesis: backfill replay generated rows with different request_ids; existing dedupe logic uses a hashed key that doesn't include ingestion_run_id, so the second replay hit the same dedupe hash and we skip writing the canonical export rows. We'll need to: a) change dedupe key to include ingestion_run_id b) add a forced-write flag for backfills c) run a one-off regen of that day's CSV for Helios.

Ashish (Infra): I can run a targeted regen now: `./infra/tools/exporter --customer helios-001 --date 2025-11-09 --force-write --output s3://support-attachments/helios/regen-2025-11-09.csv`

Sophie (Support): If you can push the regen result to that S3 path I will send corrected CSV to the customer and propose a billing credit if they want immediate adjustment.

Michael (Billing): Please cc billing@redwood when sending corrected CSV. If Helios wants a credit now we can issue a provisional credit while we fix the pipeline (adjustment will be reconciled once automatic fix is deployed).

Tara (Eng): I'll open PR to change dedupe key and add a new backfill flag. I'll add unit tests for ingest_run_id presence and e2e test that replays twice doesn't drop rows. ETA: PR by EOD PT, deploy early next week after review.

Ashish (Infra): I've kicked off the regen job, logs show success and file at s3://support-attachments/helios/regen-2025-11-09.csv (size 1.2MB). backfill-bot: attached checksum `sha256:fa3b...`

backfill-bot: Regeneration job exporter-regen-981 succeeded 2025-11-10T06:03Z -> s3://support-attachments/helios/regen-2025-11-09.csv

Sophie (Support): Sent corrected CSV and note to Helios. Told them root cause + tentative timeline for pipeline fix. Customer replied: "thank you, please keep us posted" :thumbsup:

Lina (Support): created internal incident INC-2025-123 to track the fix and billing follow-up. Assigning to Tara (Eng) and Ashish (Infra). I'll thread updates in the ticket and notify the customer once fixed.

Michael (Billing): Will prepare provisional credit entry in case Helios requests immediate refund; will reconcile after pipeline fix.

Tara (Eng): next steps: PR -> review -> canary deploy (export staging) -> verify regen for a different customer -> rollout. I'll post PR link here when ready.

Lina (Support): thanks everyone — keeping ticket open until post-deploy verification.

records.title: eng-runtime
records.text:
eng-runtime

marco: Heads-up — we saw a 99th-percentile latency spike for hosted-small around 09:12 UTC and a correlated throughput drop. Scale-controller wakeups were delayed ~6-9s. Noticed more kernel_fallback hits in runtime logs.

devon: Looking at prometheus: scale_controller.queue_length spiked, warm-pool stayed at min size. Could be autoscaler backoff or warm-pool prefetch failing. Any kernel-selection logs?

sre-bot: ALERT: latency_surge detected for service=hosted-small (09:12 UTC). Incident created: INC-412.

anya: Posting quick profiler excerpt and kernel selector snippet below — looks like many requests ended up on unoptimized kernel paths.

anya: ```
[09:12:18] kernel_selector: model=model-x seq_len=512 chosen_kernel=generic_attention_v1 fallback=true
[09:12:18] batcher: batch_size=4 latency_ms=87 kv_cache_hit=false
[09:12:19] perf: cpu_ms=45 gpu_ms=120 kv_prefetch_ms=30
```

lee: KV cache hitrate dropped from ~94% -> 62% at the same time window. That explains extra work per request and more cache prefetch pressure. Node gpu-m0 reported a memory spike and eviction noise. Might be noisy neighbor.

sara: Did we deploy any batching or kernel selector changes yesterday? I remember a batching-hysteresis tweak went out in the afternoon.

devon: We rolled batching-hysteresis to canary at 08:40 but not full. Kernel selector tweak landed in the runtime yesterday evening (PR #1987) — it added a new heuristic for seq_len routing.

marco: Traces show a pattern: requests that missed KV cache often had seq_len ~400-700 and hit the fallback kernel path which is much slower. Combined with autoscaler wakeup backoff, new capacity wasn't provisioned quickly.

anya: Another snippet from runtime logs:
```
[09:12:20] kv_cache: miss key_prefix=... prefetch_start
[09:12:20] warm_pool: prefetch_task queued for node=gpu-m0
[09:12:21] kernel_selector: no optimized kernel for seq_len=512 on model-x -> fallback
[09:12:22] container: prefetcher OOM, killed pid=4321
```

lee: That prefetcher OOM is key — if prefetcher gets killed, warmpool entries get evicted and hitrate plummets. Node-level noisy neighbor (batch job) caused memory churn.

devon: The autoscaler backoff logic has a subtle bug: when warm-pool size is changed rapidly, the controller's backoff timer doesn't reset, so wakeups are postponed. I can reproduce locally.

sara: I found the buggy condition: backoff reset checked pool_delta == 0 instead of pool_delta != 0 in v2 of the controller. Opening hotfix PR now.

marco: Immediate mitigation proposals: 1) temporarily increase warm-pool.min by +2 in affected region, 2) disable kernel_fallback for seq_len>256 (force optimized path or explicit error), 3) roll back the new kernel-selector heuristic if needed. Which order?

devon: Do 1 and 2 asap. Disabling fallback reduces perf variability even if it increases rejections slightly. I'll prepare a small change to flags.

marco: I'll scale warm-pool by +2 for us-west-2 and eu-west-1 now.

sre-bot: ACTION: warm-pool min increased for hosted-small us-west-2 at 09:24 UTC.

devon: Pushed flag to runtime to disable fallback for seq_len>256 on canary at 09:27. Monitoring.

sre-bot: UPDATE: mitigation applied. Latency trending down 09:37 UTC. Keep an eye on kernel_fallback_rate and kv_cache_hitrate.

anya: Preliminary root-cause summary for the postmortem: combination of (A) KV cache eviction due to prefetcher OOM on a noisy node, (B) increased kernel_fallback rate for mid-to-high seq_len after recent selector heuristic change, and (C) autoscaler wakeup backoff bug that delayed provisioning. All three amplified each other.

devon: Follow-ups (owners):
- devon: add kernel_fallback_rate metric + alert, gather perf traces for model-x across seq_len buckets
- sara: land autoscaler hotfix + unit test for backoff reset, schedule canary rollout
- lee: investigate prefetcher memory usage, add OOM alerts and pod qos adjustments
- anya: write full incident postmortem with flamegraphs and traces

marco: Assigning owners: devon -> kernel metrics & traces, sara -> autoscaler fix, lee -> warmpool prefetch stability, anya -> postmortem writeup. I'll follow up on rollback plan if trends don't improve.

sara: :thumbsup: PR opened for autoscaler fix and test coverage (PR #2045).

devon: I'll collect perf traces into the incident ticket and add dashboards for kernel_fallback_rate by model+seq_len.

marco: Timeline note: incident opened ~09:13 UTC, mitigation applied ~09:24-09:27 UTC, service metrics normalized by ~09:38 UTC. Closing monitoring window in 1h unless we see recurrence.

anya: Adding links: dashboard: https://dash.redwood.internal/d/hosted-small/latency, traces: https://traces.redwood.internal/trace/INC-412

lee: Quick note: we should also consider making the warmpool prefetcher more memory conservative and ensure evicted entries get rehydrated asynchronously without blocking critical requests.

marco: Good plan. Thanks everyone — we'll capture action items in the postmortem and schedule follow-ups.

sre-bot: Incident INC-412 status: mitigated. Next update in postmortem.

records.title: eng-runtime
records.text:
eng-runtime

Mike H.: quick heads-up — ran the end-to-end perf sweep on canary today, attaching brief notes below. major regression observed when kv-miss rate > 12%: tail p99 token latency jumps ~2.8x and batch formation stalls.
Anya R.: ouch. is that the new kernel hint change we rolled last week?
Mike H.: looks correlated. kernel-selection now prefers small-seq kernels for throughput; when kv-miss causes longer sequences, we fall back and recompile path which stalls batcher.
Lee J.: can you paste the flamegraph snippet or perf counters?
Mike H.: pasted the snippet from the profiler:```
# perf snippet
BatchWaitLoop
  -> assemble_batches (60%)
  -> kernel_selector (20%)
  -> kv_fetch (15%)
  -> rpc_wait (5%)
```
Anya R.: so assemble_batches dominates during high miss. means queueing/formation logic is spinning waiting for prefetched tokens?
Mike H.: exactly. continuous-batcher waits up to max_batch_delay hoping to coalesce, but with variable seq lengths and kv-miss we get a lot of tiny microbatches then a big stall when a long request finally arrives.
Dave K.: practical mitigation ideas? immediate thought: tighten max_batch_delay for lanes with low KV locality, and add a token-budget per-lane to avoid starving kernel warmups.
Lee J.: +1. also consider a soft admission early-reject for requests that would blow active_token_budget. return a soft 429 with hint to retry-after small backoff.
Anya R.: we already have soft-429 path but it's global. need per-lane and kv-locality-aware. Could we compute a kv_hit_score for incoming request and route through a 'fastpath' admit check?
Mike H.: proposal: pre-admit checks in this order:
1) estimate_tokens(request) + active_tokens_in_batch_lane <= lane_token_target? else soft-429
2) if kv_hit_est < threshold then prefer small_seq_kernel and preemptive microbatch cap = 8 tokens
3) if kernel selector triggers fallback compile, mark lane in probation for 200ms and apply aggressive reject probability p=0.3
Implementation sketch:```
# pseudo
if (active_tokens + est_tokens > token_target) return soft429("retry-ms=40");
if (kv_hit_score < 0.7) set_batch_limit(8);
if (recent_kernel_fallbacks > 0) set_reject_prob(0.3);
```
Dave K.: sounds sensible. how do we pick token_target? static or adaptive?
Mike H.: adaptive preferred. start with lane_token_target = median_tokens_per_batch * 1.6, with clamps [32, 512]. adjust every 30s based on measured tail latency and kv-miss rate.
Lee J.: need guardrails so it doesn't oscillate. add hysteresis: only change if sustained shift >10% for two consecutive windows.
Anya R.: monitoring: add new metrics: lane_token_target, kv_hit_est, kernel_fallback_count, pre_admit_soft429_rate. dashboard tile and alert if soft429>1% sustained for 5m.
infra-bot: perf_canary_deploy #17588822 completed — canary nodes with kernel-hint-optimizer v2 rolled to 10% traffic.
Mike H.: thanks. next steps: I'll draft a small PR to add pre-admit check + per-lane token budget (will target a behind-flag rollout). want Lee and Anya to review the heuristics.
Lee J.: will review tomorrow. for the PR unit tests: simulate kv-hit 0%/50%/100% and assert that batch sizes and soft429 rates behave within expected bands.
Anya R.: add e2e perf job that flips kernel hint on/off and runs a 30m sustained mix to validate no p99 regression.
Dave K.: one more note — for tracing, emit span when we return soft-429 with the reason and current lane_token_target so downstream can introspect.
Mike H.: agreed. I'll include trace annotations. thanks all :thumbsup:
Anya R.: can we also add a quick playbook entry for oncall: if p99 spikes after deploy, set lane_token_target /= 1.5 and enable kernel-hint-fallback=false, then roll back.
Dave K.: adding playbook step: "if soft429 > 5% and p99 > threshold, flip flag and reduce targets; escalate if lasting >15m"
Mike H.: putting the follow-ups in a small GH issue and linking to this thread.
Anya R.: nice. short-term mitigation + better admission controls should prevent the microburst + stall pattern.
Mike H.: closing loop — PR by EOD tomorrow, canary run, then roll to 50% if stable.

["From: Lina Ortega <finance@acme.com>

Subject: Invoice payload options and acknowledgement workflow

Hi Jordan,

Thanks for the quick onboarding call earlier. To keep momentum on the billing side, our AP team needs a clear decision on how Redwood will send invoices to Acme for production billing. We have two constraints on our side: PO matching on line 1 and automated acknowledgement for receipt (machine-readable ack).

Questions from AP:
- Can Redwood push an XML/UBL payload to our SFTP or API (preferred) that includes VAT breakdown and line-level PO matching?
- If Redwood sends PDF invoices by email, can you attach a companion machine-readable XML (or CSV) for automated ingestion?
- If portal push is used, can we still receive an email copy as archival?

Attached: sample of the invoice layout our AP system expects (invoice_sample_pdf.pdf). PO: ACME-99871 (included in attachment).

Lina Ortega

Acme Corp
(attachment: invoice_sample_pdf.pdf)

To: Lina Ortega <finance@acme.com>

Hi Lina — great to meet earlier, and thanks for the sample.

Short answer: we can support both approaches; recommended default is a portal/API push (XML) plus an automated email copy containing the PDF and a small XML attachment for ACK. That gives you machine-readable ingestion plus an archival PDF.

Notes / constraints from our side:
- Our platform can emit a UBL/Invoice XML (we use a slightly opinionated schema). I attached the schema we usually send (invoice_schema_v1.xml).
- VAT tagging: we can include line-level VAT and a total VAT block. For reverse-charge, we can populate the invoice with the proper VAT code and include a tax-evidence PDF as a separate attachment if needed.
- Delivery options: SFTP push, HTTPS POST to your invoice endpoint, or portal batch export. Email PDF with XML companion is a fallback (works but is slower for automated posting).

Proposed next steps:
1) Kimberly to validate that Acme's AP accepts our invoice_schema_v1.xml over SFTP/API and note any field mismatches.
2) Marissa to confirm whether legal needs signed invoices / DocuSign for your region.
3) Lina to confirm preferred delivery channel (SFTP/API/portal + email copy) and go-live date (you mentioned Nov 1).

Kimberly / Marissa — can you own 1/2?

Best,
Jordan Blake
Head of Revenue Operations
Redwood Inference
(attachment: invoice_schema_v1.xml)

To: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Lina Ortega <finance@acme.com>

> Our platform can emit a UBL/Invoice XML (we use a slightly opinionated schema). I attached the schema we usually send (invoice_schema_v1.xml).

Lina / Acme AP — quick ops note from our implementation playbook:
- Most enterprise AP systems accept either: (A) Peppol/UBL via SFTP or HTTPS POST, or (B) XML (custom) via SFTP. Email PDF is commonly accepted but usually requires manual keying unless accompanied by a machine-readable attachment.

- VAT/reverse-charge: we recommend including a separate tax-evidence PDF (scoped per invoice) and adding the reverse-charge note in the invoice XML in the <TaxNote> field.

Operational recommendation (my preference):
Portal/API push (SFTP or HTTPS) as primary delivery + email copy with PDF + XML companion as fallback for any partners who need it. This minimizes manual processing while keeping archives.

Action items:
- Action: Kimberly to confirm exact XML node names Acme expects for PO matching (we will map ours to yours).
- Action: Marissa to confirm if Acme requires signed/embossed invoices or if a standard PDF with tax evidence is sufficient.

--
Kimberly Park
Billing Integrations Lead
Redwood Inference
(attachment: peppol_sample.xml)
', 'From: Lina Ortega <finance@acme.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-10-20T16:45:00Z

Thanks — that plan works for us. A couple of final points from AP before we lock Nov 1: 

- Delivery: use SFTP push to our ingestion endpoint (ap-integration@acme.com / sftp.acme-corp.com) with a daily envelope. Include an email copy to invoices@acme.com for legal/archival.
- Required fields: PO must be present at line 1 and a top-level PO reference. VAT/GST breakdown must be per-line and total. For EU reverse-charge, include the note: "Reverse charge — Article 194" in the tax note.

- Reconciliation: can you include a weekly reconciliation CSV with invoice ids and amounts (CSV stub in weekly_artifact.csv)? We will ingest that for matching.

Attached: our PO for initial billing (acme_po_99871.pdf).

If you can confirm SFTP credentials and that the Peppol/UBL or the custom XML will include the fields above, we'll consider Nov 1 confirmed.

Appreciate the quick turnaround — Lina

(attachment: acme_po_99871.pdf)

Team —

We need to run a controlled preflight for the Acme Financial VPC/on-prem cutover next Thursday. Goal: validate our traffic-mirroring pipeline, failover to hosted fallback, and confirm there are no request-level regressions in latency or errors. - Run BGP flap simulation on the edge router (vendor to coordinate).

- Capture latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), and token-level error rates.

> Subject: Preflight exercise: traffic mirroring + fallback (weekend window)

Rishi Malhotra

Redwood Inference

records.title: Quarterly engagement outline — Northbridge Finance (Q1 renewal prep)
records.text:
Quarterly engagement outline — Northbridge Finance (Q1 renewal prep)

summary:
Working draft for the upcoming QBR with Northbridge Finance — focused on renewal preparation for their Dedicated + Private deployment, risk mitigation plan for model latency regressions, and a compact slide deck and ask list for the executive meeting. This file is intended to be a single-sheet narrative and playbook we can hand off to AE + SE for final rehearsals.

objectives:
Reinforce value: show cost-per-query improvements and latency stability over the last 6 months
Secure verbal renewal commitment / identify timeline for contract extension (target: signed by end of Q2)
Agree on two technical mitigations for the observed p95 tail spikes and an owners-driven remediations plan
Obtain buy-in for pilot of Redwood Optimize recommendations (quantization + batch tuning) on 2 high-volume endpoints

attendees:
Michael Yates — Head of ML Platforms, Northbridge
Sana Iqbal — Director, Fraud Ops, Northbridge
Jared Kim — CSM, Redwood
Priya Singh — Solutions Engineer, Redwood
Luis Moreno — SRE, Redwood (observability)
Account Exec: Elena Alvarez

slide_outline:
1. Welcome & Agenda — 1 min (Jared) — set expectations: 30-minute exec + 15-minute tech deep-dive
2. Partnership highlights — 2 slides (Elena) — adoption milestones, win stories from Fraud Ops
3. Usage & economics snapshot — 2 slides (Jared) — tokens/day, cost-per-1M-tokens, spend trend vs. forecast
4. Performance & reliability — 2 slides (Luis) — latency p50/p95, incident summary, SLO attainment
5. Risk areas & mitigation plan — 1 slide (Priya) — tail latency, KV cache warmup, autoscale thresholds
6. Redwood Optimize proposal — 1 slide (Priya) — expected savings and quality guardrails
7. Renewal proposal & timeline — 1 slide (Elena) — commercial options: 12/24 month, reserved capacity tiers
8. Ask & next steps — 1 slide (Jared) — decisions requested, owners, and dates

talking_points:
Open: thank you for the partnership; highlight how Redwood helped Northbridge reduce per-query cost by ~22% on their fraud-detector endpoint since Oct 2025.
Usage: call out 3 high-volume routes (fraud-detector, onboarding-chat, name-normalize) and that 68% of tokens are from fraud-detector during peak windows.
Performance: acknowledge p95 spikes in late Jan/early Feb — explain root-cause hypothesis (cache cold-start after nightly autoscale purge) and quick wins implemented (sticky-prefetch + adjusted warmup).
Reliability: confirm SLOs (99.5% p99 response < 600ms for priority endpoints) and current attainment (99.3%) — propose targeted A/B rollout of batching profile to hit 99.6%.
Optimize ask: request permission to run a 4-week Optimize pilot on the fraud-detector route (non-prod then canary prod), expected cost reduction 15–25% and <0.5% quality delta via eval harness.
Commercial: propose 12-month Reserved Dedicated with a 10% uplift on current commit in exchange for priority capacity and 4-week rollback SLA for model changes.
Decision request: Would Northbridge agree to a pilot start in 2 weeks and an IOI (intent to renew) by the end of the next month?

metrics_snapshot:
Current snapshot (rolling 30d): avg tokens/day 42.3M; peak qps 820; p50 latency 78ms; p95 latency 380ms; p99 latency 920ms; uptime 99.92%; monthly spend $86.2k; top 3 endpoints by tokens: fraud-detector (68%), onboarding-chat (18%), normalize-name (6%).

renewal_tracker_notes:
Northbridge contract renewal window: renewal notice due 2026-06-30. Current contract term ends 2026-09-30. Recommended cadence: exec QBR (this doc) -> commercial proposal sent within 10 business days -> AE to secure LOI by 2026-04-30 -> formal contract negotiation May-June. Consider 24-month discount tier only if they commit to Reserved Dedicated capacity + 1 compliance add-on (audit retention).

To: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwoodinference.com>, Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwoodinference.com>

Date: Wed, Feb 12, 2025 at 9:27 AM
Subject: Northwind AI usage discrepancy: suspected retries/stream cancellation

Looping you in on a customer escalation. Northwind is seeing ~18-25% higher usage (token totals) than their internal estimates.

Hypotheses:
- client timeouts + retry  we count each attempt
- streaming cancellation: do we count tokens emitted before cancel? do we count prompt tokens even if generation cancelled?
- dashboard aggregation maybe double-counting on certain response codes

Attachment: northwind-request-samples.csv (request ids + timestamps they provided)

Can someone from platform/usage pipeline sanity check the accounting for retries + stream disconnects?


From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwoodinference.com>
To: Priya Natarajan <priya.natarajan@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwoodinference.com>, Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwoodinference.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Wed, Feb 12, 2025 at 10:02 AM
Subject: Re: Northwind AI usage discrepancy: suspected retries/stream cancellation

Thanks. Two things:
1) usage pipeline counts per-attempt, not per logical request. If client retries, that will look inflated vs their expected.
2) prompt tokens are counted once the request is admitted; cancellation doesnt undo prompt tokens. completion tokens should be only what we actually stream.

We should confirm if their library retries on 499/timeout.

+1. Also: the UI currently groups by request_id (which is attempt id). Some customers think its an id they generate and stable across retries.

If we can add UI text: Each retry is billed as a separate attempt that might solve a bunch of these.

Customer uses a homegrown gateway and they do retry once on timeout. They assumed the timeout attempt doesnt count if they didnt get the full answer.

records.title: Introduce retrospective SLO replay service and cost-attenuation proxy
records.text:
Introduce retrospective SLO replay service and cost-attenuation proxy

description:
Motivation: We need a low-risk way to evaluate the SLO and cost impact of routing, batching and fallback policy changes against historical traffic slices without touching production runtime. This PR adds a lightweight retrospective SLO replay service (slo-replay) that replays sampled invocation traces against a ruleset engine and the same cost estimator used by the billing pipeline. The goal is to produce per-route SLO impact projections and a cost-attenuation proxy metric that observability rules can use to moderate alert sensitivity during transient rollout experiments.

What this PR does (summary): adds a new slo-replay microservice, a replay job scheduler, an adapter that feeds sampled invocations to the routing policy simulator, a cost-attenuation proxy metric emitted to the observability pipeline, a Grafana dashboard for projected-SLO vs observed-SLO scatter, and alert rule updates to use the attenuation proxy for temporary suppression during canaries.

Key design points: the replay runs offline against anonymized, sampled traces (existing sampled-context export). It uses the same token-cost and kernel-latency model that billing uses to estimate per-invocation cost and per-stage latency. Replay results are aggregated into a time-bucketed projection index keyed by route, model-version, and policy-id. The attenuation proxy is a decayed ratio (projected_error_rate / baseline_error_rate) clipped to [0,2] and emitted as a numeric label so alert rules can multiply thresholds by 1 + attenuation_factor * alpha. The service exposes a small REST status endpoint and writes projection snapshots to the telemetry tier for query.

Checklist: [x] MVP replay engine and rules simulator; [x] emit attenuation proxy metric (telemetry exporter); [x] Grafana dashboard JSON and dashboard provisioning; [x] e2e integration tests for replay -> telemetry pipeline; [x] docs: observability runbook and how-to for canaries; [x] unit tests for policy simulator.

Commits (high level): - 1a2b3c4: initial slo-replay service scaffold and job runner - 2d3e4f5: policy simulator + unit tests, tie into existing sampled-context export - 3f4g5h6: telemetry exporter for attenuation proxy + protobuf schema + index writer - 4h5i6j7: grafana dashboard panels + alert rule changes and runbook docs - 5j6k7l8: test harness and CI adjustments for e2e tests

Files changed (representative): - observability/slo_replay/service.py (new): replay scheduler, adapter to policy simulator - observability/slo_replay/simulator.py (new): deterministic policy simulator with unit tests - telemetry/exporters/attenuation_exporter.go (new): emits attenuation proxy metric with labels - dashboards/provisioning/retro-slo-projections.json (new): Grafana dashboard panels and templates - monitoring/alerting/canary_rules.yaml (modified): use attenuation proxy to suppress noisy alerts - tests/e2e/test_slo_replay_end2end.py (new): end-to-end replay smoke test - docs/observability/slo-replay.md (new): runbook and how-to

Migration and runtime safety: the replay runs only on an offline batch pool with a configurable retention window; default retention is 7 days of sampled contexts. Telemetry emission is rate-limited and namespaced under telemetry.replay to avoid collision with production metrics. The attenuation proxy is advisory by default (alert rules use a conservative alpha=0.25 until we reach 7-day stability in production projections).

Operational notes: added a small sampler config to sampled-context-export so we can increase sampling ratio for short windows when validating new policies. The replay scheduler includes a backfill mode to rerun a specific date range for re-eval.

Why this is different from existing tooling: other efforts run small synthetic replays or ad-hoc notebooks. This PR provides a repeatable, indexable, production-alike replay path with metrics surfaced in dashboards and a formalized attenuation signal that alerting rules can safely consult during rollouts.

Risks and mitigations: - Risk: attenuation proxy could be abused to mask real regressions. Mitigation: default alpha small, audit log for attenuation-enabled alerts, and gating via RBAC on who can flip advisory mode. - Risk: projection model divergence from actual runtime. Mitigation: we log a calibration delta (projection vs observed) and auto-escalate if delta exceeds threshold for 3 windows.

Next steps: collect 2 weeks of replay projections for high-volume routes, evaluate calibration, and iterate alpha per-team.

Sofia Martinez: Thanks — added a scrubber in sampled-context export and a config flag (redaction_policy) in service.py. Also switched attenuation labels to coarse enums (low/medium/high) plus a numeric factor for fine-grained calculation.
Priya Kapoor: Could we add an opt-in flag for product teams to receive projection diffs? Otherwise LGTM for the core. Please add e2e test that asserts rate-limiting of telemetry export.
Sofia Martinez: Added product opt-in metadata, and extended e2e to assert telemetry export QPS < configured threshold. CI e2e passing locally.
Liam O'Connor: Quick nit: use existing prometheus metric name prefix (telemetry.replay_) to keep queries consistent. Added an approval after the metric rename and small doc tweak.
Aiden Wu: Approved. Priya: Approved. Merging with squash once CI finishes clean run.

release_notes:

Canary alert rules can optionally consult the projection attenuation signal for temporary suppression during rollouts. See docs/observability/slo-replay.md for runbook and RBAC guidance.

records.title: Somerset Care Networks
records.text:
Somerset Care Networks

notes:
POC outcome: closed-lost. Customer compared Redwood Private + Optimize suggestions vs incumbent ClarityAI (on-prem appliance). Key decision driver: deterministic structured outputs and tool-calling reliability.

Context: Regional provider network, heavy claims and eligibility automation. Goal: replace multiple vendor chains with single inference platform to reduce latency and ops overhead. Security posture strict; on-prem preferred. Internal champion was Head of Data Ops (left role mid-eval).

POC scope: 3-week validation (2026-01-18 to 2026-02-08). Tasks: batch extraction to JSON schema v3, function/tool-calls for eligibility checks, chat assistant for first-line triage. Data: 80K redacted claims + 20K provider records.

Customer QA results (summary): - Schema conformance: Redwood failed field-level validation for required fields in ~9% of samples (missing 'member_plan_code', 'service_line_code'); ClarityAI baseline ~0.5%. - Ordering/arrays: nested procedure arrays mis-ordered causing deserialization errors in downstream ETL (~4% failures). - Tool-calling: callback idempotency issues; retries led to duplicate API invocations in 2% of cases. - Model quality: occasional non-deterministic enumerations for categorical outputs; customer called this "regression risk". Latency and cost were acceptable but secondary.

Sales/eng timeline: - Engineering proposed schema-strict mode (reject/rescore on mismatch) and server-side function signature enforcement. - Security requested detailed HSM workflow and SIEM integration sample logs; Redwood provided KMS flow but lacked documented HSM handshake used by ClarityAI appliance. - Customer asked for side-by-side run with ClarityAI on a 10K sample; Redwood offered to run automated diff but customer worried about validation effort/time.

Customer quote from final call: "We can absorb slightly higher compute cost, but we cannot accept variable JSON outputs that force re-validation of the pipeline. Clarity has been doing this in our environment for 2 years."

Follow-ups attempted: 3 emails, 1 deep-dive call (2026-02-20). Customer paused procurement due to company-wide Q1 budget hold and no active champion to push through migration. Final decision: remain with ClarityAI for continuity.

Recommended internal actions: 1) Build a schema-strict POC kit (validation hooks + sample SOW). 2) Create HSM integration docs and one-off engineering task template. 3) Run competitive regression test harness against ClarityAI on two representative datasets and publish anonymized findings for sales. 4) Check back with procurement in 6 months or after champion re-hires.

Status: Closed-lost for now. Keep on watchlist (re-engage after org stabilizes).

2025-11-02 - Discovery: heavy emphasis on deterministic outputs and on-prem deployment
2026-01-18 - POC kickoff (data ingest, schema tests, tool-calling scenarios)
2026-02-08 - Mid-POC checkpoint: anomalies surfaced in structured outputs
2026-02-14 - Final demo and security Q&A; customer requests HSM workflow
2026-02-20 - Final call: customer chooses to remain with incumbent (ClarityAI); budget freeze noted

records.title: Local runtime devkit — lightweight inference dev CLI (brainstorm)
records.text:
Local runtime devkit — lightweight inference dev CLI (brainstorm)

Top-level idea
--------------
We build a tiny developer-facing runtime / CLI that simulates Redwood inference locally for fast iteration: local-devkit.

Why?
- Fast loop for prompt engineering + integration tests without remote quotas or waiting for hosted deploys.
- Better DX on Private onboarding: customers can smoke-test integration before they provision infra.
- Lower friction for building reference apps and examples.

Core principles
- Opinionated and minimal: works out of the box for common use cases (chat, generate, embeddings).
- Reproducible: same basic config keys as Redwood API (model name, max_tokens, temperature).
- Safe defaults: telemetry opt-in, no cloud credentials by default.
- Pluggable: can proxy to a real Redwood endpoint or run a lightweight local runtime (mocked or tiny ggml-style runtime)

Primary personas
- Individual frontend/mobile engineers who need a local mock for integration tests.
- ML engineers iterating on prompts and system messages.
- Solutions engineers running PoCs in customer offices (no internet).

User stories (rough)
- As a frontend dev, I want to run local-devkit start and get a local HTTP endpoint that mirrors Redwood's /v1/chat and /v1/generate so I can call it from my app.
- As an ML engineer, I want to run local-devkit --model redwood-open-7b --quantize quick to run cheap on my laptop for prompt experiments.
- As a solutions engineer, I want an "airgap mode" that uses a packaged runtime image and no external network.

MVP feature surface
- CLI: local-devkit init, start, stop, status, logs
- Local HTTP server: /v1/chat, /v1/generate, /v1/embeddings (subset) with compatible request/response shapes
- Two backends: 1) Mock deterministic backend (fast, no model), 2) Lightweight runtime wrapper (optional, depends on user host capabilities)
- Config: ~/.redwood/local-devkit.yaml with model presets, port, telemetry=false, backend=mock|runtime|proxy
- Proxy mode: forward to Redwood hosted using API_KEY env var (useful for hybrid debugging)
- Quickstart UX: one-command demo that seeds example prompt templates and a tiny example app snippet

CLI UX notes
- Setup flow: local-devkit init (creates config + examples)
- Start: local-devkit start [-p PORT] [--profile small|dev|prod]
- Run a one-off: local-devkit run --file examples/quickchat.json -> prints response (good for CI)
- Integration test mode: local-devkit start --ci -> runs in deterministic seed mode and exits with status codes for assertions

Integration with Redwood products
- Hosted API parity: keep request/response keys aligned to minimize friction switching from local to hosted
- Private deployments: local-devkit can validate ecosystem config (routes, TLS cert format, key rotation steps) by parsing user-provided manifests
- Dedicated: allow smoke tests that validate consumed tokens and latency hooks (simulate latency ranges)

Security / privacy
- Default to telemetry=false; if enabled, only send anonymized event counters (no prompts). Explicit opt-in.
- No keys written to disk unless user runs `local-devkit configure-proxy` which stores token encrypted in OS keystore (macOS keychain, Windows cred manager).
- Airgap mode: provide a single tarball with runtime image + example data; document verification checksums.

Acceptance criteria (MVP)
- devkit can be installed via pip/npm/homebrew (pick 1 for MVP).
- local HTTP endpoint accepts a minimal Chat completion request and returns a deterministic mocked response within 50ms.
- Proxy mode correctly forwards a request to Redwood hosted and returns the same shape of response.
- Developer quickstart: <5 minute time to first response on a laptop with no cloud config.

Open questions / risks
- Do we ship a real local runtime kernel (GGML) or rely on a remote proxy + mock? Shipping a real runtime increases maintenance and binary size.
- Licensing of bundled models: can we include tiny LLM weights in an airgap tarball? Probably not unless OSS-compatible.
- CI integration: do we provide a docker image for test runners? Likely yes.
- Which package manager (pip vs brew vs npm) gives best DX for our primary persona? Survey engineering.

Technical sketch
- Language: Go or Rust for single-binary distribution (fast startup, small deps). Python wrapper for dev UX (if we want fast iteration).
- Server: tiny HTTP layer that maps Redwood API to backend impl.
- Mock backend: rule-based templating (supports system + user messages, simple string interpolation, seeded RNG for reproducibility).
- Runtime backend: thin shim around local model runner (optional plugin interface)

Telemetry & metrics for us (opt-in)
- Events: install, start, backend used, proxy-mode usage counts. No prompt payloads.
- Use to inform which features to prioritize (proxy vs runtime adoption).

Example quickstart (note to self):
1) curl -fsSL https://get.redwood.dev/local-devkit | sh
2) local-devkit init
3) local-devkit start --backend mock
4) curl localhost:8080/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer test" -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hello"}],"model":"redwood-mock"}'

TODO (short list)
- [ ] Validate exact Redwood API shapes to emulate (ask API team). (linked: JIRA-RI-4021)
- [ ] Run short survey with 10 frontend/mobile devs to pick packaging strategy (brew vs pip).
- [ ] Prototype mock backend in a small Go binary.
- [ ] Draft internal support doc for Private onboarding team: how to use devkit in airgap installs.
- [ ] Decide on naming — local-devkit vs redwood-playground-cli

Notes to self / fragments
- Could include a "seed prompts" gallery for common product patterns (summarization, Q&A, chat).
- Think about a "record-and-replay" feature to capture request/response pairs to reproduce flakiness. Might be 2.0.
- If customers ask, provide an audited minimal runtime container for on-prem PoCs.

Next steps (this sprint)
- Quick spike: 2d to implement the mock backend + start command. Demo to DX and Solutions on Wed.
- Gather packaging recommendation from infra (ask @sam-ortiz).

Slack refs / bookmarks
- #dx-local-devkit (placeholder)
- PR proto branch: github.com/redwood-inference/local-devkit-proto

End of brainstorm (rough).

records.title: Customer Signal Orchestrator & Release Commit Protocol
records.text:
Customer Signal Orchestrator & Release Commit Protocol

description:
Goal: Build a disciplined, auditable orchestration layer that converts customer escalation signals (top-account SLA breaches, executive escalations, enterprise security requests) into prioritized roadmap commitments or emergency remedies with clear SLAs and release gating. Scope includes: 1) a triage scoring model for incoming signals, 2) a routing/owner assignment matrix by signal type and severity, 3) a Release Commit Protocol (RCP) to gate changes onto the public roadmap or emergency hotfix lanes, and 4) a lightweight dashboard for stakeholders to view signal status and commit decisions. Non-goals: not building a full-blown CRM integration in this phase (we will rely on webhook payloads and CSV ingest), not replacing existing exec escalation playbooks. Rationale: Recent incidents where premium accounts requested immediate behavior fixes highlighted lack of a repeatable "commit vs short-term workaround" decision flow. This project reduces ambiguity and improves SLA transparency for top accounts while keeping engineering work scoped and prioritized.

acceptance_criteria:
A triage scoring algorithm is implemented that ingests signal attributes (account_tier, severity, upstream_impact, reproducibility) and produces a consistent priority score
Routing matrix exists and is enforceable: signals auto-assign to an owner (PM/Eng/SE) based on rules and shows reassignment history
Release Commit Protocol (RCP) document published and surfaced in Console: includes criteria for roadmap commit vs hotfix, required sign-offs, and commit SLA windows
Stakeholder dashboard prototype is accessible and shows live signals with status, owner, score, and decision timestamp
2 documented playbook runs (one simulated and one live) where an escalated top-account request is either committed to a release or moved to a hotfix lane and all steps recorded

implementation_notes:
Use deterministic weighted scoring: attributes and weights configurable via Console feature flag
Persist signal history and decision audit trail for 12 months to support customer inquiries and account reviews
Expose an API endpoint for CS/AE to trigger 'escalation simulation' to validate whether a particular signal would meet RCP commit thresholds
Dashboard will be a read-only page in Console for initial MVP with export to CSV for exec reporting

risks_and_mitigation:
Risk: Over-committing to roadmap due to noisy signals -> Mitigation: conservative score thresholds and requirement for PM+Eng sign-off
Risk: Regulatory/legal escalation requires more review time -> Mitigation: surface regulatory flag early in triage and include Security/Legal in auto-assigned approval chain
Risk: Duplicate signals from multiple channels causing churn -> Mitigation: implement dedupe heuristics on account+signature and show merged history

decision_log:
2025-02-12: Decided to use a deterministic scoring model (weighted attributes) rather than ML in phase 1 to keep auditability and debuggability (decision by PM+Eng)
2025-02-18: Agreed RCP will require at minimum: PM sign-off + Eng owner + Legal or Security sign-off if customer data is involved (security required for PII/regulated accounts)
2025-02-25: Chose to implement webhook ingest with CSV fallback instead of building two-way CRM sync to accelerate MVP rollout

records.title: architecture
records.text:
architecture

anya: Quick RFC follow-up — connection-priority plumbing at the edge. Question: do we prefer an early-accept model (frontdoor returns/starts streaming immediately while backend token refresh/validation runs async) vs deferring accept until auth/refresh completes? Latency win vs wasted work / side-effect risk. Thoughts?

sam: Early-accept is tempting for p50 latency, but worried about billing + rate-limit accounting. If we stream data and the refresh fails later, how do we signal the client? Hard to reconcile with retries. :thinking:

ravi: Also side-effects. If a call triggers downstream writes and we later abort because token refresh failed, we risk partial commits. For read-only flows maybe ok, writes are scary.

lex: Can we do a hybrid? Allow early-accept only for routes marked idempotent/read-only. Add a short "soft admit" header that indicates the response is provisional until auth-confirmation arrives. If final auth fails, we close with a trailer indicating revert/abort.

anya: Draft idea: header `x-rw-frontdoor-admit: soft` (or `strict`). trailers: `x-rw-auth-final: ok|fail`. Frontdoor still needs to surface an abort trailer for clients that support trailers.
mike: Practically: many clients don't support trailers or will ignore midstream aborts. Early-accept + hedging may double-stream same work if we hedge to another backend — cost increases. Maybe limit early-accept to small responses or short TTL streams.

kat: Observability is critical. We should tag spans with `edge.auth.window` and emit metrics for "admit-then-revoke" counts so SLOs can reflect wasted tokens.
sam: Implementation note — our current edge runtime couples auth middleware with the stream multiplexer. We should decouple: an "admit" phase that performs syntactic checks and allocates stream slot, and an async "validate" phase that can close the stream with an auth trailer or let it continue. That reduces blocking in the main accept path.

lex: Example route policy sketch (very rough):
```json
{
  "route": "/v1/embeddings",
  "early_accept": "soft", // values: "off", "soft", "strict"
  "max_stream_size_bytes": 65536,
  "require_no_sideeffects": true
}
```

ravi: Strong +1 on the "require_no_sideeffects" flag. We also need a way for downstream services to declare idempotency semantics and for platform to maintain a whitelist of safe routes.

anya: Edge cases: 1) long-lived streams (minutes) — early-accept risks long wasted GPU time if validation fails midstream. 2) billing reconciliation — if we charge per-token, we might need a refund path for aborted streams. 3) retries/hedging interactions — duplicated work.
mike: For long streams we should default to `early_accept: off` unless route explicitly opt-in. For short responses or guidance endpoints we can be permissive.

kat: Observability + billing: include a "revoke_reason" tag on aborted streams and export it to billing pipeline so we can reconcile and possibly not bill customers for aborted tokens during experiments.
deploy-bot: deploy scheduled: branch=feature/edge-auth-split env=staging at=2026-03-24T08:00:00Z (experiment: early_accept=soft on /v1/generate-preview)

ravi: SG. I'll add the whitelist and a quick test harness to simulate token refresh failures and measure "wasted token" rate.

anya: Action items: 1) I will draft a short RFC PR with header/trailer semantics + route flag. 2) Run the staging experiment (thanks @deploy-bot) and measure p50/p95 and abort-rate. 3) Instrument traces/metrics and hook billing reconciliation. I'll post RFC by EOD tomorrow.

lex: :thumbsup: I'll add unit tests for idempotency and a mock client that verifies trailer handling.

mike: One last ask — add a kill-switch per-tenant so we can quickly disable early-accept if we see regressions.

anya: Good call. Adding tenant kill-switch to RFC checklist. Thanks everyone.

records.title: Runtime shard splitting with kernel-aware steering for latency-first QoS
records.text:
Runtime shard splitting with kernel-aware steering for latency-first QoS

description:
Background: Our prefill/decode pipeline currently groups work primarily by token-phase windows which optimizes throughput but can create long-tail latency for latency-sensitive traffic. Kernel selection today is chosen per-microbatch without explicit steering for latency-critical requests. We need a scheduling policy that prioritizes latency-sensitive requests while still maintaining reasonable throughput and kernel utilization across heterogeneous hardware and model variants.

Problem statement: Latency-first customer routes (web search, chat UI) are experiencing tail latency increases during mixed workloads because: (1) large decode-heavy prefill jobs monopolize kernels optimized for throughput, (2) attention-heavy long-context prefill phases increase memory pressure causing suboptimal kernel choices, and (3) our phase grouping lacks an escape hatch to split shards when headroom is low. We also want fairness between paying customers and internal workloads without regressing cost targets.

Proposal summary: Implement a "runtime shard splitting + kernel-aware steering" policy that: (a) tags incoming requests with QoS (latency-first | balanced | throughput) and attention-cost hints (estimated KV size, attention flops estimate), (b) opportunistically splits large phases into shards when predicted completion time would violate latency SLO for in-flight latency-first requests, and (c) steers shards to kernels optimized for the desired latency/throughput tradeoff. The policy uses a lightweight estimator to predict kernel execution time per shard and picks splitting points that minimize tail latency while preserving overall token throughput.

Design details: 
- Request tagging: extend the routing layer to propagate QoS and attention-cost metadata. QoS is set by API route or user config; attention-cost is estimated from input length and model profile.
- Shard heuristic: for prefill phases longer than X ms expected on the preferred kernel and with at least Y concurrent latency-first requests, split into N shards where N is proportional to the predicted tail contribution. Shard boundaries prefer contiguous token regions that preserve attention locality to keep KV reuse efficient.
- Kernel-aware steering: maintain microbenchmarks for each kernel variant (FP16/INT8 fused attention kernels, sparse-optimized kernels) per model and sequence length. Use these to compute per-shard expected latency and choose the kernel that hits the QoS target with minimal throughput loss. If the chosen kernel cannot be scheduled within the latency window, fall back to hedged execution across two kernels (hedge window configurable).
- Fairness: introduce a proportional capacity cap for latency-first routes so shards do not starve throughput-tier work. Use a simple weighted token budget allocator that charges shards heavier for latency-first tags during high contention.
- Metrics and probing: instrument per-shard scheduler events, chosen kernel, estimated vs observed latency, and KV reuse ratio. Add alerts for shard-split churn and kernel mispredictions.

Acceptance criteria: 
- Latency-first 95th percentile reduces by at least 20% in mixed-workload synthetic replay compared to baseline (same or better than canary).
- Overall token throughput drops by <5% in steady-state mixed workload.
- Kernel selection accuracy >85% (measured as chosen kernel finishing within 1.2x predicted latency).
- No increase in error rates or token corruption.
- Feature gated and rolloutable by route or org.

Risks and mitigations: 
- Kernel misprediction causing oscillation: mitigate with conservative backoff and smoothing of kernel performance signals.
- KV cache fragmentation: choose shard boundaries that preserve contiguous KV segments and run offline microbenchmarks to measure cache hit impacts.
- Increased scheduler complexity: keep the initial implementation as a policy layer that uses existing allocator primitives; avoid deep runtime changes on first pass.

Test plan: 
- Unit tests for QoS tagging and shard boundary selection heuristics.
- Microbenchmarks across kernels with representative model sizes and sequence lengths.
- Synthetic mixed-workload replay (latency-first + throughput-heavy) in staging with production-like traffic shapes.
- Gradual canary rollout by route with circuit-breaker that disables shard splitting on regressions.

Rollout plan: 
1) Feature flag gated implementation in runtime-1.20 behind a config flag per-deployment.
2) Staging integration tests + perf benchmarks.
3) Canary by org for small cohorts (5% traffic) with observability dashboard.
4) Expand to 25% then full rollout if metrics meet acceptance criteria.

Related artifacts: design doc (https://docs.internal.redwood.com/runtime/shard-splitting-design), perf dashboards (https://grafana.redwood.com/d/abcd123/shard-splitting-experiments), prototype PR (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2418).

acceptance_criteria:
95th percentile latency for latency-first routes reduced by >=20% in mixed-workload replay
Overall token throughput drops by <5% under steady-state mixed workload
Kernel selection accuracy >85% (chosen kernel finishes within 1.2x predicted latency)
No increase in error rates or token corruption
Feature configurable per-route and behind a feature flag

comments:
2025-01-24 - Connor Blake: Spiked estimator prototype that predicts kernel latency from seq_len and kernel microbenchmarks. Early results show 30% improvement in shard latency for short tails. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2394
2025-01-30 - Priya Nair: Design review with PM and infra. PM requests explicit budget charging example for fairness; added weighted token budget section. Action: Connor to prototype budget allocator.
2025-02-05 - Elena Vostok (SRE): Raised concern about shard churn and KV cache fragmentation. Suggested adding a minimum shard lifetime and boundary heuristics to preserve locality.
2025-02-14 - Miguel Torres (ML infra): Ran microbenchmarks for fused-int8 and sparse-attn kernels across T5-3B and LLaMA-7B configs; attached numbers to design doc. Fused-int8 favored for latency on short sequences.
2025-02-20 - Connor Blake: Implemented feature-flagged runtime gate and added metrics emission (scheduler.event=shard_split, kernel.choice). Canary scheduled for 2025-02-28 on staging cluster.
2025-02-28 - Priya Nair: Observability check after staging canary: Latency-first p95 improved 24% in staging replay; throughput loss ~3.2%. Proceeding to small production canary next week.

eng-infra

ashley: FYI — after the nodepool rolling upgrade this morning we're seeing short/no-metrics windows from the dcgm exporter on a subset of GPU nodes. ML jobs spike in latency during that window.

mike: yeah saw the alerts. prometheus reported scrape failures for ~30s then recovered. looks like exporter process is up but /metrics returns 503 while it warms its device caches.

sanjay: can you paste the failing log lines?

I0318 09:12:34 exporter.go:212] starting dcgm-exporter
E0318 09:12:35 http: panic serving 10.0.5.12:503: metrics handler: no devices ready
